# CORPUS HERMETICUM

Eight editions of Ficino's book appeared before 1500; and Mead enumerates twenty-two editions of it from 1471 to 1641.

Turnebus, 1554.—*The Poemander of Hermes Trismegistus, or concerning the divine power and wisdom. The definitions of Asclepius to King Ammon. . . . Paris, 1554: at the workshop of Adrian Turnebus, royal printer.* <note>original: "Mercurii Trismegisti Poemander, seu de potestate ac sapientia divina. Aesculapii definitiones ad Ammonem regem. . . . Parisiis, M.D.LIIII: apud Adr. Turnebum typographum regium."</note>

This is the <term>editio princeps</term> <note>The first printed edition of a book that previously existed only in manuscript form.</note> of the Greek text. It contains the whole *Corpus*, I–XIV under the title *The Poemander of Hermes Trismegistus*, and XVI–XVIII under the title *The definitions of Asclepius*. One manuscript only was used; and the printed text appears to be an exact reproduction of that manuscript, which must have been closely related to *Codex D.* At the end are given about fifty variant readings, which may have been got from the margin of the manuscript.

The text printed by Turnebus is preceded by a preface, in Greek, written by Vergicius. (This preface is reprinted in Parthey's *Poemander*.) Vergicius says that 'Hermes Trismegistus was an Egyptian by race; but who his father and his mother were, no one can say. He flourished before the time of Pharaoh, as many of the <term>chronographi</term> <note>Ancient chroniclers or historians who attempted to establish a timeline of world history.</note> think.<note>1</note> Some, among whom is Cicero, suppose that he is the person whom the Egyptians called Thoth. Some reckon him a contemporary of Pharaoh; but I differ from them, for the following reason. . . . He must, therefore, have lived before Pharaoh, and consequently, before Moses also.<note>2</note>

'They say that this Hermes left his own country, and travelled all over the world . . .; and that he tried to teach men to revere and worship one God alone, the <term>demiurgus</term> <note>The "craftsman" or creator of the physical world.</note> and <term>genetor</term> <note>The father or progenitor.</note> of all things; . . . and that he lived a very wise and pious life, occupied in intellectual contemplation <note>original: "ταῖς τοῦ νοῦ θεωρίαις" (tais tou nou theoriais)</note>, and giving no heed to the gross things of the material world <note>original: "τῶν κατωφερῶν τῆς ὕλης" (ton katopheron tes hyles)</note>; and that having returned to his own country, he wrote at that time many books of mystical philosophy and theology. Among these writings, there are two of special importance; the one<note>3</note> is called *Asclepius*, and the other,<note>4</note> *Poimandres*.'

If it is so, the hooded man may be meant to stand for Plato and the Platonists, including, perhaps, Italian scholars such as Ficino.

# INTRODUCTION

Vergicius <note>Angelos Vergikios (1505–1569), a Greek scholar and calligrapher who edited the first printed edition of the Greek text</note> lays stress on the resemblances between the teaching of the *Hermetic Corpus* <note>original: "Corpus Hermeticum"; a collection of Greek texts attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus</note> and that of Christianity; and he quotes from Suidas <note>A massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek historical encyclopaedia</note> what he calls ‘the greatest and most marvellous of all the sayings of Hermes’, in which that ancient Egyptian ‘expressly teaches the doctrine of the Holy Trinity’.¹ He adds that he has found many other sayings or writings of Hermes in Stobaeus <note>Joannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler of extracts from Greek authors</note>.

In Turnebus’s <note>Adrianus Turnebus (1512–1565), a French classical scholar</note> edition, three Hermetic excerpts from Stobaeus (viz. *Excerpt* II A, *Excerpt* I, and the Greek original of *Latin Asclepius* III. 27 e) are printed as an appendage to *Corpus* I–XIV, and included under the title *Poimandres* <note>The "Shepherd of Men," the first and most famous treatise in the collection</note>.

Flussas (François Foix de Candalle), 1574.—*The Pimandras of Hermes Trismegistus restored in both languages, by the industry of Lord François Flussas Candalla. . . . Bordeaux, . . . 1574.* <note>original: "Mercurii Trismegisti Pimandras utraque lingua restitutus..."</note>

Flussas used no manuscript. His text is based on that of Turnebus. He has made a good many alterations (some of his emendations were suggested or approved by ‘Joseph Scaliger, most illustrious youth’, and other scholars); but where his printed text differs from that of Turnebus, he has, with few exceptions, given the Turnebus-reading in his margin. Thus, if we substitute the marginal readings for those of the text, we have in this edition an almost exact reproduction of the manuscript from which Turnebus printed. The *Pimandras* of Flussas² is to this day, with the exception of the scarce *first edition* <note>original: "editio princeps"</note>, the only publication in which is to be found a trustworthy printed text of those parts of the *Corpus* which have not been edited by Reitzenstein <note>Richard Reitzenstein (1861–1931), a German philologist</note>—i. e. of *Corpus* II–XII and XIV.

Flussas gives to *Corpus* I–XIV the title *Trismegisti Pimandras*, and calls the several *small books* <note>original: "libelli"</note> ‘Chapter I’, ‘Chapter II’, &c. After XIV he appends, and includes under the title *Pimandras*, a ‘Chapter XV’, which is made up of the same three Stobaeus-excerpts which had been inserted by Turnebus, with the addition of the extract from Suidas which Vergicius had quoted in his preface to the *first edition*. After this stands ‘Chapter XVI’ (our *Book* XVI), under the title *Asclepius to Ammon*. But Flussas tacitly omits the surviving fragment of *Book* XVII, doubtless because he saw that it has nothing to do with *Book* XVI, to which, in the manuscripts and the *first edition*, it is joined on as a part of the same document.

---

¹ See Suidas, *Testimonies.*
² The latest reprint of the *Pimandras* of Flussas is that which is included in the Cologne edition (1630) of Rossel’s commentary. (See below.)

He also omits *Libellus XVIII* <note>Book 18 of the Hermetic corpus</note>, probably because he saw that it could not rightly be ascribed to Asclepius <note>A legendary student of Hermes Trismegistus</note>.

In his dedicatory letter, addressed to the Emperor Maximilian II,¹ Flussas <note>François Foix de Candalle, a 16th-century French bishop and mathematician</note> says that Hermes attained to a knowledge of divine things surpassing that which was revealed to the Hebrew prophets, and equalling that of the Apostles and Evangelists. ‘Truly this man (Trismegistus) alone among those who were divinely inspired, reveals many things concerning the essence of Almighty God through very skillful discourse—the making of the world, the fashioning of man after the image and likeness of God, and moreover the fall of the same into such great misery, and finally the remedy for this fall into a greater happiness: everywhere he teaches that God is incorporeal and to be sought outside of matter. But if these things be small, and in no way surpassing the ancient messengers of the Divine will, there are many more things which were passed over in silence by Moses, the prophets, and any others preceding the revelation of Christ, which were revealed to this thrice-great Mercury. Such things as: the discourse concerning the supreme Trinity in one God;² moreover, the Divine Word as the Son of the Father;³ and that the Spirit, the God of fire and spirit, brought forth from the Father and the Word, was the worker of all things;⁴ and that the one Word was the active power <note>original: ἐνέργειαν (energeian)</note> of men who are to be reborn by Divine will;⁵ and that salvation depends solely on this effect of being reborn.⁶ Likewise, he reveals the most holy Baptism by means of a Mixing-Bowl filled with the Spirit.⁷ He promises a return to their duties for bodies that have performed their service.⁸ Finally, he commands that prayers brought forth to Almighty God be offered through the Word.’⁹ <note>original Latin: "Nimirum hic (Trismegistus) unus inter eos... per Verbum offerri iubet."</note> ‘What more’, asks Flussas, ‘is made known to us by those who were instructed by our Saviour himself? And yet this man was anterior in time, not only to the disciples of our Lord, but also to all the prophets and teachers of our Law, and, as the Ancients say, to Moses himself.’ He must then, Flussas thinks, have been inspired by God, and more fully inspired than any of the Hebrew Prophets.

# INTRODUCTION

As to the Latin *Asclepius*, Flussas <note>François Foix de Candale (1512–1594), a French bishop and mathematician who edited the Hermetica.</note> thinks it probable that Apuleius, who is known to have been a very wicked man, inserted idolatrous and impious passages² into his translation of the Greek text of Hermes, and then suppressed the Greek original, in order that his fraud might escape detection. Since the *Asclepius* has been thus polluted, Flussas decides not to include it in his edition.

He discusses the date of Trismegistus at some length, and gives reasons for thinking that he flourished about the time of Abraham.

Hannibal Rossel, *The Pymander of Hermes Trismegistus*, Cracow, 1585–1590. This is a ponderous commentary, in six volumes, on selected passages of *Corpus Hermeticum* I–VII and the Latin *Asclepius*. The passages taken from the *Corpus* are given in Latin only, and not in Greek. I have merely glanced into Rossel's commentary; but I gather from what others say about it that nothing could possibly be gained by reading it. He appears to use the sayings of Hermes merely as pegs on which to hang his own disquisitions on things in general.³

A later edition of Rossel's commentary, with a reprint of Flussas's *Pimandras* prefixed to it, was printed in Cologne in 1630.

# THE HERMETIC CORPUS

*The small books of Trismegistus, and the fragments, as many as are found, arranged in scientific order; | Three small books of the disciple Asclepius; | The mystical philosophy of the Egyptians, dictated by Plato, received and written out by Aristotle; | A scientific order of the Platonic dialogues, discovered entirely anew by Francesco Patrizzi; | Finally, many chapters in which Plato is shown to be in agreement with, but Aristotle an adversary to, the Catholic faith. | Venice, . . . 1593.*¹

Patrizzi seems to have been impelled by a genuine enthusiasm to take upon himself the task of bringing about a restoration of true religion; and he regarded the *Hermetica* <note>The body of writings attributed to the legendary Egyptian sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note> as one of the most effective instruments that could be used in the execution of this design. In his preface, addressed to Pope Gregory XIV, he says: 'In this volume I present to you five philosophies, namely (1) *our own recently established system*,² (2) *the Chaldaean philosophy of Zoroaster*,³ (3) *the Egyptian philosophy of Hermes Trismegistus*,⁴ (4) *another mystical Egyptian philosophy*,⁵ and (5) *another of Plato's pro-*

Sir John Radcliffe . . . this wonderful treasure of divine wisdom is given, dedicated, and consecrated as a mark of a grateful mind.* <note>original: "L.M.D.C.Q." stands for Libens Merito Dicat Consecratque.</note> In this republication Patrizzi's own system of philosophy is omitted; the *Hermetica* are placed at the beginning of the volume, as being first in importance, and two of Patrizzi's other additions are appended to them. But the second (Corpus XVIII. 1-10), although the third seems to depend upon it, might be considered a forgery.*'

⁵ The work reprinted by Patrizzi under the title *Mystical Egyptian . . . philosophy* is a Latin version of a treatise entitled 'The Theology of Aristotle', which had been translated from Greek into Arabic about A. D. 840, and was well known and highly esteemed among the Arabs, who supposed it to be a genuine work of Aristotle. The bulk of it is a paraphrase of portions of Plotinus, *Enneads IV-VI*; but in the introductory chapter Aristotle is made to speak in his own person, and refers to 'my earlier book, the Metaphysics'. Ueberweg (*History of Philosophy*, English translation 1880, i, p. 425) says that it 'was known in a Latin translation to the Scholastics'. Soon after 1500 Francesco Roseo found an Arabic manuscript.

# INTRODUCTION

*Plato's exoteric teaching.*¹ <note>original: "priam." - likely a transcription error for "prim." or "primam," referring to the first type of philosophy mentioned previously.</note> ... In our day, men laugh at philosophers; and it is commonly said "So-and-so is a philosopher, he does not believe in God". The reason of this is, that the only philosophy studied is that of Aristotle, which, as men know and are told, denies the omnipotence and providence of God. Yet Hermes said *that without philosophy it is impossible to be perfectly pious.*² <note>original: "sine philosophia impossibile esse summe esse pium."</note> Reflecting on this saying, I thought that it might be possible to discover a truer philosophy, by which we might return to God who made us. I threw myself into the search for it; ... and after much toil and resolute effort, I think I have brought it to completion.

'I have appended to my own philosophy the other four (i. e. those numbered (2), (3), (4), and (5) above); for all these alike *have as their proposed end that they should teach that God is the founder, ruler, caretaker, and provider of all things, and that men should know both Him and themselves, and learn by what means human souls may return to God the creator, and enjoy eternal blessedness with Him.* <note>original: "propositum sibi finem habent, ut doceant Deum rerum esse conditorem, rectorem, curatorem ac provisorem, et ut homines tum illum, tum seipsos cognoscant, et addiscant, quibus modis ad creatorem Deum animae humanae redeant, aeternaque apud eum beatitudine fruantur".</note>

of it at Damascus, and got Moses Rouas to translate the Arabic text into Italian; the Italian of Rouas was translated into Latin by Petrus Nicolaus ex Castellaniis; and the Latin version thus produced was printed at Rome in 1519, under the patronage of Pope Leo X, with the title *The Theology or Mystic Philosophy of the Most Wise Aristotle the Stagirite, Recently Rediscovered According to the Egyptians and Most Correctly Rendered into Latin.* <note>original: "Sapientissimi Aristotelis Stagiritae Theologia sive mistica Philosophia Secundum Aegyptios noviter Reperta et in Latinum Castigatissime redacta."</note> A revised edition of it, in more polished Latin, was published by Carpentarius at Paris in 1572; but Patrizzi preferred to reproduce the edition of 1519, as more faithfully representing the original. Fr. Dieterici has published the Arabic text (*The so-called Theology of Aristotle*, 1882), and a German translation of it (1883). Dieterici says that the Latin version of 1519 (i. e. that which Patrizzi reprinted), 'judged from the present standpoint of Arabic philology, is worthless'.

Patrizzi saw that the doctrine of this treatise is what is commonly called Neoplatonic; yet he contrived to retain his belief that it had been written by Aristotle. His theory about it is as follows. Plato studied for thirteen years under the Egyptian priests at Heliopolis (Strabo 806), and was permitted by them to read the writings of Hermes Trismegistus. After his return to Athens, Plato taught two distinct philosophies—an 'exoteric' <term>exoteric: intended for or likely to be understood by the general public</term> philosophy, which is given in his written Dialogues, and an 'esoteric' <term>esoteric: intended for or likely to be understood by only a small number of people with a specialized knowledge</term> philosophy, based on the ancient wisdom of Egypt, which he imparted orally to his pupil Aristotle. The latter wrote down day by day the secret teaching which he received from the lips of Plato; and the *Mystic philosophy* consists of the notes which he thus wrote down. Afterwards, Aristotle quarrelled with Plato and his followers, and started a school of his own in opposition to them; and the books commonly known as Aristotle's writings are those which he wrote during that period of his life. But in his old age he returned to the true Platonic faith. The book in which this 'mystic philosophy' was written down by Aristotle was lost, Patrizzi thinks, immediately after his death, but was found again in the time of Ammonius Saccas, the teacher of Plotinus; and the Neoplatonists borrowed from it.

Why are those parts alone of Aristotle’s philosophy studied which are hostile to God and his Church, while these *pious helpers* <note>original: "piae adiutrices"</note> are disregarded? Assuredly the treatise of Hermes *on piety and philosophy*¹ contains more philosophy than all the works of Aristotle taken together. . . . “Poemander (i. e. *Corpus Hermeticum* I) embraces the creation of the world and of man, almost identical to the Mosaic account. And he explains the mystery of the Trinity far more clearly than Moses himself. Many of the small books found in Hermes are most full of both true piety and true philosophy; these both can and should be substituted for the impious works of Aristotle.”

‘Many of Plato’s dialogues also may be publicly taught “without any danger of impiety, and with much aid to piety” <note>original: "sine impietatis periculo ullo, pietatis adiumento multo"</note>; especially the Philebus, Timaeus, Sophista, Parmenides, and Phaedo. “All the books of Plotinus contain a certain sacred theology rather than philosophy.” (He mentions with approval Proclus and Damascius also.)

‘Almost all the early Fathers, “because they knew that with a few changes the Platonists could easily become Christians, . . . preferred Plato and these followers of his to all other philosophers, and mentioned Aristotle only with infamy. But about four hundred years ago² the Scholastic Theologians strove for the opposite, and used Aristotelian impieties as the foundations for the faith. ‘I would have you then, Holy Father, and all future Popes, give orders that some of the books which I have named³ shall be continually taught everywhere, as I have taught them for the last fourteen years at Ferrara. You will thus make all able men in Italy, Spain, and France friendly to the Church; and perhaps even the German protestants will follow their example, and return to the Catholic faith. It is much easier to win them back in this way than to compel them by ecclesiastical censures or by secular arms. You should cause this doctrine to be taught in the schools of the Jesuits, who are doing such good work. If you do this, great glory will await you among men of future times. And I beg you to accept me as your helper in this undertaking.’

# INTRODUCTION

In an introduction to that part of his book which contains the *Hermetica* <note>The collection of writings attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus</note>, Patrizzi says, ‘It appears that this Hermes Trismegistus was indeed a contemporary of Moses, but a little older. . . Moreover, there will appear from these small books and fragments of Hermes a certain pious philosophy toward God, for the most part in harmony with the dogmas of the faith. It will also appear that all the Greek philosophies—the Pythagorean and Platonic in divine and moral dogmas,¹ the Aristotelian and Stoic in physics, and even the first principles of medicine—were taken both from these and from his other books which have perished.’ <note>original Latin: "Videtur Hermes hic Trismegistus coetaneus quidem fuisse Mosy... fuisse desumptas." Patrizi was arguing that Greek philosophy actually originated from Egyptian Hermetic wisdom.</note>

‘For which reason (it will appear) that it would be far better and much more advisable and useful for Christian men if the dogmas of Hermes, rather than those of Aristotle—which everywhere abound in great impiety—were sometimes read in public schools and in the monasteries of monks who are too much devoted to Aristotle. So that this might be done more conveniently, we have rearranged the small books into an order according to the sequence and series of their subject matter, as we have said.’ <note>original Latin: "Quamobrem (apparebit) longe satius... in ordinem redegimus." Patrizi was part of a Renaissance movement seeking to replace Aristotelian scholasticism with a "pious" Platonic-Hermetic philosophy.</note>

He has rearranged the *Hermetica*, and placed them in the following order: Stobaeus <note>Johannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler of extracts from Greek authors</note> I. 41. 1 (which I have divided into the two distinct excerpts *II B* and *XI*): *Corpus* I, III, X, V, VI, XIII, VII, II, XI, XII, IV: *The Virgin of the World* <note>original Greek: "Kore Kosmu"</note>, followed by eight other Stobaeus-excerpts: *Corpus* IX: six Stobaeus-excerpts: *Corpus* VIII: *Corpus* XIV: fragments from Cyril, Stobaeus, etc.: the Latin *Asclepius*. Then follows, as a separate work by a different author, the *Definitions of Asclepius to Ammon* <note>original Greek: "ὅροι Ἀσκληπιοῦ πρὸς Ἄμμονα"</note> (i. e. *Corpus* XVI–XVIII). In regarding the several documents contained in the *Corpus* as unconnected *small books* <note>term: libelli (Latin for "little books" or pamphlets)</note>, Patrizzi made a decided advance beyond the position of the earlier editors; but there is not much to be said for the order in which he thought fit to arrange the Hermetic writings.

What were the sources from which Patrizzi got his text of the *small books* of the *Corpus*? He certainly used the printed editions of Turnebus and Flussas. But Reitzenstein <note>Richard Reitzenstein (1861–1931), a prominent German scholar of ancient religions</note> has found reason to think that Patrizzi based his text on a manuscript <note>term: MS. (abbreviation for manuscript)</note> other than that used by Turnebus, and that he merely introduced here and there the readings of the earlier editors. The question is, however, of little importance; for as Patrizzi has made many arbitrary alterations in the text, and does not tell us whether the reading which he adopts is derived from some authority or is of his own invention, his edition furnishes no material that can be used as an aid to textual criticism.²

# CORPUS HERMETICUM

Casaubon, 1614.—*Sixteen Essays by Isaac Casaubon... On the Prolegomena of Cardinal Baronius to the Annals... London... 1614.* In *Essay* I. 10, pages 70 and following, Casaubon discusses the date and origin of the *Sibylline Oracles* and the *Hermetic writings*; and in this short treatise we find for the first time a view of the Hermetic writings which is, in the main at least, historically sound. As compared with all who had previously written on the subject, from Lactantius to Patrizzi, Casaubon <note>original: "οἷος πέπνυται, τοὶ δὲ σκιαὶ ἀΐσσουσιν"</note> **is the only one who possesses wisdom, while the rest flit about like shadows.** <note>A Homeric reference to the ghost of Tiresias in the underworld.</note> He does not deny that there may have been a man named Hermes Trismegistus who lived before Moses; but he sees that the *Hermetica* cannot have been written by any such person. He says, ‘The book... which began to be circulated several centuries ago under the name of Mercury Trismegistus (i.e. the Corpus Hermeticum) we do not hesitate to pronounce, and confirm with every assurance, to be <term>pseudepigraphal</term> <note>original: "ψευδεπίγραφον"; a work falsely attributed to a past author</note>’: and he concludes that it was written about the end of the first century after Christ.<note>1</note> ‘Now let us prove by certain arguments... that the book which even today is a favorite among many scholars and held in great value as if it were truly by Mercury Trismegistus, is <term>pseudepigraphal</term> and a mere <term>fabrication</term> <note>original: "πλάσμα"</note>. . . . We therefore... affirm that in that book is contained not the Egyptian doctrine of Mercury, but partly Greek doctrine taken from the books of Plato and the Platonists, and indeed very often in their own words: and partly Christian doctrine<note>2</note> sought from the sacred books.

‘What kind of philosophy was once in use among the ancient Egyptians can be understood from the books of Eusebius... and other ancient writers. But the method of philosophizing of this Pseudo-Mercury is of an entirely different kind:<note>3</note> for both the matters and the words savor of the school of Plato, those things only excepted which he mixes in from the divine books. Lest we seem to rashly contradict the opinion of so many scholars, let us demonstrate in a few words what we are saying.’ (Here he goes into details, and discusses particular passages in the *Corpus*.)

‘Then, moreover, if this book were truly by Mercury, it would be necessary that either he himself wrote it in Greek, or someone translated it from the Egyptian language. We most firmly deny that either of these things happened: the former, because the style of this book is most foreign to that language in which—

> **2** He ought rather to have said *Jewish*. (See *Corpus* I and III.)
> **3** More is now known about the modes of thought of the ancient Egyptians; but Casaubon’s opinion on this point is confirmed by the results of modern Egyptology. Traces of the influence of indigenous Egyptian thought, if not entirely absent, are rare in the *Hermetica*.

# INTRODUCTION

The Greeks contemporary with Hermes used. . . . Here (i.e. in the *Hermetica*) there is absolutely no trace of antiquity: . . . on the contrary, there are many words here which even the older form of Greek <note>original: "Hellenismus"</note> would not recognize—that which flourished around the birth of the Lord. . . . Who among the earlier writers ever said "materiality" <note>original: ὑλότης (hylotes)</note>, "essentiality" <note>original: οὐσιότης (ousiotes)</note>, and other things of that kind?

"I also deny that these works were translated from another language: I maintain that they are original <note>original: αὐτοφυῆ (autophye)</note> and were first written in Greek. No version was ever so successfully crafted that it did not betray its foreign origin and demonstrate it by certain signs. Here there is nothing of the sort. Everything is genuinely Greek, and in the Greek style of the age I have designated, its own character is consistent throughout . . . .

"It is therefore false, indeed most false, what that impostor <note>original: "planus"</note> in the *Letter to Ammon* (*Corpus* XVI) wants to persuade us; that these things were first written by Mercury in the Egyptian language. It is also most false, what the learned and unlearned alike seem to have believed until now; either that these were written by Hermes Trismegistus, the most ancient sage of Egypt, or were translated from his writings. We have proved both of these to be by far the most absurd."

In one important matter, however, Casaubon's view requires correction. He thinks, as his predecessors thought, that the *Corpus* contains distinctively Christian doctrines; and he thence infers that the *Hermetica* were, like the *Sibylline Oracles* <note>A collection of oracular utterances written in Greek hexameters ascribed to the Sibyls, often used by early Christians to find prophecies of Christ in paganism.</note>, forged by a Christian ('or rather', he adds, 'a semi-Christian'), with the object of recommending the doctrines of his religion to his Pagan neighbours by making it appear that they were vouched for by the authority of an ancient and venerated name.<note>1</note> This is true of some of the *Sibylline Oracles*; but it is not true of the *Hermetica*. The authors of the small books <note>original: "libelli"</note> collected in the *Corpus* were Pagans; and apart from a few interpolated words, the resemblances to Christian doctrine which we find in the Hermetic writings are to be accounted for, not by assuming that the writers borrowed from the New Testament or from other Christian sources, but by recognizing the fact that, at the time when the *Hermetica* were written, there were many matters on which Christians and Pagan Platonists thought and spoke alike. We must, therefore, substitute 'a number of Pagan writers' for the 'Christian or semi-Christian' author of whom Casaubon speaks. With this

Casaubon’s opinion as to the period in which the *Hermetica* <note>The collection of philosophical and religious texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> were written gradually prevailed, and came to be adopted by all competent scholars;¹ and, deprived of the prestige which their supposed antiquity had conferred on them, the Hermetic writings lost their hold on men’s interest, and sank into comparative neglect.² Translations of the *Collection* <note>original: "Corpus"</note> continued to appear from time to time;³ but from 1630 to 1854, no reprint of the Greek text was issued.

Des Mousseaux, *Magic in the Nineteenth Century* <note>original: "La magie au dix-neuvième siècle"</note>, 1860, p. 343, speaking of the passages about ‘making gods’ in *The Latin Asclepius, Book III* <note>original: "Ascl. His book is ably written, and contains much interesting matter.

The time of the Deluge is the earliest time to which I have found the Hermetic teaching assigned in Europe. But Arabic writers dated it still earlier; for they identified Hermes with Enoch, and his teacher the Good Spirit <note>original: "Agathos Daimon"</note> with Seth, son of Adam.

Ménard, 1866.—*Hermes Trismegistus. Complete translation, preceded by a study on the origin of the Hermetic books. By Louis Ménard. . . . Paris, . . . 1866.* The *Translation* is a free translation of *Corpus* I–XIV, the Latin *Asclepius*, twenty-six Stobaeus-excerpts, some fragments from Cyril, etc., and *Corpus* XVI–XVIII. Ménard does not stick closely to the (often meaningless) words of the traditional text, but expresses in fluent French what he rightly or wrongly takes to have been the author's meaning. His introductory *Study* (111 pages) is a sensible and well-written treatise on the Hermetica. For those who wish to make acquaintance with the Hermetists, but do not read Greek and Latin, Ménard's book is, I think, to be recommended in preference to any other work on the subject that has yet been published.

Reitzenstein, 1904.—*Poimandres. Studies in Greek-Egyptian and early Christian literature. By R. Reitzenstein. Leipzig, . . . 1904.* <note>original: "Studien zur griechisch-aegyptischen und früh-christlichen literatur"</note> As an appendix to the book is printed Reitzenstein's critical edition of *Corpus* I, XIII, and XVI-XVIII.

The publication of Reitzenstein's *Poimandres* <note>The "Shepherd of Men," the first and most famous treatise in the Corpus Hermeticum.</note> marks the beginning of a fresh stage in the study of the Hermetic writings. Working as a pioneer in what was, for modern scholarship, almost a new and untouched field, he has made some serious mistakes; but he has put the study of the *Hermetica* on a scientific footing, and all later work on this subject must be based on his investigations.

Reitzenstein has also discussed some passages of the *Corpus* in *The Hellenistic Mystery-Religions, their Basic Ideas and Effects, 1910.* <note>original: "Die hellenistischen Mysterienreligionen, ihre Grundgedanken und Wirkungen"</note>

Among recent publications may be mentioned *Thrice-Greatest Hermes. Studies in Hellenistic Theosophy and Gnosis <term>Gnosis: a Greek word for "knowledge," specifically spiritual or mystical insight into the nature of reality</term>. Being a Translation of the Extant Sermons and Fragments of the Trismegistic Literature, with Prolegomena <note>Introductory remarks</note>, Commentaries, and Notes. By G. R. S. Mead. London and Benares. The Theosophical Publishing Society, 1906* (three volumes). Mr. Mead's point of view is indicated by these words in his preface: 'Along this ray of the Trismegistic tradition we may allow ourselves to be drawn backwards in time towards the holy of holies of the Wisdom of Ancient Egypt. The sympathetic study of this material may well prove an initiatory process towards an understanding of that Archaic Gnosis.'

A strange and quite untenable theory as to the dates of the *Hermetica* has been put forward by Dr. Flinders Petrie, in a paper printed in the *Transactions of the Third International Congress of the History of Religions, 1908*, pp. 196 and 224. He puts the date of the *Virgin of the World* <note>original: "Kore Kosmu"</note> (which he calls 'the earliest Hermetic document') at 'about 510 B. C., or certainly before 410 B. C.'; that of *Corpus* XVI at 'about 350 B. C.'; and that of the original of the Latin *Asclepius* at 'about 340 B. C.'. And he says that 'if the longest Hermetic writings thus belong to the Persian age' (i. e. to a time before 332 B. C.), 'it is probable that the whole group are not far removed from that period'. In a book entitled *Personal Religion in Egypt before Christianity, 1909* (ch. 3, 'The dateable Hermetic writings'),

He thinks (*ibid.*, pp. 85–91) that *Corpus Hermeticum* II, III, V, VI, VII, VIII, and X, were probably written before the time of Alexander, and between 450 and 350 <term>B.C.</term> <note>Before Common Era</note>; that *Corpus Hermeticum* XII ‘must’ be earlier than 332 <term>B.C.</term>; that *Corpus Hermeticum* IV ‘belongs to about 300 <term>B.C.</term>’; that *Corpus Hermeticum* XIII ‘seems to be of the same date or rather later’; and that the date of *Corpus Hermeticum* I, which ‘seems to be the last of the longer writings of this class’, may very well be about 300–200 <term>B.C.</term> ‘The Hermetic books as a whole’, he says (p. 102), ‘seem to hang together, and to belong to one general period, 500–200 <term>B.C.</term>’ If these dates were proved to be right, there would necessarily result from them an astounding *overturning* <note>original: "bouleversement"</note> of all commonly accepted views as to the history of Greek thought. But the arguments by which he endeavours to support his datings are not such as to be worth serious attention.¹

Josef Kroll, *The Teachings of Hermes Trismegistus* <note>original: "Die Lehren des Hermes Trismegistos"</note>, Münster in Westphalia, 1914. In this book Kroll's aim is ‘to trace in detail the connexion of the Hermetic doctrines with Greek or Hellenistic doctrines in general, and to assign to the several notions (which present themselves in the *Hermetica*) their place in the history of religious and philosophic thought’. For that purpose, he arranges the teachings of the *Hermetica* under a series of subject-headings; and in dealing with each subject, he brings together what is said about it in the several Hermetic *short books* <term>libelli</term>, and quotes or refers to parallels in other writings. He concludes (pp. 386–9) that in the main the doctrines of the *Hermetica* belong to ‘the sphere of Hellenistic thought—the general philosophy of the culture-world of that time’, and that among the sources from which the Hermetists drew, special importance is to be assigned to Posidonius; that their thoughts have been little, if at all, affected by Egyptian influence; that their doctrines are in many respects similar to those of Philo, and that here and there are to be found in them distinctively Jewish notions; and that there is in the *Hermetica* ‘no trace of any influence of Christianity’.²

# CORPUS HERMETICUM

As to the dating of the Hermetic writings, Kroll says (p. 389) that, for most of them, any date after the time of Philo <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who blended Greek philosophy with biblical tradition.</note> is possible, but that there are some pieces, one of which is *Corpus* I, that cannot have been written before the time of Numenius (A. D. 150-200) <note>Numenius of Apamea, a philosopher who influenced Neoplatonism.</note>. He adds, ‘the dating in detail (of the several *small books* <note>original: "libelli"</note>) must be carried out by some one who undertakes the attractive but difficult task of distinguishing the different strata of the doctrines, and considering each of the different tractates in itself, and their relations to one another’.

That is precisely what I have aimed at doing in the present edition. There was no one Hermetic school or sect, and no one body of Hermetic doctrine. What we have before us is a number of *small books* <note>original: "libelli"</note>, written by a number of different men, each of whom had his distinct and separate point of view and mode of thought. There is in their teachings a certain general similarity, but there is also much divergence; and it is, for most purposes, more profitable to take the Hermetic *small books* <note>original: "libelli"</note> one by one, and investigate the doctrine of each of them separately, than to lump them all together.

C. F. G. Heinrici, *The Hermes-Mysticism and the New Testament* <note>original: "Die Hermes-Mystik und das Neue Testament"</note>, edited by E. von Dobschütz, Leipzig, 1918. Heinrici died leaving the book unfinished, and von Dobschütz published Heinrici’s manuscript almost unaltered, merely adding some pages of *supplements* <note>original: "Nachträge"</note> written by himself.

The purpose of this book is to determine the relation between the teachings of the *Hermetica* <note>The collection of Greek and Latin texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> and those of primitive Christianity as presented in the New Testament. With that purpose in view, Heinrici, in Part II, examines the Hermetic documents one by one (in that respect his method is preferable to that of J. Kroll), and in each of them looks for similarities in word or thought to things said in the New Testament. In Part III, he arranges the teachings of the *Hermetica* in general under a series of subject-headings, and under each heading compares the teachings of the New Testament on the same subject. His conclusions may be summed up by saying that he finds in the *Hermetica* many passages that are parallels to passages in the New Testament, but little that is *borrowed* from the New Testament.¹

He does not undertake to examine the relations between the *Hermetica* and Greek philosophic writings; his book is intended

# INTRODUCTION

to be a complement to that of J. Kroll, in which that subject was dealt with.

Heinrici's book contains some useful suggestions; but it does not throw much fresh light on the Hermetic writings. I have found in it mistakes on particular points,¹ some of which are of considerable importance. And taking the book as a whole, Heinrici does not seem to understand rightly the main drift of the Hermetic teaching, and the relations in which it stands to other religious and philosophic movements of the time. The term ‘Hermes-Mysticism’ <note>original: "Hermes-Mystik"</note>, employed by him in the title and throughout the book, is ambiguous. Of ‘mysticism’ in the sense of aspiration towards union with God, there is much in our *Hermetica*; but of the sacramentalism of the Pagan mystery-cults, and of *ritual magic* <term>theurgia: the practice of rituals intended to invoke the presence of gods or achieve union with them</term> in general, there is hardly anything; and Heinrici, though he here and there shows some recognition of this fact, is too much inclined to bring the philosophic *Hermetica* into connexion with mystery-cults and magical practices which he includes under the vague term *Mysticism*, but with which they have in reality little or nothing in common.² He begins by contrasting *Mysticism* (which he defines as ‘revelation-literature’) with philosophy, and coupling together the names Orpheus and Hermes as representative of this *Mysticism*. It would be truer to say that the name Hermes (as far as the *short books* <note>original: "libelli"</note> of the *Hermetic Corpus* <note>original: "Corpus Hermeticum"</note> and the other documents of the same class are concerned) stands for philosophy, or for a religion based on philosophy, and that of Orpheus (the reputed founder of the mystery-cults, and supposed author of the *Orphic poems* <note>original: "Orphica"</note> revered by the later Neoplatonists) stands for *ritual magic* as opposed to philosophy. He refers to Plato now and again; but he does not adequately recognize the fact that the doctrines of these *Hermetica* are, in the main, derived from Platonism, and that all the other ingredients together are of comparatively small amount.

# THE LATIN ASCLEPIUS

THE *Asclepius* has come down to us in the form of a Latin dialogue attributed to Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius (c. 124 – c. 170 AD), a Platonist philosopher and author of 'The Golden Ass'.</note>. This Latin dialogue is a translation of a Greek original, which was known to Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD) who often quoted Hermetic texts to support Christian doctrine.</note> and others, but is now lost.

The manuscript tradition of the Latin text has been thoroughly investigated by P. Thomas; and the results of his researches are incorporated in the text which he has published in his edition of the philosophic writings of Apuleius (*The surviving works of Apuleius volume III, Books on philosophy, edited by P. Thomas, Teubner, Leipzig 1908*). Thomas's edition supersedes all earlier publications of the text; and I have used it as my sole authority for the readings of the manuscripts.

Thomas classifies the more important manuscripts in two groups, as follows:

->I. *Manuscripts of the better sort*:<-

(1) B = Brussels 10054-10056; written early in the eleventh century. Collated <term>Collated: The process of comparing different manuscript copies of the same text to identify variations and errors.</term> by Thomas. This manuscript is very decidedly superior to all the rest. The hands of several correctors can be distinguished. One of these, B 2, who made his corrections at or near the end of the eleventh century, seems to have been a well-instructed man. In a few instances he alone gives what is certainly or probably the true reading; but Thomas concludes that his emendations are merely conjectural. The other correctors of B contribute nothing of value.

(2) M = Munich 621; twelfth century. Collated by Goldbacher for his edition of Apuleius, 1876, and again by Thomas.

(3) V = Vatican 3385; twelfth century. The text of the *Asclepius* contained in this manuscript has not yet been collated. But as V very closely resembles M (being, in Goldbacher's opinion, a more carelessly written copy of the same original from which M was copied), it is not likely that its collation will add largely to the material at our disposal for textual restoration. M and V are closely

Besides these two groups, Thomas mentions a manuscript in the British Museum (Add. 11983, twelfth century), which he has found to be of very little value; and a large number of 'interpolated manuscripts', which he has deliberately disregarded.

Thomas has reconstructed the text of the archetype <note>term: Archetype — the lost original manuscript from which all surviving copies are descended</note> from which our manuscripts are derived. But that is only the first stage on the road to the discovery of the Hermetic teacher's meaning. The text of the archetype itself was corrupt; and even if we could restore the Latin to the exact form in which it came from the hand of its first writer, we should still be far from the completion of our task. We have to do with a Latin translation of a Greek document. The Greek text was probably already damaged when it came into the translator's hands; the translator was very imperfectly qualified for his work, and it is certain that he has frequently blundered. Our first business is to work back to the Latin text as the translator wrote it; but having done this, we have still to guess what was the Greek which the translator had before him, and thence to infer the meaning which the writer of the lost original intended to convey. Thomas has brought together the results of the previous work of other scholars in the emendation <note>term: Emendation — the process of correcting errors in a text by logical deduction</note> of the text, and has added much of his own that is of high value; but he has still left much to be done. Not only have both the Greek original and the Latin translation been damaged by errors of transcription; but it is evident that either the original or the translation has been mutilated in a quite exceptional way. Some passages have been lost, some have been misplaced, and many words, phrases, and sentences have been transposed from a context in which they made sense to a context in which they make nonsense. If the Latin text had once

The ordinary causes of corruption <note>Common errors made by scribes, such as misreading letters or skipping lines.</note> do not suffice to explain its condition. The facts might perhaps be accounted for by assuming that the translator never wrote out a fair copy of his work, but left it full of erasures and corrections, with words and phrases, representing his second thoughts, scribbled in wherever he could find room for them; and that this confused mass of words was afterwards copied out by some one who mechanically wrote down what he saw before him, without regard for the meaning.

The text which results from my attempts to restore the original order of the words is still very faulty, and I hope that it will be further emended by others; but in spite of the many problems which remain unsolved, I think that it is near enough to the original to enable us to recover the thoughts of the writer (or writers) of the Greek treatise in the main, though not in every detail.

In order that the reader may have before him the continuous text in the traditional arrangement, each word, phrase, or passage which I have transposed (with the exception of a few of the longest of these passages) is printed between doubled rectangular brackets [[ ]] at the place where it stands in the manuscripts, and repeated between doubled brackets of a different shape ⟨⟨ ⟩⟩ at the place to which I have transferred it.

In the foot-notes to the text, I have adopted the notation employed by Thomas:
> $\omega$ = *the consensus of all manuscripts*. <note>original: "omnium codicum consensus"</note>
> $\varsigma$ = *interpolated manuscripts*. <note>original: "codices interpolati"; these are manuscripts containing later additions or alterations not found in the original.</note>
> *Roman Edition* = *the first printed edition from Rome*, 1469. <note>original: "editio princeps Romana"</note>

In the English translation which faces the Latin text, I have aimed at expressing what I suppose to have been the meaning of the original Greek, rather than the meaning—or, too frequently, the absence of meaning—of the Latin.

***The component parts of the ASCLEPIUS.*** It appears from internal evidence that the dialogue has been made up by putting together three distinct and unconnected documents—which I have named respectively ‘*Asclepius I (On Man)*’, ‘*Asclepius II (On the Origin of Evil)*’, and ‘*Asclepius III (On the Worship of the Gods)*’—and adding a ‘*prologue*’ and an ‘*epilogue*’.

# INTRODUCTION

which I call *Asclepius I* (namely chapters 2 through 14 a) is a well-constructed whole, the parts of which are arranged and linked together with some skill. It is a treatise "concerning the whole of the highest reality" <note>original Latin: "de tota summitate"</note> (chapter 7 c)—concerning *God*, the *World*, and *Man*, and their inter-relations;—but the writer deals with this all-embracing subject from a definite point of view, and according to a definite plan. Throughout the discussion, *Man* is the central figure; <margin>1</margin> and the teacher nowhere loses sight of his practical aim—that of urging men to live the life to which, as men, they are called. To this end he describes man's origin and nature (partly cosmic and partly beyond the cosmos), and his station among and relations to beings of other grades (2-7); the twofold function assigned to him in accordance with his twofold nature (7 end-11 a); and the destiny which awaits him according as he fulfils his function or neglects it (11 b-12 beginning). The subdivisions in the treatment of the theme are clearly marked, and yet are so connected that we pass on from each to the next without a break. There are two subordinate topics on which the writer has a special message to deliver, namely the call to renounce possessions (11 a), and the mischief of a certain method of philosophic teaching (12 end-14 a). But each of these topics is introduced without breach of continuity. The renunciation of possessions is spoken of as a thing required with a view to the fulfilment of man's function; and the corruption of philosophy is coupled with the love of possessions, as one of the hindrances to the realization of man's high destiny. Thus the concluding paragraph, on philosophy, is made to arise naturally out of the main subject; and so the discourse ends appropriately with a description of that teaching which the writer holds to be the true philosophy, and of which the treatise itself is a specimen.

*Asclepius I*, then, is a well-ordered whole, complete in itself. There can, I think, be little doubt that the Greek original of *Asclepius I* at first existed as a separate document, of the same type as the *Hermes to Asclepius short books* <note>original Latin: "libelli"</note> preserved in the *Collection* <note>The "Corpus Hermeticum," a primary collection of Greek Hermetic texts</note>; and it may be presumed that it once formed part of the collection of discourses known to Stobaeus <note>A 5th-century compiler of extracts from Greek authors</note> as *The Works of Hermes to Asclepius*.

*The sources of ASCLEPIUS I.* In this treatise, as in most of the *Hermetic writings* <note>original Latin: "Hermetica"</note>, there is little novelty or originality in the doctrines taught; and the discourse of Hermes contains few statements to

which parallels cannot be found in earlier Greek writings. Yet the teaching of *Asclepius* I is not a mere repetition of traditional formulas; the writer's words ring true, and are alive with genuine feeling. If he has adopted his beliefs from others, they are none the less his own.

The influence of Plato is manifest throughout. The fundamental articles of the writer's creed—the doctrine of a supracosmic <note>Existing above or beyond the physical universe.</note> God, who is the maker and ruler of the universe, and that of a supracosmic element in the human soul—have been transmitted to him from Plato; and verbal echoes of phrases used by Plato may be recognized (see for instance the reminiscences of the *Timaeus* <note>Plato's famous dialogue concerning the creation of the world.</note> in chapter 8). But there is ample evidence of dependence on Greek writers of later date than Plato. The terms *matter* <note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle)</note> and *quality* <note>original: "qualitas" (Latin) or "ποιόν/ποιότης" (Greek)</note>, as employed in *Asclepius* I, did not come into use until after Plato's time. The cosmology <note>The study of the origin and development of the universe.</note> of chapters 2-6 is largely Stoic <note>Referring to the school of philosophy founded by Zeno, emphasizing reason and harmony with the natural order.</note>. The notion of a lower and mortal soul which is either composed of fire and air, or inseparably connected with those elements, must have been arrived at by a blending of Platonism with Stoic physics. The terms *that which is carried upward* and *that which is carried downward* <note>original: "quod sursum versus fertur" and "quod deorsum fertur" (Latin); "τὸ ἀνωφερές" and "τὸ κατωφερές" (Greek)</note>, chapter 2—*form* <note>original: "species" (Latin) or "εἶδος" (Greek)</note> in the sense of an individual, or the group of qualities distinctive of an individual, chapters 2 (end) to 4—*spirit* <note>original: "spiritus" (Latin) or "πνεῦμα" (pneuma, Greek)</note>, chapter 6—and the statement that plants are *soulless* <note>original: "ἄψυχα" (apsycha)</note>, chapter 4, are of Stoic origin. The phrase *(intellect)* *which is the fifth part granted to man alone from the ether* <note>original: "(νοῦς) quae quinta pars soli homini concessa est ex aethere"</note>, chapter 6 (end), seems to have been derived from the Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> Critolaus, perhaps through the syncretic <note>Blending different beliefs or schools of thought.</note> Platonist Antiochus.¹

The writer of *Asclepius* I says that man has been embodied on earth "in order that he may tend the things of earth" <note>original: "ἵνα τὰ ἐπίγεια θεραπεύῃ" (hina ta epigeia therapeuē)</note>; and it is in the treatment of this theme, if anywhere, that he shows independence. The earliest Pagan writer in whom I have found this thought expressed is Cicero; and he probably got it from Posidonius. In this part of *Asclepius* I, therefore, the influence of Posidonius may be suspected.

The modification of a fundamentally Platonic system of thought by an intermixture of Stoic physics, such as we find in this document as well as in most of the other *Hermetica* <note>A body of mystical and philosophical texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, must have been derived from Antiochus and Posidonius, or from writers subsequent to them and influenced by them.

# INTRODUCTION

There seems to be nothing distinctively Egyptian in the doctrine of *Asclepius* I <note>The *Asclepius* is a Latin dialogue traditionally attributed to Hermes Trismegistus; "Ascl. I" refers to the first section of this work.</note>. The religious fervour of the writer is characteristic of his Egyptian nationality; but there is nothing in his dogmas that cannot be derived from Greek philosophy.

There are several phrases which show some resemblance to passages in the first two chapters of *Genesis*. See notes on ch. 3, *the world . . . was prepared by God* <note>original: "mundus . . . praeparatus est a deo"</note> (i. e. <term>matter</term> <note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle)</note> has been created by God); ch. 7, *the part (of man, namely the Mind), which we call the form of the divine likeness* <note>original: "pars (hominis, sc. the νοῦς), quam vocamus divinae similitudinis formam"</note>; ch. 8, *and it appeared to be beautiful (to God)* <note>original: "καλὸς δὲ (τῷ θεῷ) ἐφάνη ὢν (ὁ κόσμος)"</note>; *ibid.*, *and he commanded all such to be* <note>original: "talesque omnes esse praecepit"</note> (which implies the making of a 'first man'); *ibid.*, *man has been embodied so that he might . . . govern earthly things* <note>original: "ut possit . . . gubernare terrena"</note>. There is, then, a possibility that the writer was to some slight extent affected by Jewish influence; but as each of these thoughts may very well have been suggested in some other way, it remains a possibility only.

The writer uses the term **the Lord** <note>original: "ὁ κύριος" (ho kyrios)</note> as a name or title of the supreme God (ch. 8). Is this to be regarded as a result of Jewish influence? The word **Lord** (with a dependent genitive) was applied to Zeus by Pindar, *Isthmian Odes* 4 (5). 67: *Zeus dispenses these things and those, Zeus the Lord of all* <note>original: "Ζεὺς τά τε καὶ τὰ νέμει, Ζεὺς ὁ πάντων κύριος"</note>; and according to Liddell and Scott, **Lord** occurs 'in inscriptions, as a name of divers gods, Zeus, Hermes, Kronos, &c., see *Corpus Inscriptionum* Index III; so **Lady** <note>original: "Κυρία" (Kyria)</note> of Artemis, &c., *ibid.*' But it was not commonly used by Greek philosophic writers with reference to the supreme God. There is no instance of this use of it in Diels' *Fragments of the Presocratics*, in Plato, in Aristotle, or in Diels' *Doxographi Graeci*^1. But it was employed by the translators of the **Septuagint** <note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, abbreviated as LXX.</note> as a rendering of the Hebrew name of God; and where it is similarly used by Pagan writers, it may have been taken over by them from Hellenistic Jews. It occurs frequently in the books of magic; e.g. the god is addressed as **Lord** <note>original: "κύριε" (kyrie)</note> in Dieterich *Mithrasliturgie*, pp. 8, 10 (thrice), 14 (twice), and Dieterich *Abraxas*, p. 177, &c. Its use in such cases is comparable to that of the Hebrew names (e.g. **Sabaoth** <note>original: "Σαβαώθ", a Hebrew title for God meaning "of Hosts"</note>, *Abraxas* p. 176) employed in magic invocations.

I have failed to find the slightest trace of Christian influence in *Asclepius* I.

*Date of the Greek original of ASCL. I.* The only definite limit—

Hermias, *ibid.*, p. 652, in a statement of the doctrine of Anaxagoras: *the Mind is the beginning of all things, and this is the cause and Lord of the whole* <note>original: "ἀρχὴ πάντων ὁ νοῦς, καὶ οὗτος αἴτιος καὶ κύριος τῶν ὅλων"</note>. # THE LATIN ASCLEPIUS

*from whom* <note>original: "a quo"</note> is that which is given by the fact that the writer mixes Stoic physics with his Platonism. This sort of syncretism <note>The blending of different beliefs or schools of thought into a single system.</note> began in the time of Antiochus and Posidonius, i. e. in the first half of the first century B.C. It is therefore certain that the treatise cannot have been written before 100 B.C. But it was probably not written until much later.

A *limit before which* <note>original: "terminus ante quem"; a chronological point before which an event must have happened.</note> may, perhaps, be inferred from the absence of any recognition of the existence of Christianity. The attitude of the writer of *Asclepius* I presents in this respect a contrast to that of the writer of *Asclepius* III. The latter, writing about A. D. 270 (see below), regards the advance of Christianity with horror and dismay; it is already clear to him that the Christians will soon get the upper hand, and that the Pagan cults will be abolished. But the writer of *Asclepius* I, when he asks himself (chapters 12 f.) what is the most serious obstacle in the path of those who seek salvation, finds it in the fact that certain Pagan teachers attach too much importance to the study of mathematics. If he had been aware that the very existence of his religion was threatened by the spread of Christianity, he could hardly have omitted to mention at this point a danger in comparison with which the error of which he speaks would have seemed to him a negligible trifle. This seems a sufficient reason for putting the date of *Asclepius* I earlier than that of *Asclepius* III. *Asclepius* I was probably written at a time when Christianity was not yet strong or aggressive enough to cause grave alarm or distress to the adherents of the old religions; *Asclepius* III was written at a time when it had already become apparent to the writer, not only that a danger was impending, but that the total extinction of Pagan religion was inevitable. For reasons given below, I think that a man in the situation of the writer of *Asclepius* I would not have been likely to ignore this danger at any time later than A. D. 260. We may therefore fix on 100 B.C. and A. D. 260 as the extreme limits between which the date of *Asclepius* I must be placed; and we might with strong probability restrict the range somewhat more narrowly, and say that the date must lie between 50 B.C. and A. D. 250.

I can find no internal evidence which would enable us to fix the date of *Asclepius* I more exactly; but on the ground of considerations which apply to the *Hermetica* <note>A body of mystical and philosophical writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> in general, I am inclined to think that this *little book* <note>original: "libellus"</note> is not likely to have been written before the second century A. D.; and perhaps we should not be far wrong in conjecturing that the writer was a contemporary of Clement, who was teaching in Alexandria between A. D. 190 and 200.

<summary>The author argues that Asclepius I was likely written between 50 B.C. and A.D. 250, noting that its lack of concern regarding Christianity suggests an earlier date than the more alarmist Asclepius III. The text likely dates to the 2nd century A.D., possibly contemporary with Clement of Alexandria.</summary>

# INTRODUCTION

*The circumstances of the writer.* The author of *Asclepius* I <note>The first section of the Latin Asclepius, a Hermetic dialogue</note> was probably an Egyptian by race. He can hardly have been a priest; for he takes no interest in theurgic ritual <note>Rituals intended to invoke the presence of gods or spirits</note>; and the worship of 'demons' <note>original: "daemons"; here referring to local temple-gods rather than evil spirits</note> (i.e. temple-gods) is, in his eyes, a comparatively low form of religion, though better than none. It may be inferred that he had not been trained in the schools of the Egyptian priests, but had received a Greek <note>original: "Hellenic"</note> education in Alexandria. Perhaps he had attended the lectures of one of the professional teachers of Platonism in that city, and is speaking from his own experience when he complains that such teachers put difficulties in the way of a seeker after God by including in their curriculum a compulsory course of mathematics. But in spite of these difficulties, he succeeded in learning as much of Greek philosophy as he needed for his purpose; and we may suppose that he afterwards retired to some more secluded place, where he could live the contemplative life in companionship with a small group of congenial spirits, at first, perhaps, as a pupil of some older teacher of the spiritual knowledge <note>original: "gnosis"</note>, and afterwards as a teacher in his turn. The instruction in these little communities must have been chiefly oral, and carried on, for the most part, by means of conversations between the master and a single pupil at a time; and when one of the teachers committed his thoughts to writing, no doubt he reproduced, in the form of imaginary dialogues between Hermes and Tat or Asclepius, the method and contents of his own talks with this or that disciple.

If the writer of *Asclepius* I practised what he preached (ch. 11), he must have renounced all private possessions; and it almost necessarily follows from this that the brotherhood to which he belonged, and of which he was perhaps the head, held property in common, and that the produce of their labours was thrown into a common stock, from which the wants of all the members were supplied. They must have divided their time between the "care of earthly things" <note>original: "cultus terrenorum"</note> and the "worship of heavenly things" <note>original: "cultus caelestium"</note>; that is, they must have been occupied partly in tilling the piece of land which they owned collectively, and partly in adoration of the "heavenly gods" <note>original: "di caelestes"</note> (especially in the form of hymn-singing, ch. 9), and in drawing near to the supreme God by private prayer and meditation, and by such talk between teacher and pupil as is exemplified in our *Hermetica* <note>The collection of writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>. They felt that, in living such a life as this, they were doing the work which God had sent them down to earth to do; and they looked forward with trustful hope to the time when they would be 'released from the bonds of mortality',

<summary>This page discusses the likely background of the author of Asclepius I, suggesting he was an Alexandria-educated Egyptian who led a communal, contemplative life focused on both manual labor and spiritual devotion.</summary>

# THE LATIN ASCLEPIUS

and, by God's grace, permitted to return to their true home above.

*Asclepius II.* That part of the composite dialogue which I call *Ascl.* II deals with the origin of evil; the writer seeks to account for the existence of evil by attributing it to the operation of matter <note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle); in Hermetic philosophy, this refers to the raw, often chaotic physical substance of the universe</note>. This discussion is not in any way connected either with the contents of *Ascl.* I or with those of *Ascl.* III; and the dualism <note>The belief that the universe is under the control of two opposing principles, such as good and evil or spirit and matter</note> of *Ascl.* II is irreconcilable with the monism <note>The belief that all existence is derived from a single source or substance</note> of *Ascl.* I and *Ascl.* III. There can, therefore, be little doubt that the Greek original of *Ascl.* II was in existence before it was made use of to form a part of the *Asclepius*. It appears to be complete in itself; but whether it was an independent little book <note>original: "libellus"</note>,<note>1</note> or a piece extracted by the compiler of the *Asclepius* from a longer document, we have no means of knowing.

There is no indication of any definite date for the Greek original of *Ascl.* II. We may suppose it to have been written in the same period as the Greek originals of *Ascl.* I and *Ascl.* III, i. e. probably about A. D. 150-270; and this supposition is to some extent confirmed by the resemblance between the teaching of *Ascl.* II and that of Numenius and Hermogenes (A. D. 150-200) <note>Middle Platonist philosophers who influenced early Christian and Hermetic thought regarding the nature of matter</note> on the same subject.

*The contents of ASCLEPIUS III.* That part of the traditional text which I have named *Ascl.* III presents, at first sight, a mere chaos of passages not only unconnected with *Ascl.* I and *Ascl.* II, but also unconnected with one another. But this confusion may be in part, if not wholly, a result of the mutilated and disordered state in which the Latin text has come down to us; and it seems probable that the Greek original of *Ascl.* III existed as a single document before the composite dialogue was compiled.

It appears that a number of passages were somehow severed from their context, but were preserved as detached fragments; and that these fragments were collected into two blocks (27 b-29 b and 33-6), which have been inserted into the text at the two places at which we find them. I have transposed these passages to what I conjecture to have been their original positions; and the contents of *Ascl.* III, as rearranged by me, may be tabulated as follows:

# THE LATIN ASCLEPIUS

respect, *Asclepius* III stands in marked contrast to *Asclepius* I.) The treatise as a whole has little unity; and it is difficult to describe its subject in a single phrase. But every part of it contributes in some way to the exposition of what the writer holds to be the true religion; and in some parts at least he is occupied in explaining what gods are to be worshipped, and how men ought to worship them. In the Prophecy he laments the impending abandonment of the old cults; his repeated assertion that men make gods (23 b, 37) is a defiant justification of the usages of Pagan worship in the face of Christian hostility; and the passage on time and eternity (26 b-32) leads up to a mention of that vision of the Eternal in which all worship culminates. Perhaps then the loosely connected discussions of which *Asclepius* III is composed may be fairly comprehended under the title *On the Worship of the Gods* <note>original: "De cultu deorum"</note>.

*The sources of ASCLEPIUS III.* The influence of Plato is manifest throughout. The fundamental conceptions of the writer—that of a supracosmic God, and that of an incorporeal <term>Mind (nous)</term>—are derived from Plato. The notion of eternity (26 b-32) is Platonic; and the use of the word *eternity* <note>original: "aeternitas"</note> (<term>Aeon (aion)</term>) to express this notion comes from the *Timaeus*. The doctrine of <term>intelligible things (noeta)</term> and <term>forms (eide)</term> contained in chapters 17 b, 18 b, 19 a c, 34 b-36, is based on the teaching of Plato; and the distinction between <term>intelligible forms (noeta eide)</term> and <term>sensible forms (aistheta eide)</term> (17 b and 35) belongs to a stage of Platonism which can hardly have been reached before the time of Antiochus (first century B.C.). The daemonology of 27 e-29 a must have been taken over from some Platonic authority. The use of the term <term>matter (hyle)</term> (17 a) originated among the pupils of Plato. In 16 b, the Cosmos is described as a *sensible god* <note>original: "sensibilis deus"</note> (<term>perceptible god (aisthetos theos)</term>, *Plato's Timaeus*).

To Stoic influence must be ascribed the use of the term *spirit* <note>original: "spiritus"</note> (<term>pneuma</term>) in 16 b, 17 a, 18 b, and the doctrine of <term>fate (heimarmene)</term> in 39, 40 a. The definition of *voice* <note>original: "vox"</note> (<term>phone</term>) in 20 a is Stoic. In the words *that which is said to be outside the world* <note>original: "quod dicitur extra mundum"</note>, 33 a, the writer refers to the Stoic doctrine of a void outside the Cosmos. The statement that no two individuals are alike (ch. 35) is derived from the Stoics of the second century B.C., who maintained this doctrine in opposition to the Academics; and the astral explanation of individual differences (*ibid.*) would hardly have been found in the writings of any Stoic earlier than Posidonius. The terms <term>restored (apokatestesen)</term> and *rebirth* <note>original: "regenitura"</note> (<term>regeneration (palingenesia)</term>) in the last paragraph of the Prophecy, 26 a, are Stoic, and the contents of this paragraph are probably derived in part from a Stoic source. # INTRODUCTION

The statement that *mind* <note>original: "νοῦς" (nous)</note> is *the divine part of the world* <note>original: "divina pars mundi"</note>, ch. 22 b, is due to the influence of Stoic materialism, but may perhaps have been transmitted to the writer by the Peripatetic <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> Critolaus and the Platonist Antiochus. The remarks on circular movement in 31 *at the end* and 40 b may perhaps have been derived from Aristotle.

The contents of chs. 20, 21 (God is *nameless* <note>original: "ἀνώνυμος" (anonumos)</note> or *all-named* <note>original: "παντώνυμος" (pantonumos)</note>—God is *male-female* <note>original: "ἀρσενόθηλυς" (arsenothelus)</note>) may possibly be derived from native Egyptian sources. The views expressed in connexion with the statement that man makes gods (23 b, 24 a, and 37, 38) are Egyptian rather than Hellenic <note>Greek.</note>. In these passages, the writer formulates certain beliefs of his countrymen; he is here speaking of things familiar to him by direct and personal knowledge, and has no occasion to borrow from earlier writers.

In the list of *rulers of being* <note>original: "οὐσιάρχαι" (ousiarchai)</note> (19 b, 27 c), the notion of a system of departmental gods, and the names *Zeus*, *Fate* <note>original: "Heimarmene"</note>, indicate a Stoic source; but the terms <term>Decani</term> <note>Egyptian astrological deities who ruled over ten-degree segments of the zodiac.</note>, *Horoscopes* <note>original: "Horoscopi"</note>, and *All-formed* <note>original: "Pantomorphos"</note> are derived rather from the astral religion of Hellenistic Egypt. The combination of Stoic and Egyptian ingredients in this passage might be accounted for by the assumption that the scheme of *rulers of being* has been borrowed from the Egyptian Stoic Chaeremon.

The form of the Prophecy, 24 b-26 a, may have been suggested by earlier apocalypses, Egyptian or Jewish; but its contents, so far as it refers to contemporary events, must be original.

Analogies to Jewish teaching may be found in the exaltation of human procreation, ch. 21 (cf. Genesis 1:28, *increase and multiply* <note>original: "αὐξάνεσθε καὶ πληθύνεσθε"</note>); in the statement that man is made *from the more corrupt part of the world and from the divine part* <note>original: "ex parte corruptiore mundi et ex divina"</note>, ch. 22 (cf. Genesis 2:7, *God formed man as dust from the earth, etc.* <note>original: "ἔπλασεν ὁ θεὸς τὸν ἄνθρωπον χοῦν ἀπὸ τῆς γῆς κ.τ.λ."</note>); and in the application of the term *highest* <note>original: "summus" / "ὕψιστος" (hupsistos)</note> to the supreme God (*the highest who is called God* <note>original: "summus qui dicitur deus"</note>, 16 b); but there is no proof that the writer was in any way affected by Jewish influences.

There is not the slightest reason to think that any part of the doctrine of *Asclepius III* has been derived from Christian sources. On the other hand, the writer's attitude is to a large extent determined by his repugnance to Christianity. This repugnance finds direct

*Date of the Greek original of ASCLEPIUS III.* A consideration of the sources from which the doctrine of *Ascl.* III <note>Asclepius III refers to a specific section of the Hermetic dialogue</note> is derived makes it certain that the treatise must have been written after the time of Antiochus and Posidonius, i. e. at some time later than 100 B.C. At no earlier period could Stoic <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy emphasizing virtue and reason</note> conceptions have been blended with Platonism as we find them blended in this document. And if the writer has borrowed from Chaeremon <note>A Stoic philosopher and Egyptian priest of the 1st century A.D.</note>, the date must be later than A.D. 50.

But the Prophecy, ch. 24 f., contains references to contemporary events; and by examining these references, it may be possible to determine the date more exactly. The contents of the Prophecy may be summarized thus: 'Cruel and impious foreigners will invade the land of Egypt, and slaughter a large part of the inhabitants; thereupon, the Egyptians themselves will become cruel and impious, and the national religion will die out.' At what date were these predictions written? It is evident that the writer is describing, under the form of a prophecy uttered by Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom these writings are attributed</note>, things which had recently taken place, or were taking place before his eyes. If, therefore, we can identify the events of which he speaks, we shall obtain an approximate date for the writing of chs. 24-6 at least, if not for the whole treatise.

Let us consider first the predicted abandonment of the national religion.

Under the rule of the Persians and the Greeks, and under the earlier Roman empire, the Egyptian religion had maintained itself, not indeed unchanged, but unimpaired in strength, and unshaken by any sudden or violent transformation; and at no time could it be thought to be in danger of perishing, until it was threatened with extinction by the advance of Christianity.¹

---

¹ Under the Ptolemies <note>The Greek dynasty that ruled Egypt after Alexander the Great</note> and the early Roman emperors, the only declared opponents of Paganism in Egypt were the Jews; and they were never numerous or influential enough to cause such a feeling of impending and inevitable doom as is expressed by our Hermetist. (On the Jewish rising under Trajan, see below.)

An illustration of the attitude of the Jews towards the Egyptian religion is to be found in *Sibylline Oracles* 5. 484-503, written by an Alexandrian Jew of unknown date (possibly about the time of Trajan or Hadrian):
> Isis, thrice-wretched goddess, you shall remain by the streams of the Nile
> alone, a voiceless maenad upon the sands of Acheron,
> and no longer shall memory of you remain throughout the whole earth.
> And you, Serapis, sitting upon many useless stones,
> shall lie a mighty ruin in thrice-wretched Egypt.

# INTRODUCTION

What, then, is the earliest date at which Christianity was powerful and aggressive enough in Egypt to give rise to such gloomy anticipations as are expressed in chs. 24-5 of the *Asclepius*? <note>The 'Lament' in the Asclepius predicts the end of Egyptian religion and the departure of the gods.</note> Harnack, *Mission and Expansion of Christianity*, Book IV, has collected the evidences of the spread of Christianity down to <term>A. D. 325</term> <note>The year of the Council of Nicaea, a turning point for the Church's legal status.</note>. Celsus¹ (<term>A. D. 176-80</term>) speaks as if Christianity had been almost extirpated. Doubtless he exaggerates the success of the repressive measures of Marcus Aurelius; but he could not have spoken thus if the Christians were numerous enough to cause serious alarm. In his time, Pagans regarded Christianity with hatred and contempt, but not with fear.

Tertullian² (<term>A. D. 197-213</term>) speaks in a tone which foreshadows the coming danger to Paganism. But allowance must be made for his rhetorical style; he greatly exaggerates the numbers and power of the Christians.

> "As many as have brought a longing for Egypt into you, all
> shall weep for you miserably, having placed an immortal god in their hearts;
> they shall know you to be nothing, as many as sang praises to a god.
> And <then> one of the priests shall say, a man robed in linen:
> 'Come, let us build a beautiful temple of the true God;
> come, let us change the terrible law of our ancestors,
> for the sake of which those who made
> processions and rites for gods of stone and clay did not understand.
> Let us turn our souls, singing praises to the immortal God,
> the ruler of all, the true one, the king,
> the nourisher of the soul, the father, the great God who exists forever.'"
> <note>original Greek: ὅσσοι δ’ Αἰγύπτου... This is a passage from the Sibylline Oracles, Jewish-Christian prophetic verses.</note>

The Jewish Sibyllist here predicts the conversion of the Egyptians, as the writer of Isaiah ch. 19 had predicted it before him; but it is hardly to be thought that an Egyptian idolater would at any time have admitted that the conversion of the whole nation to Judaism was even possible, much less that it was inevitable.
