# THE LATIN ASCLEPIUS

Origen¹ (A. D. 246-9), speaking the language of sober truth, supplies the necessary corrective to Tertullian's exaggerations <note>Tertullian, an earlier Church Father, often claimed Christianity had already filled every corner of the Empire; Origen provides a more realistic statistical view</note>. He admits that there are still many people, even in the Roman empire, whose ears the preaching of Christianity has not yet reached; and that the Christians are still 'very few' as compared with the Pagans. He looks forward with confident assurance to the ultimate prevalence of good over evil, either in this world or in the world to come; but he doubts whether the universal acceptance of the true religion is possible on earth.

Harnack (*op. cit.*, p. 376) concludes that 'as regards the stages in the history of the mission-work, the great advances, after the time of Paul, were made (1) in the epoch of Commodus (A. D. 180-92) and his next successors, and (2) in the years 260-303; and it was in the latter period that the progress was most rapid'.²

From the time of the edict of toleration issued at Milan by Constantine and Licinius in A. D. 313, the victory of the new religion was assured. Eusebius,³ about A. D. 325, describes the Christians as 'the most numerous of all the nations'; and Firmicus Maternus, some twenty years later, speaks of Paganism as almost extinct.⁴

# INTRODUCTION

From the evidence of the authors so far cited, we may form some notion of the stages by which Christianity advanced in the Roman empire as a whole. Our present purpose would be better served if we could trace the progress made in Egypt. The history of Christianity in Egypt down to <term>A. D. 180</term> <note>The late 2nd century</note> is almost a blank;$^1$ concerning that period we know only that some early Christian documents were probably written there; that a ‘Gospel according to the Egyptians’ was in circulation; and that <term>Basilides</term>, <term>Valentinus</term>, and other Christian <term>Gnostics</term> <note>Followers of a diverse religious movement that emphasized secret spiritual knowledge (gnosis) over faith or ritual</note> taught in Egypt. About 180, we find a vigorous Christian Church established in Alexandria, and the Christian ‘Catechetical School’ <note>A famous center of Christian scholarship and instruction in Alexandria</note> already at work. In the time of <term>Clement</term> (from <term>A. D. 190</term> onwards), that School was attended by Pagans as well as Christians; and if Clement’s words$^2$ may be taken as specially applying to Egypt, they imply that Christianity had gained a firm footing among the people of the country. <term>Eusebius</term> (*Church History* 6. 1, 2) says that in the persecution of <term>Septimius Severus</term>, <term>A. D. 202</term>, a large number of Christians ‘from all (Lower) Egypt and all the Thebaid’ <note>The region of Upper Egypt centered around Thebes</note> suffered martyrdom in Alexandria.$^3$ <term>Harnack</term> (*cited work*, p. 454) says that ‘from the fragments of the letters of <term>Dionysius of Alexandria</term>, bishop of Alexandria (<term>A. D. 247-65</term>), and from the accounts of the persecutions (<term>A. D. 250-60</term>), we get the impression that the number of Christians in Alexandria was large, and that Christianity had spread to a considerable extent in the towns and villages of the country. After the middle of the third century, Lower Egypt was certainly one of the regions in which the Christians were especially numerous. . . . At the time of the persecution of <term>Decius</term> (<term>A. D. 250</term>) there were already Christians holding public offices in Alexandria, and many wealthy men were Christians (<term>Eusebius</term> 7. 26; <term>Boissier</term>, *The End of Paganism*, i, p. 347). <term>Libanius</term>, *On the Temples*, about <term>A. D. 384-7</term>, speaks of Pagan cults as still practised (<term>Boissier</term>, *ibid.*, ii, p. 341); the edict of <term>Theodosius</term> in <term>A. D. 392</term> (*Theodosian Code* 16. 10. 12) shows that the need of fresh enactments against them was still felt at that time; and even <term>Theodosius II</term> (*Theodosian Code* 16. 10. 22) issued an edict against *pagans who remain, although we believe that now there are none* <note>original Latin: "paganos qui supersunt, quamquam iam nullos esse credamus"</note>. In <term>A. D. 398</term>, <term>Claudian</term> (*On the Fourth Consulship of Honorius* 570 and following; <term>Otto</term>, *Priests and Temples*, ii. 281 and i. 404) describes a procession of statues of the gods in Memphis.

6. 41: 7. 11)'. The descriptions of the persecution of Diocletian <note>Roman Emperor from 284–305 AD, known for the last major persecution of Christians.</note> (A. D. 303) prove that there were at that time large numbers of Christians in the Thebaid <note>The region of Upper Egypt, named after its capital, Thebes.</note>. Dionysius of Alexandria (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* 6. 41) speaks of Christians among the native Egyptian population as well as among the Greeks; and the translation of the Bible into Coptic was probably begun, in Upper Egypt, in the second half of the third century. 'It is certain', says Harnack <note>Adolf von Harnack (1851–1930), a prominent German theologian and church historian.</note>, 'that at the time of the persecution of Diocletian the Christians in Egypt had long outnumbered the Jews; at the beginning of the fourth century their number probably exceeded a million.'

What, then, is the earliest date at which it would be possible for an adherent of Paganism in Egypt to foresee and lament the coming extinction of his religion? To this question no exact and certain answer can be given; but we may conclude that chapters 24-5 can hardly have been written before the renewed expansion of Christianity which followed on the close of the period of persecution under Decius, Gallus, and Valerian (A. D. 250-3 and 257-60). Thus from what we know of the progress of Christianity, we might fix on the year 260 as the <term>earliest possible date <note>original: "terminus a quo"</note></term> for the Greek original of chapters 24-6. A <term>latest possible date <note>original: "terminus ante quem"</note></term> is given by Lactantius's quotation from the Greek original of chapter 26 in his *Divine Institutes*, written within a few years of A. D. 310. The prophecy, then, was probably written at some time in the half-century A. D. 260-310.

But we may hope to fix the date more exactly by identifying the particular events referred to. The prophecy speaks of an invasion of Egypt by <term>foreigners <note>original: "alienigenae"</note></term>, and an immigration of 'Scythians or Indians or some such barbarians'. Who are these foreigners? The term cannot be meant to apply to Greeks or Jews; for Greeks and Jews had been resident in Egypt in large numbers ever since the time of Alexander, and the invasion spoken of is evidently recent. Nor can the Roman conquest be meant; for we are told that the foreigners will 'fill the land'; but the Roman conquest caused no large and sudden influx of foreigners; indeed, Italians were at no time numerous in Egypt. And neither Greek, Jew, nor Italian can be described as 'Scythian or Indian'.

We are also told of a vast slaughter, or series of slaughters, in which a large part of the population of Egypt perishes. The earliest incident to which this description could possibly be supposed to apply is the insurrection of the Jews under Trajan.¹ But though

# INTRODUCTION

The next incident to which the prophecy of slaughter might seem to be applicable² is the massacre of Alexandrians by order of <term>Caracalla</term>³ <note>Roman Emperor from 198–217 AD, known for his volatile temperament.</note> in <term>A. D. 215</term>. But the words *with foreigners filling the land* <note>original: "alienigenis terram complentibus"</note> and *the Indian or Scythian shall inhabit Egypt* <note>original: "inhabitabit Aegyptum Indus aut Scythes"</note> cannot be made to apply to Caracalla's soldiers.

It would seem that after this disaster Alexandria never fully recovered its former prosperity; and from this time onward, things went from bad to worse in Egypt. In <term>A. D. 252</term> we first hear of a pestilence which ravaged the empire in successive outbreaks during a space of fifteen years, and by which large numbers of Egyptians perished. But it was especially during the troubled years which followed the capture of <term>Valerian</term> <note>Roman Emperor captured by the Persian Sassanids, a unique humiliation in Roman history.</note> by the Persians in 260, that calamities fell thick and fast upon the land. We have a contemporary description of the situation in Egypt between <term>A. D. 261</term> and 265,⁴ in the letters written by <term>Dionysius</term>, bishop of Alexandria.

'When persecution had ceased', says Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the 4th-century "Father of Church History."</note>, 'Dionysius returned to Alexandria. There, civil strife and war broke out; and as the Christians were divided between the two factions, it was not possible for him to visit in person all the brethren in the city. He, therefore, at the Easter festival, communicated with them by letter, writing to them as if from beyond the borders, though he was in Alexandria.'

What was the civil strife and war <note>original: "στάσις καὶ πόλεμος" (stasis kai polemos)</note> of which Eusebius is speaking? The only recorded disturbance in Egypt which can be assigned to this time is the insurrection of Aemilianus.¹ It may be presumed, then, that one part of Alexandria was held by the troops and partisans of Aemilianus, and another part by those of the Roman commander Theodotus.²

Dionysius writes thus: 'I am obliged to communicate by letter with the members of my own church; and how my letter is to be conveyed to them, I do not know. For it would be easier to go

---

Gallienus <note>Roman Emperor, r. 253–268 AD.</note> cannot have taken effect there before 261. Dionysius died in 265 (Eusebius, *Church History* 7. 28. 3). The letters must therefore have been written between 261 and 265.

Mommsen's <note>Theodor Mommsen, a famous 19th-century German classical scholar.</note> account of these events is self-contradictory. He rightly says that Dionysius died in 265 (*Roman Provinces*, ii, p. 250, n. 2), and that the Palmyrene invasion of Egypt did not take place until after the death of Odaenathus in 266-7 (*ibid.* pp. 106, 107); and yet he speaks of the incidents described by Dionysius as if they arose out of the Palmyrene invasion (*ibid.* p. 250).

Mommsen, *Roman Provinces*, ii. 251, n. 1, rejects the evidence of Trebellius Pollio, and doubts the existence of the alleged usurper Aemilianus. But this is surely an excess of scepticism. At any rate, the contemporary evidence of Dionysius makes it certain that either Aemilianus, or some person whose name we do not know, raised 'civil strife and war' in Egypt between 261 and 265.

As the Easter letter written by Dionysius during the civil strife is followed by another Easter letter written by him when fighting had ceased and pestilence was raging, and that again by others written 'when the city was at peace again', the civil strife may be assigned with probability, if not with certainty, to the year 262.

It would seem that this fortification was still in existence, and was utilized by the combatants, in the time of Dionysius.

# INTRODUCTION

The principal street of the city is more impassable than the desert of Sinai; and the harbours of Alexandria have become like the Red Sea, for they have many times been reddened with bloodshed. The river which waters the city <note>original: "i. e. the canal by which the water of the Nile was brought to Alexandria."</note> was at one time drier than the desert; <note>original: "The regulation of the water-supply was probably neglected during the disturbances, and the water may have been purposely cut off by the besiegers."</note> at another time it overflowed its banks and flooded all the ways and lands around the city; and it is continually polluted with blood and slayings and drownings. As in the days of Moses, "the waters have been turned to blood, and the river stinks". <note>original: Exodus 7:20, 21. Compare the Latin *Asclepius* 24 b: "You will burst forth, full of rushing blood, even to the banks, and the divine waves will not only be polluted with blood, but will be totally corrupted."</note> The air is turbid with noisome vapours; earth and sea, river and harbour reek with foul exhalations; corpses lie rotting everywhere, <note>original: *Asclepius* 24 b: "Then this land... shall be most full of tombs and the dead."</note> and the dew is corrupted by their fetid juices. And yet men wonder what is the cause of these incessant pestilences! And they ask whence comes this great and manifold destruction of mankind, <note>original: *Asclepius* 24 b: "The number of tombs shall be much greater than the living."</note> and why it is that the inhabitants of our great city, young and old together, are fewer in number than the elderly persons <note>original: *ὠμογέροντας* (omogerontas), meaning old, but still vigorous.</note> alone were in times gone by. For though all from fourteen to eighty years of age have now been included in the list of those entitled to receive the public corn-dole, they are less numerous than the people from forty to seventy years of age used to be in those times. <note>original: Dionysius does not tell us of what earlier time he is speaking; it may have been any time before the massacre of Caracalla (Emperor from 198–217 AD). It appears that, for the purpose of the corn-dole, a maximum limit of number was maintained unaltered. In the time of greatest prosperity the full number had been made up by entering on the roll those between forty and seventy alone; as the population decreased, the names of younger and older persons were added to the register.</note> Men see the human race continually diminishing and wasting away, and yet they do not tremble, though the course of things is tending more and more towards their total destruction.'

Even before this, many terrible things had befallen us; first, the persecution of the Christians;² <note>The persecution under Emperor Valerian, roughly 257–261 AD.</note> . . . then, war³ and famine, which we Christians endured together with the Pagans, sharing the evils which they inflicted on each other; . . . and then, after short respite to us and them, there came on us this pestilence, a thing most terrible to them, and the most cruel of all disasters.' The Christians, Dionysius says, tenderly nursed the sick, and buried the dead; and many of them, in so doing, caught the infection and died themselves. 'But with the Pagans, it is far otherwise; they thrust away from them people who were sickening; they fled from their nearest and dearest; they flung them out into the streets when they were dying; and they cast forth corpses unburied, like offal.'

There is a striking resemblance between the situation depicted in these letters and that predicted by Trismegistus; and it seems probable enough that the writer of the prophecy had lived through the events which Dionysius describes. As yet, however, we have met with no trace of the *foreigners* <note>original: "alienigenae"</note>. But Egypt was invaded by foreigners a few years later. Odaenathus of Palmyra, who ruled over the provinces of Syria and Arabia, and some adjacent countries,⁴ nominally as <term>Leader of the East</term> <note>original: "Dux Orientis"; a high-ranking Roman military title</note> under Gallienus, but in practical independence, was murdered between August 29, 266, and August 29, 267. His widow Zenobia claimed the succession for her son Vaballathus, and ruled in his name; and, shortly after her husband's death,⁵ she sent an army under her general Zabdas to occupy Egypt, professedly on behalf of the Roman emperor. The fullest and most trustworthy account of the Palmyrene invasion is that given by Zosimus. He says (I. 44 ff.) that, after the first Gothic campaign of Claudius, 'Zenobia, seeking to extend her power, sent Zabdas to Egypt, which Timagenes, a native of the country, was endeavouring to bring under the rule of the Palmyrenes. The invading army was composed of Palmyrenes, Syrians, and barbarians, and amounted to the number of 70,000 men. The Egyptians met them with a force of 50,000, and a great battle took place. Probus, who had been appointed by the emperor (Claudius) to clear the sea of the (Gothic) pirates, hearing that Egypt was occupied by the Palmyrenes <note>The Palmyrenes were inhabitants of Palmyra, a powerful Syrian city-state that briefly formed its own empire under Queen Zenobia.</note>, proceeded thither with his force, and being joined by those Egyptians who were not of the Palmyrene faction, attacked the garrison and drove it out.¹ The Palmyrenes² once more marched against Egypt; Probus got together an army of Egyptians and Libyans to oppose them; the Egyptians (under Probus) got the upper hand, and were driving the Palmyrenes out of the country. Probus took up a position on the mountain near Babylon,³ meaning to bar the passage of the enemy there as they marched towards Syria; but Timagenes, making use of his knowledge of the locality, occupied the summit of the mountain with 2,000 Palmyrenes, and surprised and destroyed the Egyptian force. Probus was caught with the rest, and killed himself. Thus Egypt became subject to the Palmyrenes.⁴

¹ It appears that Probus, in treating the Palmyrene invaders as enemies of Rome, acted on his own responsibility, without waiting for instructions from the emperor; and Claudius, being too much occupied with the Goths to be willing to involve himself in a simultaneous war in the East, afterwards acquiesced in the *accomplished fact* <note>original: "fait accompli"</note>, and recognized Vaballathus <note>The son of Queen Zenobia and nominal ruler of the Palmyrene Empire.</note> as governor of Egypt in his name.

³ Babylon is the fortress of ‘Old Cairo’, on the eastern bank of the Nile. (See A. J. Butler, *Babylon of Egypt*, p. 23.) The most convenient route from Alexandria to Syria passes round the apex of the Delta, from which Cairo is only a few miles distant up the river; and if the Palmyrenes, at the time of their retreat from Alexandria, still held the fortress of Babylon, they would naturally choose the point guarded by it for their crossing of the Nile. ‘The mountain near Babylon’ must mean some spur of the desert heights to the north-east of Babylon, i. e. east of the modern town of Cairo. (The citadel of Cairo stands on such a spur, and its site may be the very place.) Probus posted his force here, apparently with the intention of attacking the Palmyrenes in flank as they marched northward from Babylon after crossing the river. While the attention of Probus was fixed on the river-valley below him, Timagenes stole round behind, over the desert tableland, and came down upon him from above.

⁴ These events are summarized by Trebellius Pollio, *Life of Claudius* <note>original: "Vita Claud."</note> 11, as follows: <note>original: "‘Dum haec a divo Claudio aguntur, Palmyreni ducibus Saba et Timagene contra Aegyptios bellum sumunt, atque ab his Aegyptia pervicacia et indefessa pugnandi continuatione vincuntur. Dux tamen Aegyptiorum Probatus Timagenis insidiis interemptus est: Aegyptii vero omnes se Romano imperatori dederunt, in absentis Claudii verba iurantes.’"</note> “While these things were being done by the divine Claudius, the Palmyrenes, under the leaders Saba and Timagenes, took up war against the Egyptians, and were conquered by them through Egyptian persistence and an untiring continuation of fighting. Zenobia . . . caused the land to be reconquered for the Roman empire by her general Zabda.” But there is no evidence for the existence of Probatus except this passage of Trebellius Pollio; and Mommsen (ii. 107, n. 1) is undoubtedly right in identifying the “leader of the Egyptians Probatus” <note>original: "dux Aegyptiorum Probatus"</note> of Trebellius Pollio with the Probus of Zosimus, who was not a usurper, but a Roman commander opposing the Palmyrenes in the interest of the empire.

# THE LATIN ASCLEPIUS

The war of conquest must have lasted for at least a large part of a year (A. D. 268-9). How long did the Palmyrenes <note>Inhabitants of Palmyra, a powerful Syrian city-state</note> hold the country they had conquered? Zosimus <note>A Greek historian of the 5th-6th century</note> (i. 50) says that Aurelian, after his accession (early in 270), spent some time in settling affairs in Italy and Paeonia, and then "was purposing to make war on the Palmyrenes, who by this time were masters of the inhabitants of Egypt, and of all the East as far (westward) as Ancyra in Galatia". Aurelian probably set out on his expedition to the East in 271, captured Zenobia <note>The Queen of Palmyra who challenged Roman authority</note> and received the surrender of Palmyra in the spring of 272, and, on the renewed revolt at Palmyra, destroyed that city in the spring of 273.¹ At what stage in the war did he recover possession of Egypt? Zosimus does not tell us. Vopiscus <note>One of the purported authors of the Augustan History</note> says that Egypt was reconquered for Aurelian by the future emperor Probus,² but gives no date. The most probable date seems to be

The *treachery of Timagenes* <note>original: "insidiae Timagenis"</note> by which he perished must mean the fight near Babylon <note>A Roman fortress in Egypt, not the Mesopotamian city</note>. What pretext, if any, Zenobia put forward to justify her occupation of Egypt, we do not know; but if there was any disturbance in the country which might be represented as calling for her interference, no record of it has come down to us; and Probus evidently regarded the invasion as an act of war against Rome, though Claudius subsequently found it convenient to recognize the Palmyrene as legitimate governor of Egypt in his name.

The last sentence of Trebellius Pollio <note>Another purported author of the Augustan History</note>, "The Egyptians indeed . . . swearing to the words" <note>original: "Aegyptii vero . . . verba iurantes"</note>, must be taken to mean that the Egyptians submitted to Vaballathus <note>Zenobia's son</note>, accepting him, however, not as an independent ruler, but as viceregent of the Roman emperor Claudius.

¹ Bury on Gibbon, i. 462.
² *Life of Probus* <note>original: "Vita Probi"</note> 5. 9 "(Probus) also fought against the Palmyrenes who were defending Egypt on behalf of Odaenathus and Cleopatra (that is, Zenobia), at first successfully, later recklessly, so that he was almost captured; but later, having restored his forces, he brought Egypt and the greatest part of the East back under the power of Aurelian." <note>original: "(Probus) pugnavit etiam contra Palmyrenos Odenati et Cleopatrae (i. e. Zenobiae) partibus Aegyptum defendentes, primo feliciter, postea temere, ut paene caperetur; sed postea refectis viribus Aegyptum et orientis maximam partem in Aureliani potestatem redegit"</note>. The earlier part of this passage (as Mommsen <note>Theodor Mommsen, a famous 19th-century German historian</note> has noted) suspiciously resembles the account of the conquest of Egypt by the Palmyrenes in 268-9. In that war another Probus had fought against the Palmyrenes in Egypt; and according to Zosimus's account, it might be said of him that he had fought "at first successfully, later recklessly, so that he was captured" <note>original: "primo feliciter, postea temere, ut caperetur"</note>. It seems probable, therefore, that Vopiscus has erroneously taken as referring to the more famous Probus something that he had read about the doings of the other. The statement which follows, that the future emperor Probus reconquered Egypt for Aurelian, may none the less be correct; but the evidence is open to suspicion.

Mommsen (ii, p. 108) says, "Egypt was already, *at the close of the year 270*, brought back to the empire . . . by Probus"; and he adds, "The determination of the date depends on the fact that the usurpation-coins of Vaballathus cease entirely in the fifth year of his Egyptian reign" (by which must be understood the fifth year from the death of his father Odaenathus, not from his acquisition of Egypt), "i. e. Aug. 29, 270—Aug. 29, 271; the fact that they are very rare speaks for the beginning of the year". But this merely negative evidence is hardly conclusive; and the cessation of the coins may be otherwise accounted for, by the supposition that Vaballathus died in 270-1 (Schiller, i. 864).

Mommsen, *ibid.*, p. 250, says, "When Probus, the general *sent by Claudius*, at length gained the upper hand", etc. Is this a slip of the pen? Or has Mommsen, like Vopiscus, here confused the one Probus with the other? It is certain that the Roman war against the Palmyrenes did not begin till after the death of Claudius.

An incident in this war of reconquest <gloss>1</gloss> is described by Eusebius (*Church History* <note>original: "H. E." or Historia Ecclesiastica</note> 7. 32), who speaks of it as occurring 'in the course of the siege of Piruchion <gloss>2</gloss> at Alexandria'. The Roman commander held one part of the city, and was blockading the Palmyrene faction (including, it would seem, the bulk of the inhabitants), who were cooped up in the other part, and were dying of hunger. The besieged Alexandrians were under the rule of a council (*council*, *assembly* <note>original Greek: "βουλή", "συνέδριον"</note>). An influential Christian who was amongst them induced the council to grant permission to the starving non-combatants to pass the lines and go over to the Romans, and at the same time, communicating with a friend on the other side who had access to the Roman commander, obtained from the latter a promise to spare the lives of all who came over to him. By so doing, he saved from death not only the aged, the women, and the children, but also a large number of able-bodied men, who took the opportunity to escape from the blockaded quarter, disguised in women's clothes.

The Palmyrene faction was conquered for the time, but it was not yet extinguished. # INTRODUCTION

It appears, then, that it is impossible to find any time to which the prophecy of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom various philosophical and magical texts were attributed.</note> could refer, except the time of the Palmyrene occupation of Egypt; and that the events of that time—i. e. of the five years 268-73—correspond exactly with the indications given in the prophecy.

We are told that the invading army, 70,000 in number, was composed of Palmyrenes, Syrians, 'and barbarians'. These barbarians were, no doubt, contingents sent by countries subject or allied to Zenobia <note>The Queen of the Palmyrene Empire who famously challenged Roman authority.</note>, and adventurers attracted by the prospect of pay and plunder. Among them were certainly Saraceni (Bedouin Arabs), probably Armenians, perhaps Iberians, and possibly Persians.<note>1</note> A patriotic Egyptian might naturally enough describe a body thus composed by the contemptuous phrase 'Scythian or Indian or some such person from the neighboring barbarian lands.' <note>original: "Scythes aut Indus aut aliquis talis de vicina barbaria"</note> It should be remembered that the trade-route between Egypt and India traversed the Red Sea, and consequently the inhabitants of the southern coast-lands of the Red Sea—the "Happy Arabs" <note>original: Arabes Eudaemones; referring to the inhabitants of modern-day Yemen.</note> and the Axomites <note>People of the Kingdom of Aksum, located in modern Ethiopia and Eritrea.</note>, and perhaps Blemmyes <note>A nomadic tribal group from the Nubian region.</note> also—were, from the point of view of an Egyptian, neighbours of the Indians;<note>2</note> while the Armenians, Iberians, and Persians were neighbours of the Scythians. Moreover, the conquest of the country would probably give occasion for a large influx of Arab and other immigrants in addition to the armed forces; and if to these we add the hordes of the Blemmyes pouring in over the

capital was reduced after an eight months' siege.' This, however, cannot be the event referred to in the prophecy; for there was at this time no fresh invasion of *foreigners* <note>original: alienigenae</note>.

# THE LATIN ASCLEPIUS

southern frontier, there is quite enough to account for the words ‘Foreigners filling this land’ <note>original: "Alienigenis terram istam complentibus"</note>.

The loss of life caused by war and insurrection during these five years, and by the famine and disease that war brought with it, must have been enormous; and scenes such as those described by Dionysius <note>Dionysius of Alexandria, a 3rd-century bishop who wrote about the plagues and civil strife in the city</note> a few years earlier must have recurred again and again. It might well be said that ‘the land was filled with corpses’, and ‘the waters were polluted with blood’, and even (if we make some allowance for a prophet’s rhetoric) that ‘the dead were far more in number than the survivors’.

The inhabitants were divided into two factions, the one siding with the Palmyrenes <note>The Palmyrene Empire, led by Queen Zenobia, which broke away from Rome and conquered Egypt in 269-270 AD</note>, and the other opposing them. Thus the horrors of civil war were added to those of foreign invasion; ‘Egypt itself was infected with yet worse plagues’ than those inflicted by the barbarian invader, and ‘set an example of cruelty to the world’.

And lastly, the national religion was dying out. As we have already seen, the power which Christianity had acquired by <term>A. D. 260</term> <note>Anno Domini, "In the year of our Lord"</note>, and its rapid growth from that time onward, were enough to give a worshipper of the gods of Egypt cause to anticipate the total defeat and overthrow of his religion; and the violent disturbance of native traditions caused by the shock of the Palmyrene invasion must have further promoted that general abandonment of the old cults which was already in progress. The invaders and immigrants, who at this time ‘filled the land’, were doubtless worshippers of many different gods,¹ but all of them alike must have been strangers to the national religion of Egypt, and little disposed to venerate its rites. The Palmyrene rulers, if they did not directly promote the spread of the new faith, were at any rate not hostile to it;² and a devout Egyptian might well feel, when his land fell under their dominion, that Egypt was forsaken by the gods, and that the national religion, already much impaired by the encroachments of Christianity, was now indeed doomed to perish.

# INTRODUCTION

I think then that we may take it as established that the prophecy in chapters 24-26 of the *Asclepius* <note>A famous Hermetic treatise, originally in Greek but preserved largely in Latin, containing a famous "Lament" for the decline of Egyptian religion.</note> was written under the impression produced by the Palmyrene invasion of Egypt and the events connected with it. And as there is in the prophecy no hint that the foreigner will be expelled or dispossessed, and it seems to be assumed that his occupation of the land will be permanent ('he shall inhabit Egypt' <note>original Latin: "inhabitabit Aegyptum"</note>), it may be inferred that the passage was written either before the reconquest of the country for Aurelian <note>Roman Emperor from 270–275 AD who reclaimed Egypt from the Palmyrene Empire.</note> in 271, or at any rate, before the final suppression of the Palmyrene faction in 273. The writing of the prophecy then (with the exception of two sentences added after <term>A.D.</term> <note>Anno Domini; Year of our Lord</note> 353) must be assigned to the years 268-73.

It remains to be considered whether *Asclepius* III as a whole is of the same date. It is conceivable that the prophecy might have been inserted into an already existing document. But as chapter 26, which is closely connected with the preceding predictions, passes on without a break into the main current of the treatise, I do not think this hypothesis can be admitted. It is also conceivable that different parts of the prophecy itself might be of different dates—i.e. that the prediction of the extinction of the national religion (in chapters 25 and 26) might have formed part of an *Asclepius* III which was in existence before 268, and that the references to the Palmyrene invasion ('For by foreigners... he shall be seen as a stranger' <note>original Latin: "Alienigenis enim . . . videbitur alienus"</note>, if my rearrangement of the sentences is accepted) might have been subsequently inserted in 268-73. But against this it may be said, first, that the latter passage, if not absolutely needed for continuity, at any rate fits perfectly with its context, and supplies a cause for that decay of religion of which the writer goes on to speak; and secondly, that, since we have already found reason to think the writer's conviction of the impending doom of the national religion could hardly have arisen before <term>A.D.</term> 260, the dates of the two portions of the prophecy could in any case be separated by no more than a few years at most. I conclude therefore that this hypothesis also must be rejected, and consequently, that the Greek original of *Asclepius* III as a whole was written in <term>A.D.</term> 268-73.

*Circumstances of the writer of* ASCLEPIUS III. The author of *Asclepius* III must have been an Egyptian by race; he regards Egypt as his country, and his Hellenic <note>Greek-influenced culture and education.</note> education has not diminished the intensity of his national patriotism (chapter 24 b). Seeing that he localizes the cult of the god Asclepius <note>The Greek name for the Egyptian deity Imhotep, associated with healing.</note> (chapter 37) and the ancient cult

# THE LATIN ASCLEPIUS

of the Egyptian kings (chapter 27 d) at Arsinoe-Crocodilopolis, it seems probable that he resided in or near the Fayum <note>A fertile basin in Egypt, southwest of Cairo, known for its ancient irrigation and the cult of the crocodile god Sobek</note>. His keen interest in the national temple-cults, and his grief at the prospect of their suppression, suggest that he may have been an Egyptian priest. His approval of marriage (chapter 21) makes it unlikely that he was a member of a monastic brotherhood such as that to which the writer of *Asclepius* I presumably belonged. He shows a less unworldly disposition than that writer; he values the mundane benefits which the temple-gods confer; and his hearty love and admiration of the material universe (chapter 25) seems hardly consistent with the *contempt of the world* <note>original: "contemptus mundi"</note>, and aspiration to escape from the body, which his principles required him to profess. We may imagine him then to have been a priest attached to the temple of one of the local deities of the Fayum; and we may suppose that he had assimilated the Hermetic doctrine <note>A philosophical and religious system based on writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note> without ceasing to discharge his priestly functions and to take his part in social life, and that he found in that doctrine a justification of the worship in which his interests centred, and a means of defending it against the attacks of the Christians.

## Date of the composite *Perfect Discourse* <note>original: "Λόγος τέλειος" (Logos teleios)</note>. 

The Greek original of the Latin *Asclepius* as a whole was known to Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD) who often quoted pagan prophecies to support Christianity</note>, under the title *Perfect Discourse*, about <term>A. D. 310</term>. The redactor <note>An editor or compiler who brings different texts together</note> who joined together the Greek *Asclepius* I, *Asclepius* II, and *Asclepius* III to make a single dialogue must therefore have done his work at some time between <term>A. D. 270</term> and <term>310</term>. But *Corpus Hermeticum* IX announces itself as a sequel to the *Perfect Discourse*; and if, as seems probable, this title was given only to the composite document, and not to any of its component parts before they were joined together,<margin>¹ See notes on the beginning of the Latin *Asclepius* <note>original: "Ascl. Lat. init."</note></margin> the redactor's work must have been done before *Corpus Hermeticum* IX was written. We may conjecture then that the *Perfect Discourse* was compiled about <term>A. D. 280-90</term>, and that *Corpus Hermeticum* IX was written about <term>A. D. 290-300</term>. It is possible that the same person who compiled the composite *Perfect Discourse* proceeded to write *Corpus Hermeticum* IX as a sequel to it; if so, the date of both might be about <term>A. D. 290</term>.

It may be doubted whether the concluding prayer of the *Asclepius* (41 b) formed part of the original *Asclepius* III (written about <term>A. D. 270</term>), or was added by the compiler of the *Perfect Discourse*. This prayer has been borrowed by the sorcerer who wrote one of the magic incantations preserved in the *Mimaut Papyrus* (Reitzenstein, *Poimandres*, pages 151, 156). # INTRODUCTION

Thus the prayer may have been first written about <term>A.D.</term> 270-90, and borrowed by a sorcerer a little later.

*Date of the Latin translation.* The Latin *Asclepius* has come down to us among the works of Apuleius. Now Apuleius was born about <term>A.D.</term> 125, and wrote under Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, i. e. before <term>A.D.</term> 180. If, therefore, any good reason could be shown for attributing the translation to Apuleius, it would be necessary to reconsider our conclusion as to the date of the Greek original of *Asclepius III.*

Hildebrand (*Works of Apuleius*, 1842, vol. i, pp. xlix ff.) discusses the question whether the translation was written by Apuleius, dealing with it mainly on the ground of Latin style, and states his conclusion thus: <note>original: "hunc dialogum ab Apuleio confectum esse persuasum mihi quidem est. . . Demonstrasse mihi videor, dicendi rationem quae in hoc dialogo cognoscitur ab Apuleiana non esse alienam, ac pluribus locis cum ea concordare. Inde quamquam colligi per se nequit Apuleium revera huius dialogi esse auctorem, tamen cum accedat manuscriptorum auctoritas, qui optimi quique Apuleii nomen in fronte habent, non intelligo cur nostro scriptori hic liber abiudicandus sit."</note> "I am indeed persuaded that this dialogue was composed by Apuleius. . . I believe I have demonstrated that the manner of speaking recognized in this dialogue is not foreign to that of Apuleius, and in many places agrees with it. From this, although it cannot be inferred by itself that Apuleius is truly the author of this dialogue, yet since the authority of the manuscripts is added—the best of which have the name of Apuleius at the front—I do not understand why this book should be denied to our writer."

But the incompetence shown by our translator¹ is a strong argument against identifying him with Apuleius, who would surely have done the work better. Moreover, the method of translation in the *Asclepius* differs widely (as Hildebrand admits) from that of Apuleius in his version of the Aristotelian *On the Universe* <note>original: "De mundo"</note>.² In *On the Universe*, the translation is free and fluent; in the *Asclepius*, it is literal³ and clumsy.

It may be considered certain that Augustine, who knew our translation, did not suppose it to have been written by Apuleius. In quoting from it,⁴ he says <note>original: "Huius Aegyptii verba, sicut in nostram..."</note> "The words of this Egyptian, just as [they were translated] into our [language]..."

# THE LATIN ASCLEPIUS

‘*I shall set down what has been translated into our tongue*’ <note>original Latin: "linguam interpretata sunt, ponam"</note>, without naming the translator. But in the same passage Augustine speaks of Apuleius, and contrasts the view of Apuleius with that of ‘Hermes’ (that is, the view expressed in the *Asclepius*); if therefore he had thought the Latin *Asclepius* to be the work of Apuleius, he would have mentioned the fact—as he does elsewhere in the case of the *On the World* <note>original Latin: "De mundo"</note>.

I can therefore see no reason to dissent from Goldbacher,¹ who says, ‘*I am persuaded that the dialogue of Asclepius is wrongly included among the works of Apuleius*’ <note>original Latin: "Asclepi dialogum . . . iniuria inter Apulei opera referri mihi persuasum (est)"</note>. After speaking of the passage in Augustine, Goldbacher continues, ‘*Since other very weighty matters are added to this, which Bernays² explained, I should think there would be hardly anyone who would believe that this dialogue was translated from Greek into Latin by Apuleius*’ <note>original Latin: "Quo cum accedant aliae res gravissimae, quas Bernaysius . . . exposuit, haud quemquam fore putaverim, qui hunc dialogum ab Apuleio e Graeco in Latinum conversum esse existimet"</note>. The Latin *Asclepius* was, no doubt, attributed to Apuleius in the archetype of our manuscripts: but that attribution was an error. Consequently, there is nothing to set against the conclusion at which we have already arrived, namely, that the Greek original of *Asclepius* III was written in <term>A. D. 268-73</term> <note>The period of the Palmyrene Empire's rule over Egypt</note>; and the Latin translation must have been written at some time after that date.

The <term>limit before which</term> <note>original Latin: "terminus ante quem"; the latest possible date for an event</note> for the Latin translation is given by the fact that Augustine quotes from it in his *The City of God* <note>original Latin: "De civ. Dei"</note>, about <term>A.D. 413-26</term>. If the references to penal laws against Pagan worship are contemporary with the rest of the Latin text,³ the translation must be dated between 353 and 426. If those references have been subsequently <insert>interpolated</insert> <note>inserted later by a different hand</note> into the Latin text, any date between about 280 and 426 is possible for the translation.

*Who was the translator?* That question cannot be answered with certainty; but the only man known to us to whom the translation might with some probability be attributed is C. Marius Victorinus. Jerome, in *On Illustrious Men* <note>original Latin: "Vir. illustr."</note> 101: ‘*Victorinus, an African by birth, taught rhetoric at Rome under the Emperor Constantius (A. D. 350-61)*’ <note>original Latin: "Victorinus, natione Afer, Romae sub Constantio principe... rhetoricam"</note>

---

# THE LATIN ASCLEPIUS

...an old man and most skilled in all liberal doctrines, who had read and evaluated so many works of the philosophers, a teacher of so many noble senators, who even, on account of the mark of his excellent teaching... had earned and received a statue in the Roman Forum.’ <note>This quote describes Marius Victorinus, a 4th-century grammarian and philosopher who converted to Christianity late in life.</note> Boethius, *On Porphyry’s Isagoge*, Brandt (*First Edition*), I. 1: ‘that which Victorinus, the most learned orator of his time, is said to have translated by way of Porphyry’s *Isagoge* <note>original: "Isagogen"</note>, that is, through an introduction to Aristotle’s *Categories*.’ Boethius *in the same work* (*Second Edition*), 5. 24: ‘the sequence of this book was first indeed turned into Latin speech by the rhetorician Victorinus, but afterwards by us.’ Boethius found Victorinus’s translation of the *Introduction* <note>original: "Isagoge"</note> to be inaccurate,¹ and for that reason wrote a fresh translation of it for himself.

Victorinus then, in the course of a long life which ended soon after A. D. 362, was much occupied in the study of Pagan philosophy; he translated into Latin (presumably for the use of his pupils at Rome) ‘books of Platonists’, among which were some of the writings of Plotinus and Porphyry; and his translations were read by Augustine, who, since he did not read Greek, was dependent on them for his knowledge of Neoplatonism. Such a man would almost necessarily become acquainted with the Hermetic <term>Perfect Discourse</term> <note>original Greek: "Λόγος τέλειος" (Logos teleios); the Greek title for the work known in Latin as the Asclepius</note>, and might very well think it worth while to translate a document which contained doctrines so closely related to those of his Neoplatonic creed; and the fact, made known to us by Boethius, that he sometimes misunderstood his Greek original, and made mistakes in translation, adds to the probability of the hypothesis that our Latin *Asclepius* is his work. There is no positive evidence that it was so; but it may safely be said that the translator was either Victorinus or some one who had much in common with him.

Augustine, were probably Plotinus, *Enneads* i, 2, 3, 4, 6; iii, 2; and v, 1; and perhaps also Porphyry, *On the Return of the Soul to God* and *Sentences Leading to the Intelligibles* (<term>Starting Points for the Intelligibles</term> <note>original Greek: "Ἀφορμαὶ πρὸς τὰ νοητά" (Aphormai pros ta noēta)</note>).

# THE HERMETICA IN THE ANTHOLOGY OF STOBAEUS

<margin>1</margin> JOANNES STOBAEUS, at some date not far from A. D. 500, compiled a large collection of extracts from Pagan Greek writers. The collection was divided into four books, and was entitled *Four Books of Extracts, Sayings, and Precepts* <note>original: "ἐκλογῶν, ἀποφθεγμάτων, ὑποθηκῶν βιβλία τέσσαρα"</note>. It seems to have been made up by putting together the contents of earlier collections of extracts, and adding to them passages extracted by Stobaeus himself from books which he had read. He arranged the extracts in chapters according to subjects, and placed at the head of each chapter a superscription stating the subject of the extracts contained in it.

Photius (around A. D. 850) <note>A Byzantine scholar and Patriarch of Constantinople known for his vast library and summaries of ancient books.</note> read this *anthology* <note>original: "anthologium"</note> in a copy differing little from the original as written by Stobaeus; and in his *Library* <note>original: "Bibliotheca"</note>, p. 112 a, 16 ff., he describes it as a work in two volumes <note>original: "τεύχη" (teuche)</note>, consisting of four books <note>original: "βιβλία" (biblia)</note>, and gives the superscriptions of the 208 chapters into which the four books were divided.

Our manuscripts of Stobaeus are derived from an archetype <note>The original or most authoritative manuscript from which later copies are made.</note> closely resembling the manuscript used by Photius, if not from that very manuscript. But at some time not far from A. D. 1000, the two volumes of which the archetype consisted were separated; the two parts passed into different hands, and thenceforward, each of them was copied and recopied separately. Hence the first part (Books I and II) has come down to us in one set of manuscripts, and the second part (Books III and IV) in another set of manuscripts. The two parts consequently came to be edited separately, as if they were two different works; and the editors gave to Books I and II the title *Physical and Ethical Extracts* <note>original: "Eclogae physicae et ethicae"</note>, and to Books III and IV the title *Florilegium* <note>A "gathering of flowers," or a collection of literary excerpts.</note>. Either the term *Extracts* <note>original: "Eclogae"</note> or the term *Florilegium* might serve as a title for the whole (each extract, whether in Books I and II or in Books III and IV, is an

---

> 1 The latest writer quoted by Stobaeus is the Neoplatonist Hierocles, a contemporary of Proclus (A. D. 410-85). The fact that Stobaeus ignores all Christian writings makes it improbable that he lived much later than Hierocles (Christ, *History of Greek Literature* <note>original: "Gesch. der gr. Litt."</note>, p. 848).

# STOBAEUS

In their edition, what had hitherto been called *Stobaeus's Selections* is called *The first two books of the Anthology of Stobaeus*, and what had hitherto been called *Stobaeus's Flower-gathering* is called *The last two books of the Anthology of Stobaeus*; and their correction will doubtless be henceforth accepted by all scholars.

After the separation of the two parts of the *Anthology*, the first part (Books I and II) was reduced to smaller compass by an abridger <note>term: "epitomator" — a scribe or scholar who creates a shortened version of a larger work</note>, who had a preference for philosophical writings. He copied out almost in full Book I, chapters 1-30; but from that point onward as far as his handiwork can be traced (i.e. down to Book II, chapter 9), he omitted nearly all extracts except those from Plato, Aristotle, Archytas, Porphyry, and (fortunately for our present purpose) Hermes. The last part of his *abridgment* <note>original: "epitome"</note> (Book II, chapters 10-46) is lost. It is only this mutilated *abridgment* of Books I and II, and not the full text of these two books as read by Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar who recorded summaries of many books now lost</note>, that has come down to us in the manuscripts of Stobaeus. Some of the missing passages have, however, been recovered from a *collection of maxims* <note>term: "gnomologium" — a book of pithy sayings or moral quotes</note>, partially preserved in a Laurentian manuscript (fourteenth century), the compiler of which borrowed largely from the four Books of Stobaeus at a time when they were still complete; and from that source Wachsmuth has been able to print the text of Stobaeus, Book II, chapters 15, 31, 33, and 46.

Stobaeus seems to have got his *Hermetic writings* from (1) a collection of <term>Discourses of Hermes to Tat</term> <note>original: "Ἑρμοῦ λόγοι πρὸς Τάτ"</note>; (2) a collection of <term>Discourses of Hermes to Asclepius</term> <note>original: "Ἑρμοῦ λόγοι πρὸς Ἀσκληπιόν"</note>; (3) a collection of <term>Discourses of Hermes to Ammon</term> <note>original: "Ἑρμοῦ λόγοι πρὸς Ἄμμωνα"</note>; and (4) a collection of <term>Discourses of Isis to Horus</term> <note>original: "Ἑρμοῦ λόγοι Ἴσιδος πρὸς Ὧρον"</note>. The total number of Hermetic excerpts in his *Anthology* is forty-two,¹ if we include *Excerpts* [XXVIII] and [XXIX], and count as separate excerpts the two parts of Stobaeus 1. 41. 1 (which I call *Excerpt* II B and *Excerpt* XI), and the two parts of Stobaeus 1. 41. 6 (which I call *Excerpt* IV B and *Excerpt* III). Of these, ten are taken from *small books* <note>original: "libelli"</note> which have been preserved in the *Hermetic Corpus* (*Corpus* II, IV, and X); and one (Stobaeus 4. 52. 47)

The remaining thirty-one are given in the present edition as Excerpts I, II A, II B, III, IV A, IV B, V—[XXIX]. I have arranged and numbered them, grouping together the *Hermes to Tat* Excerpts (I–XI), the *Hermes to Ammon* Excerpts (XII–XVII), the Excerpts in which there is no indication of the pupil's name (XVIII–XXII), and the *Isis to Horus* Excerpts (XXIII–XXVII); and I have divided the longer Excerpts into numbered sections.

Twenty-seven of these ‘Excerpts’, as well as all the ten extracts from *booklets* <note>original: "libelli"</note> which are extant in the *Collection* <note>original: "Corpus"</note>, occur in Stobaeus <note>Joannes Stobaeus, a 5th-century compiler who preserved many ancient texts in his anthology.</note> Book I, and two (*Excerpt* I and *Excerpt* XVIII) in what remains of Stobaeus Book II. For the text of *Excerpt* I therefore we are dependent on the manuscripts <note>original: "MSS."</note> of Books III and IV (the so-called *Gathering of Flowers* <note>original: "Florilegium"</note>), and not on the manuscripts of Books I and II (the so-called *Selections* <note>original: "Eclogae"</note>). Wachsmuth <note>Curt Wachsmuth, a 19th-century German classical scholar.</note> has now restored these misplaced passages to their original positions in Book II, chapters 1, 4, and 2.

The other four Hermetic extracts (namely *Excerpts I, II A, XXVII*, and the fragment of the Greek original of the Latin *Asclepius*) have come down to us in the manuscripts of Stobaeus Books III and IV. The chief printed editions of Stobaeus are the following:
Books I and II: Canter (*first edition*), Antwerp, 1575; Heeren, 1792-1801; Gaisford, 1850; Meineke, 1860-3; and Wachsmuth, Berlin, 1884.
Books III and IV: Trincavelli (*first edition*), Venice, 1535-6; Gesner, 1st edition 1543, 2nd ed. 1549, 3rd ed. 1559; Gaisford, 1822; Meineke, 1860-3; and Hense, Berlin, 1894-1912.

Wachsmuth and Hense have investigated the manuscripts far more thoroughly than any of the previous editors; and the edition of the *Anthology* of Stobaeus which they have produced by their combined labours supersedes all earlier publications of the text. Their edition is my sole authority for the readings of the manuscripts in the Hermetic extracts.

In my text of the *Excerpts*, and in my textual notes on them, I have used the same notation as in the *short books* <note>original: "libelli"</note> of the *Corpus Hermeticum*.¹ The readings of P² I have treated as conjectures.

# INTRODUCTION

the further task of emending the more or less corrupt text of each extract as read by Stobaeus, and so recovering, as nearly as may be, the original text of the passage as written by its author. For the performance of this task also, Wachsmuth and Hense <note>Kurt Wachsmuth and Otto Hense were 19th-century German scholars who produced the definitive modern edition of Stobaeus.</note> have given valuable help; but much remains to be done; and it is this that, as far as the Hermetic extracts are concerned, I have aimed at doing in the present edition. Starting from the text of the archetype <note>The "archetype" is the lost common ancestor from which all surviving manuscript copies of a text are descended.</note> of the Stobaeus-MSS., as reconstructed by Wachsmuth and Hense, I have tried to discover or guess, firstly, what words the author of each Hermetic passage wrote, and secondly, what he meant by the words he wrote. When one has concluded that a phrase is corrupt, the best way to deal with it is usually to attack the second of these two problems first; i. e. to infer from the context, and from parallels in other writings, what the author must have meant, and thence, if possible, to infer what words he used to express his meaning. In a matter of this kind, complete success is unattainable; but there is much that can be done, and it is to be hoped that the process of recovering the thoughts of the Hermetic writers, to which I have tried to contribute, will be taken up and carried farther by others.

->Wachsmuth, vol. i, p. xx, says: "In the Hermetic fragments (the *Hermeticum*), I have held to this rule: that I should restore not those things which it was probable the authors themselves wrote, but only those things which it seemed Stobaeus had read in his own copy." <note>original Latin: "hanc normam tenui, ut non ea quae ipsos scripsisse probabile esset, sed ea tantum quae in exemplo suo Stobaeus legisse videretur restituerem."</note><-

# TESTIMONIES

The earliest evidence for the existence of writings of a similar character to our religious and philosophic *Hermetica* <note>The *Hermetica* are a body of Egyptian-Greek texts from the 2nd and 3rd centuries AD attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note> is that of Athenagoras, <term>A. D. 177-80</term>. But that evidence is not quite free from doubt; for the statement which Athenagoras apparently ascribes to Hermes, namely that he was descended from 'gods' who were men (that is, from men who were held to have become gods after death), might have occurred in any sort of document the teaching of which was attributed to Hermes, for example in a dialogue dealing with astrology or magic.

Tertullian, in his work *On the Soul, chapter 33*, quotes a passage from a writing of the same kind as our *Hermetica*. His obscure style makes it difficult to be sure what he means in the three passages in which he mentions Hermes Trismegistus without quoting him; but it may be inferred from *Against the Valentinians, chapter 15* and *On the Soul, chapter 2* that he knew of writings of which Hermes was supposed to have been the author, and which contained doctrines resembling those of Greek philosophers, and especially those of Plato. His evidence proves then that in <term>A. D. 207-13</term> some *Hermetica* similar to ours were in existence, and were accessible to Christian readers; but it does not prove that at that time any of the extant *Hermetica* had yet been written.

In the writings of Clement of Alexandria,¹ there is no mention of any Greek *Hermetica*. What is to be inferred from this fact? Large parts of Clement's *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromateis"</note> are occupied with discussions of the relation between Greek philosophy and 'barbarian' philosophy (by which he usually means the teaching of Moses and the Hebrew prophets). He seeks to prove that the Greek philosophers were later in date than the Hebrew writers, and 'stole' from them. If he had known our *Hermetica*, and believed them to contain the

¹ Clement taught in the Catechetical School of Alexandria from about <term>A. D. 190 to 202 or 203</term>. At the latter date he quitted Egypt; he was residing in Asia Minor about <term>A. D. 211</term>, and he died in or about <term>A. D. 216</term>. The dates of his chief writings are probably *Exhortation to the Greeks*, <term>A. D. 190-200</term>; *Miscellanies books 1-4*, *The Instructor*, *Miscellanies books 5-7* (in this order), <term>A. D. 203-16</term> (Harnack, *Chronology*, volume 2, pages 3-18).

# INTRODUCTION

teachings of an ancient Egyptian sage, he could not possibly have omitted to speak of them in the course of these discussions. He could not have failed to notice the resemblance between the Hermetic doctrines and those of Plato; and he would have said, as others did, ‘Plato borrowed from Hermes’.¹ His silence concerning the Greek *Hermetica* <note>The *Hermetica* are a body of philosophical and religious texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure blending the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth.</note> can therefore be accounted for only by assuming either that they were not yet in existence; or that they were in existence but unknown to him; or that he knew them, but knew them to be of recent date, and therefore had no more reason to speak of them than of other recent writings. Now the hypothesis that no such writings were yet in existence is excluded by the evidence of Clement’s contemporary, Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 220 AD).</note>, who quotes from a philosophic *Hermeticum*; and if writings of this character were known to Tertullian, it is most unlikely that they were unknown to Clement, whose work as a teacher in Alexandria must have brought him into contact with thinkers of all kinds that were to be found in Egypt, Pagans as well as Christians. It is therefore probable that Clement knew of the existence of some Greek *Hermetica* of the same character as ours, but knew them to have been composed by men of his own time, and therefore to have no bearing on the question what sort of doctrines were taught in Egypt before the beginnings of Greek philosophy.

Arguments *from silence* <note>original: "ex silentio"</note> are often of little weight; but in the case of Clement, the force of this argument will, I think, be evident to any one who reads the following passages. *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Strom." referring to Clement's *Stromata*</note> I. 15. 66-73 (a long list of Greek philosophers who were either barbarian by race or pupils of barbarian teachers). *Miscellanies* I. 21. 134 (an item in a long list of Pagan prophets): "But also among those who were once men among the Egyptians, but became gods in human opinion, were Hermes of Thebes and Asclepius of Memphis."² <note>original: "ἀλλὰ καὶ τῶν παρ’ Αἰγυπτίοις ἀνθρώπων ποτέ, γενομένων δὲ ἀνθρωπίνῃ δόξῃ θεῶν, Ἑρμῆς τε ὁ Θηβαῖος καὶ Ἀσκληπιὸς ὁ Μεμφίτης."</note> *Miscellanies* 5. 5. 29: "And in general Pythagoras and those of his school, along with Plato, more than any of the other philosophers..." <note>original: "καὶ ὅλως ὁ Πυθαγόρας καὶ οἱ ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ σὺν καὶ Πλάτωνι μάλιστα τῶν ἄλλων φιλοσόφων"</note>

Why did not Clement mention the much more evident resemblance between the doctrines of Plato and the Greek *Hermetica*? *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Stromata"</note> 5. 12. 78: Clement quotes Plato's *Timaeus* 28 C (for it is impossible to express the Father... <note>original: "τὸν γὰρ πατέρα . . . ἐξειπεῖν ἀδύνατον"</note>), and says that Plato got this thought from *Exodus* xix, where it is shown that God is invisible and inexpressible <note>original: "ἀόρατος καὶ ἄρρητος"</note>; and he compares some verses of Orpheus, who, he says, got the same truth from the same source. (Here follows a list of the different orders of Egyptian priests, and of the subjects dealt with in the ‘Books of Hermes’ which priests of the several orders were required to study.) There are, then, forty-two books of Hermes which are absolutely necessary; of these, thirty-six, containing the whole philosophy of the Egyptians, are learned by heart by the aforementioned priests, and the remaining six by the shrine-bearers <note>original: "παστοφόροι"</note>, these being medical books . . . and such, to speak briefly, are the affairs of the Egyptians; and the philosophy of the Indians, etc. Clement evidently means by ‘Books of Hermes’ books written in the Egyptian language, and ascribed to Thoth, which were used in the schools of the priests. The notion that the Egyptians believed in *reincarnation* was probably a false inference drawn by Greeks, in or before the time of Herodotus, from the observed fact that Egyptians reverenced certain kinds of animals, and thought it wicked to kill and eat them. A Greek, knowing that Pythagoreans abstained from the flesh of animals, would be apt to think that the reason for these strange Egyptian usages must be the same that Pythagoreans gave for their abstention, viz. that they believed that a human soul was or might be incarnated in the animal. Moreover, Greeks would be told by Egyptians that in each of the individual animals worshipped in the temple-cults (e. g. the Apis-bull) some god (e. g. Osiris), who had once reigned as a king on earth, was incarnated; and this might easily seem to the Greek visitor to be merely a particular instance of the doctrine of *reincarnation* taught by Pythagoras.

If he had believed any Greek *Hermetica* <note>The *Hermetica* are a body of philosophical and religious texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure blending the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth.</note> known to him to be translations or paraphrases of ancient and genuine ‘books of Hermes’, he would necessarily have referred to them here, as the best evidence accessible to him and his readers concerning the character of the ‘Egyptian philosophy’, instead of talking of the books studied by the priests, books which he could not read, and about which he knew very little.

We must conclude then that Clement either did not know of any Greek *Hermetica* such as ours, or else, as seems more likely, knew of some such writings (not necessarily any of those which have come down to us), but knew that they were of recent date, and that their contents could not be rightly attributed to the ancient teacher Hermes.¹

Did Origen (A. D. 185–255) <note>A prominent early Christian scholar and theologian from Alexandria.</note> know any philosophic or religious *Hermetica*? No quotations from or references to Hermetic documents have been found in his writings. Origen, like his teacher and predecessor Clement, repeatedly asserts that Moses and the Hebrew prophets were prior in time to the Greek philosophers, and says that, as far as there was any borrowing, it must have been the Greeks that borrowed from the Hebrews; but he does not discuss this question at length and in detail, as Clement does; and I do not know of any passages in Origen’s works in which the course of his argument is such that, if he had known any Greek *Hermetica* and thought the teachings contained in them to be Egyptian and of ancient date, it would have been necessary for him to speak of them.²

# TESTIMONIES

It may however be said of Origen, with even more confidence than of Clement, that if any such writings were current in his time, he must have been aware of their existence. Origen was born and brought up in Alexandria, and lived and taught there as head of the <term>Catechetical School</term> <note>The famous school of Christian theology in Alexandria, which sought to reconcile the Gospel with Greek philosophy.</note> (with some intermissions) from <term>A. D.</term> 203 to 230, after which he migrated to Palestine. He had a wide and thorough knowledge of Pagan philosophic writings, and especially of those of the Platonists, down to and including Numenius. Some have thought that he was for a time a pupil of Ammonius Saccas, and a fellow-pupil with Plotinus (who was junior to him by about eighteen years). Statements to that effect seem to have arisen out of a confusion between the Christian Origen and a Pagan Platonist of the same name. But be that as it may, the fact remains that he was living in Egypt at the same time as Ammonius Saccas and Plotinus; that he *may* have been personally acquainted with one or both of them; and that he *must* have got his Platonism from the same sources that they did, or from similar sources. Among the sources from which he got it, were any *Hermetica* <note>The collection of philosophical and religious texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> included? That question we have no means of answering. There are in his writings many passages which, in the thoughts expressed, closely resemble passages in our *Hermetica*; but I have found no instances of verbal resemblance of a kind that could be held to prove direct borrowing; and the resemblances in thought prove nothing more than that both Origen and the Hermetists were familiar with Platonism.

In any case, Origen’s writings are of special significance for the study of the *Hermetica*, because he lived at the very time during which we have reason to think that most of the earlier of our extant *Hermetica* were written. He was a Platonist as well as a Christian.¹ The Platonism that is to be found in his writings is intermixed with allegorical interpretations of Bible texts, but it can, for the most part, be disentangled from them without much difficulty;² and we

---

But to any one who knew our *Hermetica*, and thought them to be ancient, it would have seemed much more evident that Plato had learnt some things from *them*.

# INTRODUCTION

The date of the sentence concerning Hermes in Cyprian (?) *That Idols are Not Gods* <note>original: "Quod idola [dii non sint]"</note> is so uncertain, that no inference can safely be drawn from it.

The author of the *Exhortation to the Greeks* <note>original: "Cohortatio ad Graecos"</note> (probably <term>A. D.</term> <note>Anno Domini; Year of our Lord</note> 260-302) quotes Hermes from the *Excerpts of Stobaeus I*; and if the conjecture 'Agathos Daimon' <note>original: "Αγαθοῦ δαίμονος" - The "Good Spirit," a frequent teacher in Hermetic texts.</note> for 'Akmon' <note>original: "Ἄκμωνος"</note> is accepted, he also knew a Hermetic dialogue in which Agathos Daimon was the teacher.

The earliest Pagan *testimony* <note>original: "testimonium"</note> is that of Porphyry, who, in his *Letter to Anebo*, written in the latter part of the third century, said that he had met with some philosophic *Hermetica* (*Response of Abammon* 8. 4 a: "in the writings which you say you have encountered . . . for those things circulating as the works of Hermes, etc." <note>original: "ἐν τοῖς συγγράμμασιν οἷς λέγεις περιτετυχηκέναι . . . τὰ μὲν γὰρ φερόμενα ὡς Ἑρμοῦ κ.τ.λ."</note>).

It might perhaps be argued that the Greek *Hermetica* may have been for some considerable time kept secret (as is enjoined in some of them), that is, may have been passed from hand to hand within the small groups of men for whose instruction they were written, but concealed from all others; and that they may therefore have been in existence long before they became known to outsiders. But that seems improbable. Among 'seekers after God', such as were the authors of our *Hermetica* and their pupils, conversions to Christianity must have been frequent; and a Hermetist who had become a Christian would no longer have any motive for concealing the writings which he had previously held sacred. There was therefore nothing to prevent these documents from becoming widely known soon after they were written.

We find then that the external evidence agrees with and confirms the conclusion to which the internal evidence points, namely, that most of the extant *Hermetica* were written in the course of the third century after Christ, and that few of them, if any, can have been written long before <term>A. D.</term> 200.

That most of them, if not all, were in existence at the end of the third century, is proved by the evidence of Lactantius.

The treatise of Lactantius *On the Workmanship of God* <note>original: "De opificio dei"</note>, his larger work *Divine Institutes* <note>original: "Divinae institutiones"</note>, and his treatise *On the Wrath of God* <note>original: "De ira dei"</note> were written between <term>A. D.</term> 303 and 311.<note>1</note> The contents of the *Divine Institutes* are

Lactantius must therefore have drawn from a source other than Cicero and Varro, and other than the Stoic writings of which Cicero and Varro made use. In that *Hermetic work*, beauty must have been spoken of side by side with utility. The only extant Hermetic passage in which the construction of the human body by God is dealt with is *Hermetic Corpus* V. 6; and that’, says Brandt (mistakenly, as it seems to me), ‘cannot be the passage referred to in the *Divine Institutes at the place cited*, because it speaks only of the beauty of the bodily organs, and not of their utility. From the time of Lactantius onward, the existence of religious or philosophic *Hermetica*, and the resemblance of the doctrines taught in them to those of Platonism, were widely known among the Christians. In the course of the Arian controversy <note>A major theological dispute in the 4th century regarding the nature of Christ's divinity.</note> of the fourth century, disputants on both sides referred to these documents. (See Marcellus of Ancyra and Pseudo-Anthimus.) They were read by Didymus (<term>A. D. 380-93</term>), and by Cyril of Alexandria (<term>A. D. 435-41</term>). Augustine (<term>A. D. 413-26</term>) read the *Latin Asclepius* in the translation which has come down to us, but does not appear to have read any other *Hermetica*. He did not read Greek; and the *Perfect Discourse* <note>original: "Λόγος τέλειος" (Logos teleios)</note> was probably the only *Hermeticum* that had in his time been translated into Latin. Lactantius, Augustine, and Cyril took for granted the antiquity and authenticity of the *Hermetica*; and it does not appear that any doubt on that point arose among Christians thenceforward down to the time of Casaubon <note>Isaac Casaubon (1559–1614), the scholar who eventually proved the Hermetica were written in the post-Christian era rather than in ancient Egypt.</note>.

The Pagan Neoplatonists paid little attention to the *Hermetica*. Porphyry spoke of them in his *Letter to Anebo*, but there is no reference to them in any of his extant writings. The author of *Abammon’s Reply* <note>original: "Abammonis responsum", better known as "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians" by Iamblichus.</note> shows knowledge of them in his reply to Porphyry. But with these exceptions, the *Hermetica* <note>The collection of philosophical and religious texts attributed to the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus.</note> are ignored in Neoplatonic literature.¹ Seeing that the doctrines set forth in the Hermetic writings are closely connected with those taught by Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD).</note> and his successors, we might have expected the Neoplatonists to be keenly interested in these documents. Why did they neglect them, and prefer to accept as inspired scriptures the *Chaldaean Oracles* and the *Orphic poems*, which would seem to us far less suitable for their purpose? Probably because they knew that the attribution of the *Hermetica* to the ancient prophet Hermes was an error. Porphyry <note>A student of Plotinus and a rigorous scholar.</note> was too good a scholar and critic to be misled in this matter; he must have seen them to be what in fact they are, namely, documents written by Egyptian Platonists in his own time, or very shortly before it. The author of *The Response of Abammon* <note>original: "Abammonis resp."; likely referring to Iamblichus's 'On the Mysteries'.</note> knew at least that they were not written by Hermes (that is implied by his phrase <note>original: "τὰ φερόμενα ὡς Ἑρμοῦ"</note> "the works circulated under the name of Hermes," 8. 4 a, which he may have taken over from Porphyry); though he mistakenly thought that they correctly reproduced the meaning of doctrines taught in books written by ancient Egyptian priests. The later Neoplatonists, if they were aware that the *Hermetica* were of recent date, would have little reason to refer to them; for all that was acceptable to them in the teaching of the *Hermetica* was to be found more fully worked out in Plotinus.

Some of our *Hermetica* were known to the alchemist Zosimus (A. D. 300–50?). Stobaeus, *c.* A. D. 500, had access to the whole mass of *Hermetica*, and made copious extracts from them. About the same time Fulgentius happened to meet with *Corpus* I; and the *Perfect Discourse* <note>original: "Λόγος τέλειος" (Logos teleios), also known as the Asclepius.</note>, and at least one other *Hermeticum*, were read by Lydus, *c.* A. D. 550. From that time onward the Greek *Hermetica*

---

¹ Malalas (Migne, vol. 97, col. 512) says that in A. D. 367–83 "Theon the most wise philosopher" <note>original: "Θέων ὁ σοφώτατος φιλόσοφος"</note> (that is, no doubt, Theon of Alexandria, the father of Hypatia) "taught and interpreted the astronomical works, and the writings of Hermes Trismegistus, and those of Orpheus." <note>original: "ἐδίδασκε καὶ ἡρμήνευε τὰ ἀστρονομικά, καὶ τὰ Ἑρμοῦ τοῦ τρισμεγίστου συγγράμματα, καὶ τὰ Ὀρφέως."</note> (See note on Hermetic fragments in Stobaeus, *Excerpts* [XXIX].) But we are not told that ‘the writings of Hermes Trismegistus’ on which Theon commented were philosophic or religious; they may have been writings on astrology or some other kind of ‘occult’ science.

Cyril of Alexandria (Migne, vol. 76, col. 548 B; see *Testimonies*) says that some man, whom he does not name, ‘composed at Athens the fifteen books entitled *Hermaica*’ <note>original: "Ἑρμαϊκά"</note>; and he quotes from the first book of that work (which seems to have been written in the form of a dialogue) a passage, put into the mouth of an Egyptian priest, in which it is said that Hermes was the founder of Egyptian civilization and science. But we do not know how long before Cyril’s time the work called *Hermaica* was written; we know nothing about its contents except the extract quoted by Cyril; and in that extract nothing is said of Hermes as a teacher of philosophy or religion.

# TESTIMONIA

seem to have been little known and seldom read, until they were brought to light again in the revival of learning which took place at Constantinople under the lead of Psellus <note>Michael Psellus (11th century), a Byzantine philosopher and historian who revived interest in Platonic and Hermetic thought.</note>. In that interval (A. D. 550-1050) most of them perished; and (apart from extracts and quoted fragments) those only survived which were, at some date unknown to us, put together to form the *Corpus Hermeticum* <note>The primary collection of Greek Hermetic writings.</note>. The Latin *Asclepius* may have owed its preservation to the fact that it was mistakenly ascribed to Apuleius <note>Author of 'The Golden Ass'; the 'Asclepius' was often bundled with his philosophical works in medieval manuscripts.</note>, and handed down together with his writings.

But while the reputation of Hermes as a philosopher and teacher of religion dwindled in Europe, it lasted on undiminished in another region. The centre in which it most strongly maintained itself, and from which it spread afresh, was Harran,¹ an important city in northern Mesopotamia, situated on the main road between Babylonia and the West. When Christianity, in the course of the fourth century, became the dominant religion in the neighbouring regions of the Roman empire, the majority of the Harranians refused to be converted, and continued to worship in their heathen temples as before;² so that Harran came to be spoken of by Christians as a 'city of Pagans' <note>original: "Ἑλλήνων πόλις" (Hellenon polis) — literally 'City of the Greeks,' a term used by early Christians to mean 'City of Pagans.'</note>.³ When Syria and Mesopotamia were invaded and conquered by the Arabs (A. D. 633-43), a large part of the Harranians were still Pagans; and under Moslem rule they adhered to their religion with the same pertinacity. We hear little of them for nearly two centuries; but they emerge into light again in the reign of the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mún (son of Hárún ar-Rashíd). In A. D. 830, al-Mamun, setting out from Bagdad, his
