According to Chwolsohn, the people called ‘Sabians’ by Mohammed were the Mandaeans, a sect residing in the marsh-lands near the head of the Persian Gulf. (See Brandt, *Mandaean Religion*, 1889, and *Mandaean Writings*, 1893.) These people called themselves Mandaeans, a name derived from *mandâ*, which means <term>knowledge <note>original Greek: ἡ γνῶσις (he gnosis)</note></term>; but their neighbours called them Sabians, a Semitic word meaning ‘people who wash themselves’, or ‘baptists’. A few thousands of Mandaeans were still to be found in the neighbourhood of Basra in the nineteenth century; but they are probably by this time almost, if not quite, extinct. The sect may have been in existence as early as the second century A. D. Their scriptures are written in an Aramaic dialect, and contain a mixture of Babylonian, Jewish, and Zoroastrian ingredients, slightly modified by Christian influence. These writings, in the form in which they are now extant, may perhaps have been composed about the seventh or eighth century A. D., but were doubtless compiled out of documents of earlier date. In the ninth century, so little was generally known about this sect, that it was possible for the Pagans of Harran, who had no connexion whatever with them, to claim the name of Sabians without fear of contradiction, and thereby to get for themselves a legal status similar to that of Jews, Christians, and Magians (i. e. Zoroastrians) under Moslem rule.

There is, however, some doubt whether Chwolsohn was right in identifying the ‘Sabians’ of the Koran with the Mandaeans. De Goeje (*Acts of the 6th International Congress of Orientalists*, Pt. ii, section 1, Leyden, 1885, p. 289) says that the people called Sabians in the Koran were ‘a Christian sect strongly impregnated with Pagan elements, the Elkasaïtes, who existed in Babylonia, and who, while having much resemblance to the Mandaeans, are not identical with them, as Chwolsohn thought they were’. But whether the sect denoted by the name Sabians before A. D. 830 was that of the Mandaeans or some other, it was in any case a sect with which the Pagans of Harran had nothing to do.

They called themselves Sabians, and were thenceforward officially recognized by the Moslem government as entitled to toleration under that name.<note>The superscript 1 refers to the footnote below.</note>

But in order to make good their claim to this legal status, it was necessary for them not merely to call themselves by a new name, but also to put forward a Book on which it could be said that their religion was based, and a Prophet or Prophets to whom the contents of that Book had been revealed. sagacious tolerance, Mamun recognized no distinction of creed or race; all his subjects were declared eligible for public offices, and every religious distinction was effaced. . . . Carra de Vaux, *Avicenna*, p. 30, tells a story (reported by Masudi <note>Al-Masudi, a famous 10th-century Arab historian and geographer.</note>) of a group of Manichaeans arrested and put to death as heretics by Mamun’s order.

<margin>1</margin> Hence, from <term>830 AD</term> <note>original: "A. D. 830"</note> onward, the name Sabians had a new and different meaning. Some Arabic writers were aware that there were people ‘in the marshes’ near the head of the Persian Gulf who were called Sabians; but the name was henceforward more commonly used to denote the Harranian Pagans. And since these were the only Pagans with whom the Moslem Arabs of the Baghdad region were directly or personally acquainted, the name Sabians came to be habitually used (from about <term>1000 AD</term> <note>original: "A. D. 1000"</note> onward) to signify Pagan polytheists or ‘star-worshippers’ in general. (The Arabs were inclined to think that all Pagans were star-worshippers; this notion they probably got by generalizing from what was known to them about the local cults of Harran.) An Arabic writer says, for instance, that Constantine was converted from ‘Sabism’ to Christianity; and another says that Pharaoh was a ‘Sabian’.

The name ‘Sabians’ then had three different meanings. (1) Before <term>830 AD</term>, it meant the Mandaeans, or some other sect of similar character. (2) From <term>830 AD</term> to about 1000, it meant the Harranian Pagans. (3) From about <term>1000 AD</term> onward, it meant Pagans in general, of all places and all times. But most Moslems were not aware of these distinctions; and it is often difficult to decide whether an Arabic writer is using the name in the second or the third sense.

# INTRODUCTION

Now the religion of the Pagan Harranians of the ninth century was the indigenous religion of heathen Syria, more or less modified by Hellenic <note>Greek</note> and perhaps by Persian and other influences. For the mass of the people, religion must have been, there as elsewhere, a matter of cult <note>ritual practice</note> far more than of doctrine. Of the local cults of Harran some descriptions have come down to us in Arabic writings; but these are mostly vague and meagre, and some of the more definite statements are evidently due either to gross misunderstanding or to malicious invention. We learn from them, however, that there was at Harran a temple of the Moon-god Sîn,¹ and that among the deities worshipped by the Harranians the seven planet-gods were prominent; and there are also descriptions of a cult² which seems to show some resemblances to Mithraism <note>A mystery religion centered on the god Mithras, popular in the Roman Empire</note>.

But there were among the Pagans of Harran learned men who were well acquainted with Greek philosophy; and in those times Greek philosophy meant a religious philosophy founded on Plato and Aristotle—that is, in one word, Neoplatonism.³ The religion

¹ The cult of the Moon-god Sîn must have been firmly rooted at Harran ever since what may be vaguely called ‘the time of Abraham’; and this Harranian cult was in high repute under the Roman empire. D. 363, Julian, halting at Harran on his way to war against the Persians, worshipped in the temple of the Moon-god (Ammianus Marcellinus 23. 3. 1). This worship seems to have continued without intermission under Moslem rule, until the temple of Sîn at Harran was finally destroyed, either in A. D. 1032, or according to another authority, at the time of the Tartar invasion in A. D. 1230.

Boys were admitted into a crypt, and were there terrified by weird sounds and voices. Women were excluded from the rites. There was a sacrament in which cakes were eaten (we are told that these cakes were made of meal mixed with the blood of a slaughtered baby; but that is doubtless a calumny, like similar accusations against the early Christians; and in both cases alike, the accusation may have been based on a too literal interpretation of symbolic actions and metaphorical phrases used in the ritual); and there was also a sacramental drinking of some liquid out of seven cups.
In this description there is much that reminds one of Mithraism. It must have been in some region not far distant from northern Mesopotamia that the Mithraic cult which spread over the Roman empire first took shape; and after it had spread westward, it might have been brought back to that same region and revived there by Roman soldiers and merchants.

And when the Pagan Harranians were required, on pain of death or merciless persecution, to name a Book on which their religion was based, it would necessarily fall to the learned men among them to find an answer to the question, and to speak on behalf of the whole body. They might have said with some truth that their religion (i. e. the philosophic religion of these learned men themselves, though not the religion of the mass of Pagans) was based on Plato’s Dialogues; but they preferred to name what were believed to be the more ancient writings from which Plato had derived his wisdom—that is, the Greek *Hermetica*. ‘Our Scriptures’, they must have said to the Moslem officials, ‘are the Hermetic writings; and our Prophets are those whose teaching is recorded in those writings, namely, Hermes Trismegistus, and his teacher Agathos Daimon <note>Greek for "Good Spirit"</note>.’¹

The Moslems did not set any fixed limit to the number of ‘prophets’ acknowledged by them (among those whom they recognized as prophets were Adam, Seth, Enoch, Noah, Abraham, &c., and we are told by one authority that the total number of prophets amounted to 313, Chw. i. 626); and there might be no great difficulty in adding two more to the list; but it would be easier to get these two accepted if they could be identified with prophets already well known to Mohammedans. It was probably for this reason, and at the suggestion of Harranians, that Agathodaimon came to be identified with Seth son of Adam, and Hermes with Idrīs, whom Moslems held to be identical with Enoch (*Koran* 19. 57 and 21. 85).

The fact that the Harranian Pagans, when required to name a Scripture, chose the *Hermetica*, proves that in A. D. 830 a collection of *Hermetica* was known and read in Syria; and the fact that they named Agathodaimon as a prophet together with Hermes proves that their collection included some dialogues (now lost, and known

# INTRODUCTION

It may be inferred from the occurrence of the names Tat, Asclepius, and Ammon in conjunction with that of Hermes in Arabic writings,¹ that these Harranians <note>A pagan community in Upper Mesopotamia known for preserving Hellenistic star-worship and philosophy.</note> had in their possession Hermetic *booklets* <note>term: libelli (small books or treatises)</note> in which the pupils were so named; and among these were presumably some that are now lost, as well as those which have come down to us.

In the ninth century, Hermetic documents were most likely known to some scholars at Harran in the original Greek; but the *Hermetica* <note>The body of philosophical and magical writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> had probably been translated into Syriac <note>A dialect of Aramaic used as a literary and liturgical language by Christians in the Near East.</note> long before that time, and were doubtless usually read in Syriac by Harranians and their neighbours at Edessa and elsewhere.²

---

¹ 'Tat son of Hermes' is repeatedly spoken of in Arabic writings; and Asclepius is mentioned as one of the prophets recognized by the Harranians (Chwolsohn, i. 229, ii. 523, etc.), and is called a follower of Hermes (Chw., i. 243). Of Ammon there is at least one mention; al-Qifthī, A. D. 1248 (Chw., i, p. 787, and ii, p. 533), wrote a book containing, *among other things* <note>original: "inter alia"</note>, biographies of Idris (that is, Hermes), *King Amon*, Asclepius, Empedocles, and Plato.

² We know from Ephraim the Syrian <note>original: "Ephraim Syrus," a prominent 4th-century Christian theologian and hymnwriter.</note> (see *Testimonies*) that *Hermetica* were known in Syria *around* <note>original: "c." (circa)</note> A. D. 365, and that at that time a Syrian who probably did not read Greek had some knowledge of their contents (but perhaps only at second hand). De Boer, *History of Philosophy in Islam*, 1901, says that translation of secular <note>original: "profane"</note> writings from Greek into Syriac began in or about the fourth century. In the fifth century, there was in Edessa a flourishing academy, furnished with a large library of Greek and Syriac books (Chw., i. 172-4), and there can be little doubt that among those books were the *Hermetica*. We hear of works of Aristotle translated into Syriac in the fifth century (Chw., *ibid.* <note>original: "ib." (in the same place)</note>). The school at Edessa, having become infected with Nestorianism <note>A Christian doctrine deemed heretical by the Roman Church, which emphasized the disunion of Christ's divine and human natures.</note>, was suppressed by the emperor Zeno in A. D. 489 (C. de Vaux, *Avicenna*, p. 41), and there seems to have been thenceforward no one central seat of learning for Syrian Christians; but the work which had been centred at Edessa was still carried on in other Syrian cities (for example, at Nisibis). Meanwhile, Harran was the chief seat of learning for Syrian Pagans, and continued to be so down to the end of the ninth century. The Arabs got their knowledge of Greek science and philosophy partly from Syrian Christians (orthodox, Monophysite, and Nestorian), but (from A. D. 830 onward, if not before) partly also from Syrian Pagans of Harran.

Masudi (*according to* <note>original: "ap." (apud)</note> C. de Vaux, *Avicenna*, p. 38) reports from a lost work of al-Farabi (who died in A. D. 950) the following sketch of the history of learning: 'The chief seat of human knowledge was transferred from Athens to Alexandria in Egypt. The emperor Augustus, after destroying Cleopatra, established two centres of teaching, Alexandria and Rome; the emperor Theodosius put a stop to the teaching at Rome, and brought back the whole of it to Alexandria. Under Omar son of Abd-el-Aziz (A. D. 705-10), the chief seat of teaching was transferred from Alexandria to Antioch; and later on, in the reign of Mutawakkil, it was transferred to Harran.' The caliph Mutawakkil, 'the Nero of the Arabs', was a drunken debauchee, and a rigidly orthodox Mohammedan (Ameer Ali, *Short History*, p. 288). Why is he, of all people, mentioned in this connection? Apparently because it was in his reign (A. D. 847-61) that the learning of the Harranians first became widely known among the Arabs. From the time of the Arab conquest until A. D. 830, the date at which their religion was granted legal recognition, the learned Pagans of Harran had been forced to remain in concealment.

# TESTIMONIA

From that time onward, for about two centuries (A. D. 850-1050), we hear much of the Harranian Pagans. Some of them rose to positions of high eminence, and played an important part in the intellectual life of Bagdad <note>Modern Baghdad, the capital of the Abbasid Caliphate and a major center of medieval learning</note>.

The most famous of them is Thabit ibn Qurra,¹ who was born A. D. 835, and died *c.* A. D. 901. During the earlier part of his life he resided in Harran, as a money-changer. But shortly before A. D. 872, there was a schism in the community² of ‘Sabians’, as the Harranian Pagans were now called; Thabit’s party was defeated, and he was expelled, and forced to leave the city. After some years he settled at Bagdad, was introduced to the caliph, and attained to high favour at court; and he got the government to recognize him and his companions as a separate and independent community of ‘Sabians’, with a head of its own.³ Most of the learned men of Harran probably migrated to Bagdad and joined him. The community thus established at Bagdad must have been a sort of school of Pagan Neoplatonism,⁴ in some respects analogous to the school of Pagan Neoplatonism which had flourished at Athens until suppressed by Justinian about 350 years before.⁵ But there

# INTRODUCTION

were doubtless considerable differences; and one of the differences was this, that whereas the Neoplatonists of Athens had ignored the *Hermetica* <note>A collection of mystical and philosophical texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, the Harranian Neoplatonists of Bagdad recognized the *Hermetica* as their 'Scripture', and regarded the Hermetic teaching as the source whence their philosophy was derived.

Thabit lived on at Bagdad, occupied in teaching and writing, till his death about <term>A. D. 901</term> <note>The year 288 in the Islamic calendar</note>. We are told that towards the end of his life he was forced to become a Mohammedan; but his sons remained Pagans, and the Pagan community which he had founded in Bagdad continued its activities after his death.

Thabit's work as a writer extended over a wide range of subjects. He is spoken of as highly distinguished in mathematics, astronomy, logic, and medicine, as well as in philosophy. His mother tongue was Syriac, but he knew also the Greek and Arabic languages. Barhebraeus <note>A famous 13th-century Syriac scholar and bishop</note> says that Thabit wrote about 150 works (translations included?) in Arabic, and 16 in Syriac. He translated Greek writings, and corrected earlier translations made by others; and according to an Arabic writer, it was said that 'no one would have been able to get any benefit from the philosophic writings of the Greeks, if they had not had Thabit's translations'.$^1$ Among his writings on philosophy and logic were the following: a *Treatise on the argument ascribed to Socrates* <note>original: "Tractatus de argumento Socrati ascripto"</note>; a *Treatise on the solution of the mysteries found in Plato's Republic* <note>original: "Tractatus de solutione mysteriorum in Platonis Republica obviorum"</note>; a translation of part of Proclus's commentary on the *Golden Verses* <note>original: "Aurea carmina"</note> of Pythagoras; an *Introduction to logic* <note>original: "Isagoge in logicam"</note>; commentaries on Aristotle's *On Interpretation* <note>original: "Περὶ ἑρμηνείας"</note>, and a part of Aristotle's *Physics* <note>original: "Φυσικὴ ἀκρόασις"</note>; extracts from *Aristotle's Categories*, *Prior Analytics*, and *On Interpretation*. But he was, like the Neoplatonists of Athens, interested in Pagan cults (more especially, perhaps, but not exclusively, the local cults of Harran), as well as in philosophy; and under this head may be placed the following titles given in the list of his writings: *Book on the law and canons* (ceremonial law and ritual?) *of the Pagans* <note>original: "Liber de lege et canonibus... ethnicorum"</note>; *Book on the burial of the dead*; *Book on the confirmation of the Pagan religion*; *Book on purity and impurity*; school either at Athens or at any other place'. Is it certain that Damascius did not settle down at Harran and teach there? He could hardly find any other place where he would feel so much at home as in that 'city of Pagans'. He was a Syrian, born at Damascus, whence he got his name.

*The Book of Animals Fit for Sacrifice*; *The Book of the Hours of Prayer*; *The Book of Readings to be Recited, Adapted to Each of the Seven Planets*; *The Book of Repentance and Supplication*; *The Book of the Religion of the Sabians*; *The Book of the Laws* <note>original: "legibus"</note> (ceremonial regulations?) *of Hermes, and of the Prayers* <note>original: "orationibus"</note> used by the Pagans <note>original: "ethnici"</note>. From one of these books (perhaps the *Book of the Confirmation of the Religion of the Pagans*) must have been taken the following passage, quoted from Thabit by Barhebraeus <note>A 13th-century Syriac Orthodox scholar and historian</note>: ‘We are the heirs and propagators of Paganism. . . . Happy is he who, for the sake of Paganism, bears the burden (of persecution?) with firm hope. Who else have civilized the world, and built the cities, if not the nobles and kings of Paganism? Who else have set in order the harbors and the rivers? And who else have taught the hidden wisdom? To whom else has the Deity revealed itself,¹ given oracles, and told about the future, if not to the famous men among the Pagans? The Pagans have made known all this. They have discovered the art of healing the soul; they have also made known the art of healing the body. They have filled the earth with settled forms of government, and with wisdom, which is the highest good. Without Paganism the world would be empty and miserable.’

Thabit seems to have also dabbled in the ‘occult’ sciences; he paid some attention to astrology, and he wrote a commentary on a ‘Book of Hermes’ concerning the *doctrine of letters and names* <note>original: "doctrina litterarum et nominum"</note>—probably a treatise dealing with the cryptic significance or magic efficacy of letters of the alphabet.² It is very likely that he knew other books also on such subjects (e.g. on astrology) that were ascribed to Hermes, and assumed them to have been written by the same Hermes that he believed to be the author of the teachings recorded in the religious and philosophic *Hermetica* <note>A collection of Greek and Latin texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, blending Egyptian and Greek philosophy</note>.

Thabit’s son Sinán was a physician of high repute, and held by official appointment the position of head of the medical profession in Baghdad. Masudi <note>A famous 10th-century Arab historian and geographer</note> says that Sinan had a thorough knowledge of mathematics, astronomy, logic, metaphysics, and the philosophic systems of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle.

Chwolsohn (i. 577 sqq.) enumerates twenty-seven other ‘Sabians’ (i. e. Harranian Pagans) whose names have been preserved. One of them, al-Battáni (A. D. 877–918), was a famous astronomer and mathematician, known as Albategnus in medieval Europe.³

# INTRODUCTION

It appears that the ‘Sabians’ <note>A religious group from Harran who identified as "Sabians" to gain protected status under Islamic law; they were renowned for their knowledge of Greek science and philosophy.</note> lived on at Baghdad, and continued to be known there as a separate sect, for about 150 years after the death of Thabit <note>Thabit ibn Qurra (d. 901 AD), a famous Sabian mathematician and astronomer.</note> (A. D. 900-1050). At that time the ‘Golden Age’ of the great caliphs (al-Mansur, ar-Rashid, and al-Mamun, A. D. 754-833) was past, and the vast empire over which they had ruled had fallen to pieces. The decline may be said to have begun in the reign of Mutawakkil, *c.* A. D. 850. There was a period of confusion, in the course of which caliphs at Baghdad were helpless in the hands of Turkish praetorians <note>Elite Turkish guard units who exerted significant political control over the caliphs.</note>, and provincial governors made themselves independent and established local dynasties. But shortly before A. D. 950 one of these local rulers, a son of Buwayh, who had got possession of a large part of Persia, made himself master of Baghdad; and thenceforward (until the coming of the Seljuks in 1055) the Buwayhids governed there as ‘Mayors of the Palace’, and the caliphs, reduced to impotence, retained only a shadowy dignity as pontiffs. Thus during the greater part of the century A. D. 950-1050 Baghdad was under a tolerably firm and settled government, and though shorn of much of its earlier glory, was still the chief city of a considerable dominion (Mesopotamia, Iraq, and western Persia).

During these political changes, students pursued their work without intermission, some at Baghdad, and others at the place of residence of this or that local dynast; and it was not until after the political decline had begun that Arabic learning reached its highest level.

In the intellectual activity of A. D. 900-1050 the Sabians of Baghdad took their part. During that time, or at least during the earlier part of it, there was still under Muslim rule much freedom of thought; and non-Muslims, though subject to occasional ill-usage or annoyance, were often well received at court, and found the highest careers open to them. But from about A. D. 1050 we hear no more of these Sabians; and their disappearance is probably to be accounted for as the result of a gradual increase in the strictness with which Mohammedan <note>An older term for Islamic.</note> orthodoxy was enforced.

Among ‘the two and seventy jarring sects’ <note>A reference to a famous line from the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam regarding the many divisions within religion.</note> of Islam, there were, and had been from the first, two main tendencies in conflict. There was a school of theologians (the ‘orthodox’ theologians as they may be called) who relied wholly and solely on the authority of

<margin>on the *Four Books* <note>original: "Tetrabiblos"</note> of Ptolemy, and revised the *Greatest Compilation* <note>original: "Almagest"</note> and several works of Archimedes’.</margin>

# TESTIMONIA

revelation—that is, on what God had revealed to Mohammed—and refused to diverge from this or go beyond it; and opposed to them there was a school of ‘liberal’ theologians, who, while accepting the authority of the Koran <note>The central religious text of Islam, believed by Muslims to be a revelation from God.</note>, claimed a right to the use of human reason in the interpretation of the sacred text, and exercised that right to a varying extent. In the ninth century, when the Arabs had got access to Greek learning, there arose, side by side with the two schools of theologians, a third school, that of the ‘philosophers’.¹ Philosophy meant, for the Arabs, not a search for truth in any direction, but adherence to those philosophic doctrines which they had learnt from the Greeks—that is, to Neoplatonism <note>A strand of Platonic philosophy that emerged in the 3rd century, heavily influencing early Christian and Islamic thought with its mystical focus on "the One."</note>; so that the ‘philosophers’ were, in fact, a sect among other sects. They were professedly Mohammedans (differing in this from the Sabians, who were not Mohammedans in any sense), and they did not openly reject the Koran; but they disregarded it as far as they could with safety, and when obliged to take notice of it, contrived some sort of compromise between their Neoplatonic doctrines and those of Moslem theology. Meanwhile, the liberal theologians also read the philosophic writings, and got from them arguments which they employed in their controversies with the more rigidly orthodox. Thus the ‘orthodox theologians’ and the ‘philosophers’ came to stand opposed to one another as the two extremes, while the ‘liberal theologians’ held an intermediate position between them.

Under the great caliphs <note>The civil and religious leaders of the Muslim community who succeeded the Prophet Mohammed.</note>, the liberal theologians had, on the whole, the upper hand, and men of all ways of thinking could express their opinions openly. But as time went on, the orthodox party grew in strength, and asserted itself more and more. The tenets of this party, or of a comparatively moderate section of it, were formulated by al-Ashari (who died <term>935 AD</term> <note>original: "A. D. 935"</note>, that is, about half a century after the founding of the Sabian community in Bagdad); and his followers, known as ‘the Asharites’, carried on the struggle until they brought it to a victorious conclusion. From the school of the Asharites issued Ghazali (<term>1058-1111 AD</term>), who ‘crushed the philosophers’, and finally established the system of Mohammedan orthodoxy which has, in the main, been in force from his time down to our own day.

# INTRODUCTION

Thus, about <term>A. D. 1050</term> <note>The mid-11th century, a period of increasing religious orthodoxy in the Islamic Caliphate</note>, the forces hostile to freedom of thought were already prevailing. Men such as the <term>Sabians</term> <note>A group of pagans from Harran who claimed the Hermetic writings as their scripture to gain "People of the Book" status under Islamic law</note> of whom I have been speaking could no longer venture to speak out; they could escape ill-treatment only by remaining in obscurity; and they were probably soon absorbed into the mass of orthodox <term>Moslems</term>.

Now the time at which the Sabians disappear at <term>Bagdad</term> (*c.* <term>A. D. 1050</term>) is just about the time at which documents of the *Corpus Hermeticum* <note>The foundational collection of Greek texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, after an interval of five centuries during which nothing has been heard of them in Europe, reappear at <term>Constantinople</term>, in the hands of <term>Psellus</term> <note>Michael Psellus (1017–1078), a Byzantine monk, scholar, and politician who led a revival of Greek philosophy</note>. Is there not something more than chance in this? It may be that one of the Sabians of Bagdad, finding that his position under Moslem rule was becoming unendurable, migrated to Constantinople, and brought in his baggage a bundle of Greek *Hermetica*—and that our *Corpus* is that bundle. If so, the line along which the *libelli* <note>original: "libelli" — small books or treatises</note> of the *Corpus* have been transmitted to us from <term>Egypt</term> runs through <term>Harran</term> and Bagdad. This is merely an unproved hypothesis; but it is one that agrees well with the facts known to us. The Pagans of Harran almost certainly possessed the whole collection of *Hermetica* (including many documents that are not now extant) in Greek, at the time when they adopted these writings as their Scriptures, in <term>A. D. 830</term>; and there can be little doubt that <term>Thabit</term> <note>Thabit ibn Qurra, a famous 9th-century Sabian mathematician and translator</note>, who was a good Greek scholar, still had a copy of them in Greek at the end of the ninth century. During the 150 years which had since elapsed, knowledge of Greek must have almost, if not quite, died out at Bagdad, and the *Hermetica* must have been now read only, or almost only, in <term>Syriac</term> or <term>Arabic</term> translations. But a man such as the Sabian I am supposing would, even if he did not himself know the Greek language, have good reason to preserve with care, and to take with him when he migrated to a place where Greek was spoken, any portions of his Scriptures, in the original Greek, that had chanced to escape destruction and to come into his hands; and it is just such a chance collection of specimens that we have in the *Corpus*.

Moreover, if we choose to indulge in yet further conjectures, there is nothing to prevent us from supposing that it was the arrival in Constantinople of a few such Sabian <term>Neoplatonists</term> <note>Followers of a mystical form of Platonic philosophy that flourished in late antiquity</note> from Bagdad, and the writings which they brought with them, that first started that revival of Platonic study in which Psellus¹ took the leading

Al-Kindi (who died about <term>873 AD</term> <note>original: "A. Shahrastani (died <term>1153 AD</term>), Katibi (died <term>1276 AD</term>), and other Arabic writers give summaries of the philosophic teaching of the Harranian Sabians; and the contents of these summaries are probably derived (either directly or through Muslim intermediaries) from some of the writings of Thabit and his associates. The doctrines which these Arabic writers ascribe to the Harranian Sabians are for the most part such as are to be found in our *Hermetica*, or might have been found in *Hermetica* now lost; but we have no means of knowing whether the Sabian writers got them from the *Hermetica*, or from Platonic sources of the same kind as those from which the Hermetists drew.

Among the Arabic writers whose *testimonies* <note>original: "testimonia"; evidence or historical witnesses</note> are known to me, the only one who shows any considerable knowledge of the contents of the Greek *Hermetica* is the mystic Suhrawardi (died <term>1191 AD</term>). The statements of Arabic writers concerning Hermes show that, down to the twelfth century and later, his name was widely known among them, and was held in high repute as that of a teacher of philosophic religion; but they add nothing to our knowledge of the Greek *Hermetica*. There has come down to us, however, one document which may be called an Arabic *Hermeticum*; namely, *Hermes on the Chastisement of the Soul* <note>original: "Hermes de castigatione animae"</note>, a translation of which is given at the end of the *Testimonies*. There are many passages in it which contain teaching that closely resembles that of some of the Greek *Hermetica*. It seems probable that most of these passages are extracts from the writings of men who knew the Greek *Hermetica* (or Syriac or Arabic translations of them), and that some of them have been translated, with little alteration, from Greek originals. It is possible that some of these Greek originals were *Hermetica*; but it cannot be said with certainty of any passage in the *Chastisement of the Soul* that it is a translation of a Greek *Hermeticum*.

# TESTIMONIA

contains a <term>gnomologium</term> <note>A collection of maxims or aphorisms, from the Greek 'gnome' (opinion/maxim) and 'logos' (word).</note> in which are reported *sayings* <note>original: "dicta"</note> of several sages (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, etc.), one of whom is Hermes. Among the thirty-six sayings ascribed by him to Hermes are the following: 'Desire is slavery; renunciation is freedom.' 'He who publicly reprimands any one deserves blame and contempt.' 'Let nothing of the advantages which the Creator has given you be small in your eyes, that you may not lose that which is already given.' 'Leave the liar and his company, for you get nothing that is of use from him; he is like the mirage in the desert, which shines, but does not quench your thirst.' 'He who scorns another on account of his sins finds no forgiveness.' 'For the merciful, the repentance of the offender is a sufficient advocate.' 'Death is like an arrow (that is already) in flight, and your life lasts only until it reaches you.' 'The height of magnanimity is to be merciful to fools.' Gnomic sayings such as these have nothing to do with the Greek *Hermetica* <note>The philosophical and religious treatises attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note>. It is evident that the name Hermes has here been employed at random, and it is a mere chance that these sayings are ascribed to him, and not to Socrates or some other sage. This document therefore is, for our present purpose, significant only as showing that in the ninth century Hermes was, in the circle to which Honein <note>Hunayn ibn Ishaq (809–873 AD), a famous scholar and translator in Baghdad.</note> belonged, reputed a 'wise man' in the same sense as the chief Greek philosophers.

Bardenhewer, in his introduction to the *Chastisement of the Soul* <note>original: "Castig. an." (Castigatio animae)</note>, says that there is an unpublished writing of Mubashshiri b. Fatik (*Catalogue of the Library of the Academy of Leiden* <note>original: "Cat. bibl. Acad. Lugd.-Bat."</note> iii, p. 342) which contains a *collection of sharp sayings* <note>original: "collectio acute dictorum"</note> (doubtless a <term>gnomologium</term> resembling that of Honein), and in which *Hermes plays a serious role* <note>original: "Hermes gravem agit personam"</note>; and that there are other similar and partly identical Arabic collections of gnomic sayings.

<note>The name "Poimandres" is often interpreted as "Shepherd of Men," though it may derive from an Egyptian phrase meaning "Knowledge of Ra."</note>

Once on a time, when I had begun to think about the things **1** that are, and my thoughts had soared high aloft, while my bodily senses had been put under restraint by sleep,—yet not such sleep as that of men weighed down by fullness of food or by bodily weariness,—methought there came to me a Being of vast and boundless magnitude, who called me by my name, and said to me, ‘What do you wish to hear and see, and to learn and come to know by thought?’ ‘Who are you?’ I said. ‘I,’ said he, ‘am **2** Poimandres, the Mind of the Sovereignty <note>original: "the Mind of the Sovereignty" refers to the supreme divine power or Absolute.</note>.’ ‘I would fain learn,’ **3** said I, ‘the things that are, and understand their nature, and get knowledge of God. # CORPUS HERMETICUM

**30** As for me, I recorded within myself the benefit received from Poimandres <note>The "Shepherd of Men," a divine being representing the Mind of the Sovereignty</note>, and having been filled with what I desired, I was exceedingly glad. For the sleep of my body became the sobriety of my soul, and the closing of my eyes became true vision, and my silence became pregnant with the Good, and the barrenness of my speech <note>original: "aphoria" - a state of being unable to produce words</note> became the birthing of good things. This happened to me because I received from Poimandres—that is, from the Mind of the Sovereignty—the Word <note>original: "Logos"</note>, through which I became divinely inspired <note>original: "theopnous"</note> and arrived at the truth.

Therefore, I give praise to God the Father with all my soul and strength.

**31** Holy is God, the Father of all things, who exists before the beginning.
Holy is God, whose will is accomplished by His own powers.
Holy is God, who wishes to be known, and is known by His own.

Holy are You, who by the Word <note>Logos</note> established all things that exist.
Holy are You, whom nature has not darkened.
Holy are You, of whom all nature is an image.

Holy are You, who are stronger than all domination.
Holy are You, who are greater than all excellence.
Holy are You, who are beyond all praise.

Accept pure spiritual sacrifices from a soul and heart stretched out toward You, O Unspeakable, Unutterable One, who is invoked by silence.

**32** Grant my prayer that I may not fall away from the knowledge <note>original: "gnosis"</note> that fits our essence; and empower me, so that by obtaining this grace, I may enlighten those of my race who are in ignorance—my brothers, and Your sons.

And I inscribed in my memory the benefaction of Poimandres <note>The "Shepherd of Men," a personification of Divine Mind</note>; and I was exceeding glad, for I was fed full with that for which I craved. > ‘Holy is God the Father of all, who is before the first beginning; <note>i.e., who was before the world began to be.</note>
> holy is God, whose purpose is accomplished by his several Powers;
> holy is God, who wills to be known, and is known by them that are his own.
> Holy art Thou, who by thy word hast constructed all that is;

> holy art Thou, who art greater than all pre-eminence;
> holy art Thou, who surpassest all praises.

> I pray that I may never fall away from that knowledge of thee which matches with our being; grant Thou this my prayer. And put power into me, that so, having obtained this boon, I may enlighten those of my race who are in ignorance, my brothers and thy sons.

<meta>This page begins Libellus II of the Corpus Hermeticum, a foundational text of Hermetic philosophy. It follows the introductory Poimandres (Libellus I) and initiates a dialogue between the sage Hermes Trismegistus and his disciple Asclepius regarding the nature of motion, space, and the divine.</meta>

CORPUS HERMETICUM

->*BOOK II*<-

### 〈The Discourse of Hermes Trismegistus to Asclepius.〉

**1** Everything that moves, O Asclepius, is it not moved in something and by something? — *Certainly.* — And must not that in which it moves be larger than the thing being moved? — *It must.* — [Therefore, the mover is stronger than the moved. — *It is indeed stronger.* — ] And must not that in which it moves have a nature contrary to the nature of the thing being moved? — *Entirely so.* —

**2** Great then is this universe <note>original: "kosmos"</note>, than which there is no larger body. — *That is agreed.* — And it is solid; for it is filled with many other great bodies, or rather, with all bodies that exist. — *That is the case.* — And is the universe a body? — *It is a body.* —

**3** And is it moved? — *Certainly.* — How large then must the space be in which it moves, and of what nature? Must it not be much larger, so that it can accommodate the continuity of the motion, and so that the thing moved is not cramped by the narrowness and have its motion hindered? — *It must be something immense, O Trismegistus.* — And of what nature? Must it not be of the contrary nature, O Asclepius? And the nature contrary to body is the incorporeal <note>The "incorporeal" refers to that which has no physical substance or dimensions, often equated here with the void or the divine mind.</note>. — *That is agreed.* — Space, therefore, is incorporeal.

**4b** Now the incorporeal is either something divine || or it is God. By "something divine" I do not mean that which is generated, but that which is ungenerated. If, then, it is something divine, it is essential <note>original: "ousiodes"; having the nature of essence or being.</note>; but if it is God, it becomes even beyond essence <note>original: "anousiaston"; transcending the category of substance or being.</note> [...]. In another sense, space is intelligible <note>original: "noetos"; capable of being understood by the mind/intellect rather than the senses.</note>; for it is intelligible...

---

II. 6b-9: Stobaeus 1. 19. 2, volume i, page 163 W (*Eclogues* I. 398 H): "From Hermes, from the discourse to Asclepius. Everything that moves not in... carries two bodies."
II. 10-13: Stobaeus 1. 18. 3, volume i, page 158 W (*Eclogues* I. 386 H): "In the same (namely, Hermes from the discourses to Asclepius). Not one of the things that are... to each one of all things that are."
Manuscripts of Stobaeus: **F** (Farnesinus, 14th century), **P** (Parisinus, 15th century).

# BOOK II

->*BOOK II*<-

### A discourse of Hermes Trismegistus to Asclepius.

<margin>1</margin> *Hermes.* Is it not true of everything which is moved, Asclepius, that it is moved *in* something, and is moved *by* something?— *Asclepius.* Assuredly.—*Herm.* And is not that in which the thing is moved necessarily greater than the thing moved?—*Ascl.* Yes.—*Herm.* And that in which the thing is moved must be of opposite nature to the thing moved.—*Ascl.* Certainly it must.—

<margin>2</margin> *Herm.* Now this <term>Kosmos</term><note>The universe conceived as a perfectly ordered and harmonious system.</note> is great; there is no body greater than the Kosmos.—*Ascl.* Agreed.—*Herm.* And it is massive; for it is filled with many other great bodies, or rather, with all the bodies that exist.—*Ascl.* It is so.—*Herm.* And the Kosmos is a body, is it not?—*Ascl.* Yes.—*Herm.* And a thing that is moved?—*Ascl.* Assuredly.—*Herm.* Of what magnitude then <margin>3</margin> must be the space in which the Kosmos is moved? And of what nature? Must not that space be far greater, that it may be able to contain the continuous motion of the Kosmos, and that the thing moved may not be cramped through want of room, and cease to move?—*Ascl.* Great indeed must be that space, Trismegistus.—*Herm.* And of what nature must it be, <margin>4 a</margin> Asclepius? Must it not be of opposite nature to the Kosmos? And of opposite nature to body is the incorporeal.—*Ascl.* Agreed.—*Herm.* That space then is incorporeal.

<margin>4 b</margin> Now that which is incorporeal is either something that appertains to God, or else it is God himself. (By 'a thing that appertains to God' I mean, not a thing that comes into being, but a thing without beginning.) If then the incorporeal thing is something that appertains to God, it is of the nature of eternal substance; but if it is God himself, it must be distinct from substance, <unclear>(. . .)</unclear>.¹ Space is an object of thought, but not in the <margin>5</margin>

# THE HERMETIC CORPUS

God is primarily for himself, but space <note>original: "topos"</note> exists for us, not for himself. For that which is intelligible <note>capable of being understood by the mind</note> is intelligible to the one who thinks. [God falls under the category of perception] Therefore, space is not intelligible to itself—for it is not [something other than the thing being thought] thought by itself—but it is intelligible to us. [[It is something else **6 a**]] [For this reason it is thought by us]. But if space is intelligible, it is not so in the same way as God, [but space] [and if God is not like space] but rather as a containing energy <note>original: "energeia chorētike," a capacity to hold or contain things</note>, then space is something other than God.

**6 b** Everything that is moved is moved not in something that is moving, but in something that stands still. Even the mover itself stands still; for it is impossible for it to be moved along with the object it moves.

—How then, O Trismegistus <note>Hermes "Thrice-Greatest"</note>, are the things here <insert>that move</insert> moved along with the things being moved? For you said that the wandering spheres <note>the planets</note> are moved by the fixed sphere <note>the firmament of stars</note>.

—That is not, O Asclepius, a "moving-with," but a "counter-movement"; for they do not move in the same way, but in opposition to one another. This opposition <insert>of movement</insert> has the resistance <note>original: "antereisin"</note> of the movement standing still; **7** for the reaction <note>original: "antitypia," or striking back</note> is the stillness of the motion. Therefore, the wandering spheres, moving in opposition to the fixed sphere, are moved by one another through the contrary encounter, driven by the very opposition of the stationary force. And it is impossible for it to be otherwise. For these Bears <note>the constellations Ursa Major and Minor</note> that you see, which neither set nor rise, [but turn around the same point,] do you think they move or stand still?

—They move, O Trismegistus.

—What kind of movement, O Asclepius?

—The kind that turns around the same point.

—But a revolution around the same point is a movement held fast by stillness. For "around the same" prevents "beyond the same," and if "beyond the same" is prevented, <insert>if it stands still</insert>, it results in "around the same." Thus, the contrary motion **8 a** stands firm, supported by its own opposition. I will give you an example that falls right before your eyes, I mean the animals on earth. For instance, the—

->CORPUS HERMETICUM<-

Consider a man swimming: for as the water is carried along, the resistance of his feet and hands becomes a point of stability <term>stasis; a state of standing still or rest</term> for the man, so that he is not carried away with the water. —The example is clear, O Trismegistus.—

<margin>8 b</margin> Therefore, all motion is moved within stability and by stability. <note>The text has a small lacuna or gap here in the original Greek.</note> Thus the motion of the cosmos, and of every material living being, does not happen to be caused by things outside of the body, but by things within moving toward the outside—namely by the soul, <insert>or spirit</insert>, or some other incorporeal <term>non-physical</term> thing. For a living body is not moved <insert>by a body</insert>; nor is a body moved at all, even if it is <margin>9</margin> inanimate <term>without a soul or life-force</term>. —How can you say this, O Trismegistus? Are not wood and stones and all other inanimate things the bodies that do the moving?— Not at all, O Asclepius. For that which is inside the body, which moves the inanimate thing, is not itself a body. That internal force is what moves both things: the <insert>body</insert> of the one carrying and the thing being carried. <insert>Since</insert> an inanimate thing, by itself, moves nothing. You see, then, how the soul is weighed down when it alone must carry two bodies. <insert>So</insert>, it is now clear both in what things move, and by what they are moved.—

<margin>10</margin> But must not things that move, move in a vacuum <term>kenon; an empty void</term>, O Trismegistus? —Speak words of good omen <note>original: "Εὐφήμει" (Euphemei); a ritual command to avoid unlucky speech, similar to "Hush!" or "God forbid!"</note>, O Asclepius. Not one of the things that exist is empty; only that which does not exist is empty. <insert>For that which exists</insert>, by the very logic of its existence, <insert>can never become empty</insert>. That which is could not be "being" if it were not full of existence. —Are there then no empty spaces, O Trismegistus, such as an empty jar—

Thus it is that you see the soul distressed by the weight of its burden, when it bears two bodies at once.

I have now explained to you what is that *by which* things are moved, as well as what is that *in which* things are moved.—

Nothing that is, is void; it is only that which is not, that is void. # CORPUS HERMETICUM

...is an empty jar, or a ceramic vessel, or a <insert>whole river</insert>, or a wine-vat, and all other such things? <note>Hermes is challenging the common perception of "emptiness" by listing common containers.</note>—Alas for such a great error, Asclepius! Those things which are actually the most full and most complete,

**11** do you consider these to be empty?—How do you mean, O Trismegistus?—Is the air not a body?—It is a body.—And does this body not permeate through all things that exist, and by permeating them, fill them? And does a body not consist of a mixture of the four bodies <note>The four classical elements: earth, water, air, and fire.</note>? Therefore, all the things you call empty are actually full of air; and if they are full of air, they are full of the four bodies. It follows that the opposite of your argument is revealed: that all those things you call "full" are actually empty of air, because they are crowded by other bodies and have no space to receive the air. Therefore, these things which you say are empty should be called "hollow," not empty; for they are full of existence [of air and spirit].—Your argument is irrefutable, O Trismegistus.—

**12 a** What then shall we call the Place in which the universe moves? We call it incorporeal, Asclepius.—Then what is this "incorporeal"?—It is Mind, a whole consisting entirely of itself, containing itself, free from the <term>error of the body</term> <note>original: "somatikēs planēs" — referring to the deceptive nature of physical matter</note>, impassible, untouchable, standing fixed within itself, capable of containing all things and the preserver of all beings, the light of the soul.—

**12 b** What then do you say the Good is?—The archetypal light, of which Mind and Truth are like the rays. <note>Hermes uses the metaphor of the sun to explain the relationship between the ultimate Good and human intellect.</note>

# BOOK II

of an empty jar, or pot, or . . . ,<gloss>1. Perhaps, ‘mortar’ <note>original Greek: ὅλμος</note></gloss> or trough, and the like? Are not such things void?—*Hermes.* How far you are in error, Asclepius! Do you suppose these things to be void? The truth is rather that they are completely full.—*Asclepius.* What do **11** you mean, Trismegistus?—*Hermes.* Is not air a body? <note>In ancient physics, "body" refers to anything made of matter that occupies space.</note>—*Asclepius.* Yes.—*Hermes.* And does not that body permeate all things that are, and fill them by its permeation? And are not bodies composed of a mixture of the four elements? <note>Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> All things that you call void then are filled with air; and if with air, they are filled with all four elements. Thus we are led to a conclusion opposite to what you said; we must say that all those things which you call full are void of air, because the presence of other bodies in them leaves no space unoccupied, and so they have no room to admit the air. Hence the things which you call void ought to be called hollow, not void; for they are full of something that exists.—*Asclepius.* There is no gainsaying that, Trismegistus.—

*Hermes.* Now what was it that we said <gloss>2. See section 4a.</gloss> of that Space in which **12 a** the universe is moved? *Asclepius.* Tell me then, what is the Good?—*Hermes.* The Good is **12 b** the archetypal Light; and Mind and Truth <gloss>3. Or ‘Reality’.</gloss> are, so to speak, rays emitted by that Light.—

->CORPUS HERMETICUM<-

**13** What, then, is God? — He is that which is neither of these <note>original: "μηδέτερον τούτων" — referring to the categories of being and non-being or specific material qualities discussed previously</note>, but who is the cause of being for them, and for all things, and for each individual thing among all that exists. For He left nothing behind, except that which is non-existent. All things that come to be <note>original: "γινόμενα" — things in a state of becoming or generation</note> arise from the things that exist, not from the things that do not exist. For things that do not exist do not have the nature of being able to become anything, but rather the nature of not being able to become anything. And conversely, things that exist do not have the nature of ever not being. God, therefore, is not Mind <note>original: "νοῦς" — the higher intellect or divine consciousness</note>, but is the cause of Mind’s existence. <insert>He is not Spirit, but the cause of Spirit’s existence; He is not Light, but the cause of Light’s existence.</insert>

**14** Therefore, one must worship God with these two names, which belong to Him alone and to no one else. For neither any of the others called "gods," nor any humans, nor any spirits <note>original: "δαιμόνων" — daemons, intermediary beings between gods and humans</note> can be good in any degree whatsoever, except God alone. <insert>And He alone is this, and nothing else.</insert> All other things are incapable of containing <note>original: "ἀχώρητά" — unable to receive or hold</note> the nature of the Good. For they are body and soul, which have no place capable of containing the Good.

**15** For the magnitude of the Good is as great as the existence of all things that are, both bodily and incorporeal, both sensible <note>perceived by the senses</note> and intelligible <note>perceived by the mind</note>. And this is God alone, and nothing else. Do not, therefore, call anything else "good" <insert>except God alone</insert>, for you would be impious; nor ever call God anything else except "the Good," for again you would be impious.

**16** Now, the word "Good" is spoken by everyone, but what it actually is is not understood by everyone. For this reason, God is not understood by everyone either. Out of ignorance, people call both the gods and certain humans "good," though they can never be so, nor could they ever become so.

# BOOK II

*Asclepius.* What then is God?—*Hermes.* God is He that is neither **13** Mind <note>original: "Nous"</note> nor Truth,¹ but is the cause to which Mind and Truth,¹ and all things, and each several thing that is, owe their existence. Nothing is left over, except that which is not. And all things that come into being come out of things that are, not out of things that are not. For not such is the nature of things which are not, that they can come to be something; their nature is such that they cannot come to be anything. And not such is the nature of things which are, that they can ever cease to be. God is not Mind then, but the cause to which Mind owes its being.

And so, in our worship of God, we ought to call him by **14** these two names;² they belong to Him alone, and to none beside him. None of the other beings called 'gods', nor any man or <term>daemon</term> <note>In this context, a "daemon" refers to a spirit or lesser divine being, not necessarily an evil entity.</note>,³ can be good in any degree. God alone is good; all other things⁴ are incapable of containing such a thing as the Good. Neither body nor soul has room enough in it to contain the Good; for such is the greatness of the Good, that it is **15** coextensive with the existence of all things that are, things <term>corporeal</term> <note>Physical or bodily things.</note> and things <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Spiritual or non-physical things.</note>, objects of sense and objects of thought together. And God is the Good, and nothing but the Good.⁵ Call nothing else good then, nothing but God; it would be impious. And never call God anything but the Good; that also would be impious. All men speak of the good, but some **16** do not understand what the Good is; and hence it is that some do not understand what God is. And in their ignorance they call the gods good, and they call certain men good; whereas gods and men can never be good, and cannot possibly become good.

---

¹ Or 'Reality'.
² Namely 'God' and 'the Good'. But the writer of section 17 a took the two names to be 'the Good' and 'the Father'.
³ Perhaps, 'None of the other beings, whether men or daemons, that are called good'.
⁴ Perhaps, 'can be good in any degree, but God alone. <insert>God is good, inasmuch as he gives all things and receives nothing;</insert> but all other things', etc.
⁵ Or perhaps, 'And God alone <note>original: "monos"</note>, and nothing but God, is the Good'.

->THE HERMETIC CORPUS<-

For the Good is entirely foreign to these things <note>referring to material or worldly qualities mentioned on the previous page</note>, and it is inseparable from God, being God himself. Now, all the other gods <note>original: "theoi"; here referring to the celestial bodies or lesser divinities</note> are called good [immortal] because they are honored with the title of God. But God is called the Good not as a matter of honor, but by his very nature. For the nature of God is one with that of the Good [and they are of one kind, from which all other kinds of things arise]. [For God is good, as he gives all things and receives nothing.] [Therefore, God gives all and receives nothing.] Therefore, God is the Good, and the Good is God.

<margin>17 a</margin> The other title for him is "Father," again because of his power to create all things; for it is the part of a father to create. For this reason, the procreation of children is the greatest and most sacred concern in life for those who think rightly. It is the greatest misfortune and impiety for someone to depart from human life childless; <insert>such a person is cursed by the Sun.</insert> This person pays the penalty to the spirits <note>original: "daimosin"; in this context, these are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits who execute divine justice</note> after death. The punishment is this: the soul of the childless person is condemned to enter a body that has the nature of neither man nor woman. [[Such a person is cursed by the Sun.]] Therefore, Asclepius, do not congratulate anyone who is childless, but on the contrary, pity their misfortune, knowing what punishment awaits them.

<margin>17 b</margin> Let these things, and things of this kind, be said to you, Asclepius, as a sort of foreknowledge of the nature of all things.

### The Sacred Discourse of Hermes Trismegistus.

That God is the first of all things, and the universe is divine, and nature is divine.

<margin>1 a</margin> God is the Beginning of all beings, and of mind, and of nature, and of matter; <insert>having made all things</insert> for the manifestation of his wisdom, being the Beginning of all. Nature is the <insert>activity</insert> of the divine, functioning by necessity, and for the sake of an end, and for renewal.

# BOOK II

<meta>catchword: 2806</meta>

For the Good is utterly alien to gods and men; <note>The translator suggests the original Greek might have meant: "they call certain men good; whereas men can never truly be so."</note> but it is inseparable from God, for it is God himself. All the other gods are called good merely because men have sought to honour them by giving them a title which belongs to God; but God is called the Good not by way of honouring him, but because that is his nature; for the nature of God is one and the same with the nature of the Good. God then is the Good, and the Good is God.

<margin>17 a</margin>
And <note>This section was likely added by a later commentator or different author.</note> the other name of God is 'Father'. He is called the Father, because he is the maker or begetter of all things; for it is the part of a father to beget. And for this reason the begetting of children is held by those who think aright to be the most weighty concern in human life, and the most pious of deeds. That a man should depart from life and leave no child is a great misfortune, and a great sin; it is a thing accursed in the sight of the Sun. Such a one is punished by the <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, daemons are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or divine agents who oversee the soul's journey.</note> after death; and the punishment is this, that the soul of the man who has no child is condemned to enter a body that is neither that of a man nor that of a woman. Therefore, Asclepius, never be glad on behalf of any man that he is childless, but pity his misfortune, knowing what manner of punishment awaits him.

<margin>17 b</margin>
Let this suffice. What I have taught you to-day, Asclepius, is a beginning of knowledge of the nature of all things.

->*BOOK III*<-

### A holy discourse of Hermes Trismegistus. <note>The original manuscripts for this Book are highly corrupted and required significant reconstruction to be intelligible.</note>
### *That God is the first of all things, and the universe is divine, <note>Meaning derived from or dependent upon God.</note> and nature is divine.*

<margin>1 a</margin>
God is the source of all that is; He is the source of mind, and of nature, and of matter. To show forth his wisdom has He made all things; for He is the source of all. And nature is a force by which God works; nature operates in subjection to necessity, and her work is the extinction and renewal of things.

# BOOK III

There was darkness in the deep,¹ and water without form; and there was a subtle breath,² intelligent, which permeated³ the things in Chaos with divine power. Then, when all was yet undistinguished and unwrought, there was shed forth holy light; and the elements came into being. All things were divided one from another, and the lighter things were parted off on high, the fire being suspended aloft, so that it rode upon the air; and the heavier things sank down, and sand was deposited beneath the watery substance, and the dry land was separated out from the watery substance, and became solid.

And the fiery substance was articulated,⁴ with the gods therein; and heaven appeared, with its seven spheres <note>The seven planetary spheres of the ancient cosmos: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>, and the gods, visible in starry forms, with all their constellations. And heaven revolved,⁵ and began to run its circling course, riding upon the divine air.

And each god,⁶ by his several power, put forth that which he was bidden to put forth. And there came forth four-footed beasts and creeping things and fishes and winged birds, and grass and every flowering herb, all having seed in them according to their diverse natures; for they generated within themselves the seed by which their races should be renewed.

(. . .⁷ And God ordained the) births of men, and bade mankind increase and multiply abundantly. And He implants each soul in flesh by means of the gods who circle in the heavens. And to this end did He make men, that they might contemplate heaven, and have dominion over all things under heaven, and that they might come to know God’s power, and witness nature’s workings,

¹ Or perhaps, ‘upon the deep’.
² Or ‘a fine airy substance’, or ‘a subtle spirit’.
³ Or perhaps, ‘which was moving upon’.
⁴ Or ‘was organized’; that is, the mass of fire was fashioned into an ordered whole made up of distinct and interdependent parts.
⁵ Or ‘was wrapped round (the world)’.
⁶ The ‘gods’ here spoken of are earth, water, and air, i. e. three of the four elements. (Fire, the fourth element, has already been deleted with.)
⁷ The making of man must have been here described in a passage now lost.

# BOOK III

and that they might mark what things are good, and discern the diverse natures of things good and bad, and invent all manner of cunning arts.

And it is the lot of men to live their lives <note>The original Greek suggests a sense of being born into these lives.</note> and pass away according to the destiny determined by the gods who circle in the heavens <note>referring to the planetary deities or celestial spheres</note>, and to be resolved into the elements. For the whole composition of the universe is dependent on God, being ever renewed by nature's working; for it is in God that nature has her being.

# LITTLE BOOK IV

You must understand then that God is pre-existent, and ever-existent, and that He, and He alone, made all things, and created by his will the things that are. For inasmuch as He is good, <note>The text is fragmentary here; it likely read: "He willed that all things should be good."</note>

<margin>3</margin>The Universe <note>The text is missing a phrase, perhaps: "is a divine being"</note>; but man has this advantage over all other living beings, that he possesses speech and mind. In Hermetic thought, this refers to higher intuitive intellect or divine consciousness, rather than just logical reasoning.</note> he did not impart to all. Not that he grudged it to any; for the grudging temper does not start from heaven above, but comes into being here below, in the souls of those men who are devoid of mind.—*Tat.* Tell me then, father, why did not God impart mind to all men?—*Hermes.* It was his will, my son, that mind should be placed in the midst as a prize that human souls may win.—*Tat.* And where did he place it?—*Hermes.* He filled a great <margin>4</margin>basin <note>term: "Basin" (Greek: Krater). A symbolic vessel or mixing bowl, often used in ancient mysteries to represent a source of spiritual purification or initiation.</note> with mind, and sent it down to earth; <note>Or perhaps, "and set it among men."</note> and he appointed a herald, and bade him make proclamation to the hearts of men: 'Hearken, each human heart; dip yourself in this basin, if you can, <note>Perhaps, "if you will."</note> recognizing for what purpose you have been made, and believing that you shall ascend to Him who sent the basin down.' <note>Perhaps, "Him who sent you down to earth."</note> Now those who gave heed to the proclamation, and dipped themselves in the bath of mind, these men got a share of *knowledge*; <note>term: "Gnosis" (Greek: gnosis). # CORPUS HERMETICUM

...those who failed to heed the proclamation <note>The "proclamation" refers to the invitation to dip oneself in the mixing bowl of Mind mentioned on the previous page.</note>, these are the ones who possess **reason** <note>original: "logos"</note> but have not yet received **Mind** <note>original: "nous"; in Hermetic thought, "reason" is the common human ability to speak and think, while "Mind" is a higher, divine faculty of spiritual perception.</note>. These people, being ignorant of why they were created and by whom, possess senses similar to those of irrational animals. They are gripped by anger and lack of self-control, admiring nothing that is truly worth seeing, but instead devoting themselves to the pleasures and appetites of their bodies; they believe that man was created for these things alone.

But those who have shared in the gift from God, these men, O Tat, are immortal rather than mortal when compared to the others. For they have embraced all things in their own Mind—things on earth, things in heaven, and whatever may exist above heaven. Having raised themselves to such a height, they have seen the Good; and having seen it, they consider their stay here on earth a misfortune. Despising all things corporeal and incorporeal, they hasten toward the One and Only <insert>Good</insert>. This, O Tat, is the <insert>activity</insert> of the Mind: an abundance of the knowledge of divine things and the contemplation of God.

— And I too, O Father, wish to be baptized in the mixing bowl. <note>The "mixing bowl" (crater) is a metaphor for the immersion in divine consciousness.</note>

— Unless you first hate your body, my child, you cannot love yourself. But once you have loved yourself, you will possess Mind, and possessing Mind, you will also partake in **knowledge** <note>original: "episteme"; here meaning a direct, spiritual understanding rather than mere data.</note>.

— How can you say this, O Father?

— Because it is impossible, my child, to be devoted to both: that is, to things mortal and things divine. For there being two kinds of things—the corporeal and the incorporeal, in which reside the mortal and the divine—the choice of one is left to him who wishes to choose. It is not possible to grasp both at once. When one choice is diminished, it makes manifest the power of the other. Therefore, the choice of the better part not only turns out to be the most beautiful for the one who chooses it, by saving the man, but it also demonstrates piety toward God. But the choice of the lesser part destroys the man...

# BOOK IV

Those who failed to heed the proclamation, these are they who possess speech indeed, but have not received mind <note>The Greek term *Nous*, often translated as "Intellect" or "Divine Mind."</note> also. It is not possible to take both; and when the one is slighted, then the working of the other becomes manifest. # BOOK IV

Destruction comes to the man, and it is likewise an offense against God; for just as processions pass through the midst of the people but can do nothing themselves, and only obstruct the way for others, even so these men merely pass in procession in the <term>Kosmos (the ordered universe)</term>, led along by bodily things. This being so, my son, God has done His part toward us, and will continue to do it; it is for us to do our part accordingly, and not to fall short. For God is blameless; it is we who are to blame for our evils, if we choose the evils in preference to the goods.

<margin>8 a</margin>
... You see, my son, through how many bodily things in succession we must make our way, and through how many troops of <term>daemons (intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil)</term> and courses of stars, so that we may press on to the one and only God.<note>Perhaps, 'to Him who alone is good', or 'to that which alone is good'.</note> ...<note>Perhaps, '(But when we have once attained to the Good, it will never fail us)'.</note> For we can never reach the farther boundary of the Good; it is limitless and without end; and in itself, it is without beginning, though to us it seems to begin when we gain knowledge of it. For the thing to be known does not itself begin to exist when we gain knowledge of it; it is only for us that our knowledge makes it begin. Let us then lay hold on this beginning, and make our way there with all speed; for it is hard for us to forsake the familiar things around us and turn back to the old home from which we came.<note>That is, to the world of the 'incorporeal' and 'divine', from which we were 'sent down' to earth.</note> Things seen delight us, and things unseen give rise to disbelief. Now the things that are evil are more manifest to sight; but the Good cannot be seen by manifest things;<note>That is, by our bodily eyes.</note> for it has no form or shape. It is impossible that an <term>incorporeal (non-physical)</term> thing should be manifested to a thing that is corporeal; because the incorporeal is like to itself, but unlike to all else.<note>The writer assumes that a thing can be seen or known only by that which is like it.</note>

<margin>9</margin> ["He is as much greater as the name of God is great."] <note>This bracketed sentence is likely a later scribal insertion or a corrupted variant of the opening of section 10</note> For who else is the father of all things? Is it not he alone? And this is his very function: to be a father. And if I must say something even more daring, his very essence <term>essence: *ousia*, the fundamental nature of a thing</term> is to move all things and to make them. Just as it is impossible for anything to come into being without a maker, so too must he not exist unless he is always making all things—in heaven, in the air, on the earth, in the deep, in every part of the cosmos, in all that is and all that is not. For there is nothing in the whole universe that is not him. He himself is both the things that are and the things that are not; for the things that are he has made manifest, but the things that are not he contains within himself.

<margin>10 a</margin> This is the one who is greater than the name of God. This is the invisible one, yet the most manifest. This is the one who is contemplated by the mind, yet visible to the eyes. This is the incorporeal one, the one of many bodies—or rather, the one of every body. There is nothing that he is not; for all things that are, he is. And for this reason, he has all names, because all things belong to him as their one father; and for this reason, he has no name at all, because he is the father of all.

See how many crafts have been <margin>7</margin> employed on one material, and how many works of art are enclosed within one compass! No one says <margin>8</margin> that a statue or a portrait has come into being without a sculptor or a painter; and has such a work as this come into being without a Maker? How blind men are! Nay, if I needs must speak with some boldness, I will even say that it is his very being to set all things in motion <note>The translator notes that the original manuscripts read "to give birth to all things."</note>, and to make all things; and as it is impossible for anything to come into being without a maker, so too it needs must be that He does not exist, if he is not ever making all things, in heaven, in air, on earth, and in the deep, in every part of the <term>Kosmos</term> <note>The universe conceived as a perfectly ordered and beautiful system.</note>, in all that is and in all that is not. He is both the things that are and the things that are not; for the things that are He has made manifest, and the things that are not He contains within himself.

Such is He who is too great to be named God. He is hidden, <margin>10 a</margin> yet most manifest. He is apprehensible by thought alone, yet we can see Him with our eyes. He is bodiless, and yet has many bodies, or rather, is embodied in all bodies. There is nothing that He is not <note>Alternatively: "that is not He."</note>; for all things that exist are even He. For this reason all names are names of Him, because all things come from Him, their one Father; and for this reason He has no name, because He is the Father of all.

->*BOOK VI*<-

### Of Hermes the Thrice-Greatest.

#### That the Good is in God alone, and nowhere else.

<margin>1 a</margin> The Good, O Asclepius, is in nothing except in God alone. Or rather, God himself is the Good eternally.
If this is so, the Good must be an essence devoid of all motion and generation <note>meaning it does not change or "become" something else</note>, but possessing a stable energy centered upon itself, lacking nothing, and untouched by <term>passions</term><note>original: "pathon". Refers to external influences or suffering.</note>.

Therefore, it is impossible for the Good to exist in "becoming," but only in the Unbegotten.

<margin>2 b</margin> Just as a participation in all things is granted in matter, so it is with the Good. In this way, the world is "good" insofar as it also makes all things, so that in its capacity of making, it is good. But in all other respects it is not good; for it is subject to passion and motion, and it is the maker of things subject to passion.

<margin>1 b</margin> And this belongs to none save God alone. There is nothing that God lacks, so that he should desire to gain it, and should thereby become evil. There is nothing that God can lose, and at the loss of which he might be grieved. There is nothing stronger than God, to do him wrong, and so provoke him to quarrel. God has no consort, to excite in him the passion of love; no disobedient subject, to rouse anger in him; there is none wiser than God, to make him jealous. And since his being admits of none of these passions, what remains, save only the Good?

<margin>2 a</margin> But as no evil can be found in such a being, even so the Good cannot be found in any other. In all other things all is evil, in things small and great alike, in each thing severally, and in the one living being that is greater than all, and mightiest of all.<note>1</note> For all things that come into being are full of perturbations <note>original: "passions" or "disturbances" of the soul/matter</note>, seeing that the very process of coming into being involves perturbation. But wherever there is perturbation, there the Good cannot be, and wherever the Good is, there no perturbation at all can be; even as wherever day, night cannot be, and wherever night is, day cannot be. Hence the Good cannot be in things that come into being, but only in that which is without beginning.<note>2</note>

<margin>2 b</margin> Yet as participation in all (the ideal <term>archetypes</term> <note>The original patterns or forms upon which all material things are modeled</note> of things) is distributed in the world of matter, so also participation in the Good. But in all other respects the Kosmos is not good; for it is subject to perturbation, and the things which it makes are subject to perturbation. It is impossible then <margin>3 a</margin> for things in this world to be pure from evil; and that which is is 'in God'.

<margin>3 b</margin> The Good, then, is in God alone. In man, that which is called good is so called in comparison with evil; for that which is not evil beyond measure is named good. Thus in men, Asclepius <note>The disciple to whom this discourse is addressed; in Hermetic tradition, he represents the seeker of wisdom</note>, it is only the name of the Good that is present; the thing itself is nowhere to be found. And what is worst of all, Asclepius, each of these things of which I have spoken is in this world believed to be the greatest good, whereas it is rather an evil than which none is greater. This error it is that leads the train of <note>original: "supplies" or "furnishes"</note> all the evils. And for my part, I thank God for this <margin>4 a</margin> thought that he has put into my mind, even the thought that the Good is absent, and that it is impossible for it to be present in the Kosmos <term>Kosmos: the ordered universe or material world, often viewed in this context as a place of limitation</term>. For all things which the eye can see are mere phantoms, and unsubstantial outlines; but the things which the eye cannot see are the realities, and above all, the ideal form of the Beautiful and the Good. And as the eye cannot see God, so it cannot see the Beautiful and the Good. For the Beautiful and the Good are parts of God; they are properties of God alone; they belong to God, and are inseparable from him; they are without blemish, and most lovely, and God himself is in love with them. ->*BOOK VII*<-

### [Of Hermes the Thrice-Greatest.]

#### That the greatest evil among humans is ignorance concerning God.
