# BOOK VI

The Good is inimitable <note>original: "inimitable"; possibly "unspeakable" or "ineffable"</note>, even as God himself is. As then you apprehend God, even so you must apprehend the Beautiful and the Good. For they are incommunicable to all other things, because they are inseparable from God. If you seek knowledge of God, you are also seeking knowledge of the Beautiful <note>The original text likely implies "the Beautiful and the Good" as a single concept</note>. For there is one road alone that leads to the Beautiful, and that is piety joined with knowledge of God.

<margin>6</margin>
Hence those who have not that knowledge, and have not traveled on the road of piety, are not afraid to call a man "beautiful and good" <note>The Greek phrase *kalos kagathos* was a common idiom for a "gentleman" or a person of high social standing, which the author here critiques as a superficial use of divine terms</note>; and that, though the man has never even in a dream seen anything that is good, but is encompassed by every kind of evil, and has come to believe that the evil is good, and in this belief, is insatiable in his dealings with evil, and fears to be deprived of it, and strives with all his might not only to keep it, but to increase it. Such, Asclepius <note>A legendary figure in the Hermetic tradition, addressed here as a student of wisdom</note>, are the things which men deem good and beautiful. And we cannot shun these things nor hate them; for the hardest thing of all is this, that we have need of them, and cannot live without them.

## CORPUS HERMETICUM
<note>The "Corpus Hermeticum" is a collection of Greek texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth. These texts explore the nature of the divine, the cosmos, and the human soul.</note>

**2 a** Therefore, do not be swept away by the great flood; instead, make use of the backcurrent. You who are able to reach the harbor of salvation, moor your ship there and seek a guide who will lead you to the doors of Knowledge <note>original: "gnosis" — spiritual insight or direct knowledge of the divine</note>. There, the light is brilliant and pure of darkness; there, not a single person is drunk, but all are sober, looking with the heart toward Him who wishes to be seen. For He cannot be heard, nor spoken of, nor seen with the eyes, but only with the mind and the heart.

**2 b** But first, you must tear off the garment you are wearing—the <insert>dark covering</insert>, the web of ignorance, the support of wickedness, the bond of corruption, [[the dark covering]], the living death, the sensible corpse <note>original: "aisthetikon nekron" — a body that feels but is spiritually dead</note>, the portable tomb, the resident thief, the <insert>enemy</insert> who hates you through the very things you love and envies you through the things you desire.

**3** Such is the enemy garment you have put on. It strangles you and pulls you down toward itself, so that you might not look up and behold the beauty of the Truth and the Good that dwells there. It wants you to hate its own wickedness, having understood the plot it has laid against you. It makes the so-called organs of sense <note>original: "aistheteria"</note> into organs of no-sense, blocking them with a mass of matter and filling them with loathsome pleasure, so that you might neither hear what you ought to hear, nor see what you ought to see.

# BOOK VII

Do not allow yourselves then to be borne along downstream by the strong current, but avail yourselves of a backflow, those of you who are **2 a** able to reach the haven, and cast anchor there, and seek a guide to lead you to the door of the House of Knowledge.<note>original: "Gnosis"—referring to a direct, experiential knowledge of the Divine, which implies union with God.</note> There you will find the bright light which is pure from darkness; there none is drunken, but all are sober, and they look up and see with the heart Him whose will it is that with the heart alone He should be seen. For He cannot be known by hearing, nor made known by speech; nor can He be seen with bodily eyes, but with mind and heart alone.

But first you must tear off this garment<note>A metaphor for the physical body, viewed here as a heavy burden or a disguise.</note> which you wear,—this **2 b** cloak of darkness, this web of ignorance, this support of evil, this bond of corruption,—this living death, this conscious corpse, this tomb you carry about with you,—this robber in the house, this enemy who hates the things you seek after, and grudges you the things which you desire. Such is the garment in which you have **3** clothed yourself; and it grips you to itself and holds you down, that you may not look upward and behold the beauty of the Truth,<note>Or "of Reality."</note> and the Good that abides above, and hate the evil of this thing, discovering its ill designs against you. For it makes senseless what men deem to be their organs of sense, stuffing them up with the gross mass of matter, and cramming them with loathly pleasures, so that you may neither hear of the things you ought to hear of, nor see the things you ought to see.

# THE HERMETIC CORPUS

->*BOOK VIII*<-

### Of Hermes the Thrice-Greatest.

->That none of the things that exist are destroyed, but people mistakenly<-
->call these changes "destructions" and "deaths."<-

**1 a** We must now speak, my son, concerning the soul and the body: in what manner the soul is immortal, and of what nature is its activity <note>The Greek text here is fragmented; the editor suggests a missing section regarding how bodies are composed and dissolved</note> in the composition and dissolution of the body.
**1 b** For death has nothing to do with any of these things. Rather, the term "death" is either an empty name or a hollow effect. <insert>Or perhaps "death" is so named by the removal of the first letter, standing for "immortal."</insert> <note>original: "thanatos" (death) vs "athanatos" (immortal). The author plays on the idea that death is merely a linguistic privation.</note> For death implies destruction, yet nothing in the cosmos is ever destroyed. For if the cosmos is a "second God" and an immortal living being, it is impossible for any part of an immortal being to die; and all things within the cosmos are parts of the cosmos. <insert>And man, the rational living being, is especially immortal.</insert>

**2** For first of all beings, and truly eternal and unbegotten, is God, the Creator <term>Demiurge: the divine craftsman or architect of the universe</term> of all things. Second is the one made by Him in His image; having been brought into being by Him, and being sustained and nourished by Him, this second being is ever-living, as it is endowed with immortality by the Father who is eternal. For the "ever-living" differs from the "eternal." For the Father was not brought into being by another; and if He was, He was brought into being by Himself. Rather, He never "became," but always *is*. The cosmos, however, is always "becoming" <note>The author distinguishes between the timeless existence of God and the continuous, cyclical process of the physical universe</note>. For the Father is the cause of the existence of the whole; but the Father is His own cause. Thus the cosmos has been made immortal by the Father, who is eternal.

**3** And as much of matter as was subject to His will,

### BOOK VIII

## A discourse of Hermes Trismegistus.

*That nothing that exists perishes, but men are in error when they call the changes which take place ‘destructions’ and ‘deaths’.*

<margin>1 a</margin>
Hermes. We have now to speak, my son, of soul and body; I must explain in what way the soul is immortal, and by the working of what sort of force <note>The original Greek text is fragmented here; the translator suggests it likely discussed how bodies are composed and dissolved.</note> of the composition and dissolution of a body.

<margin>1 b</margin>
. . . For death has nothing to do with any of them <note>Referring to the various parts or beings within the universe.</note>. The word ‘death’ is a mere name, without any corresponding fact. For death means destruction; and nothing in the <term>Kosmos</term> <note>The universe viewed as a complex, ordered system.</note> is destroyed. For seeing that the Kosmos is the second God, and an immortal being, it is impossible that a part of that immortal being should die; and all things in the Kosmos are parts of the Kosmos.

<margin>2</margin>
First of all things, and in very truth eternal and without beginning, is God, who is the Maker of the universe; and second is the Kosmos, which has been made by God in his image, and is kept in being and sustained by God. The Kosmos is ever-living; for it is made immortal by the Father, who is eternal. ‘Ever-living’ is not the same as ‘eternal’. The Father has not been made by another; if he has been made at all, he has been made by himself; but it ought rather to be said that he has never been made, but ever is. But the Kosmos is ever being made. For the cause of the existence of the universe is the Father; but the Father is the cause of his own existence. The Kosmos then has been made immortal by the Father, who is eternal.

<margin>3</margin>
The Father took all that part of matter which was subject to his

# CORPUS HERMETICUM
<note>The "Corpus Hermeticum" is a collection of Greek texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, blending Egyptian and Greek philosophy.</note>

The Father, having given body and bulk to the All, made it spherical, endowing it with this specific quality—which is itself immortal—and possessing an eternal materiality. Furthermore, the Father, having sown the qualities of living beings into the sphere, enclosed them as if in a cave, wishing to adorn that which was without quality <note>original: "apoion"</note> with every quality. He wrapped the entire body in immortality, so that matter, should it wish to separate from this composition, might not dissolve into its own disorder <note>original: "ataxia"</note>. For when matter was incorporeal, my son, it was disordered; and even here it retains a certain disorder that revolves around the smaller living beings—that process of increase and decrease [which men call death]. This disorder occurs among the earthly living beings. For the bodies of the celestial beings possess a single order, which they received from the Father in the beginning; this is preserved indissolubly by the restoration <note>original: "apokatastasis," referring here to the cyclical return of stars to their positions</note> of each. The restoration of earthly bodies, however, occurs when their composition is dissolved; and by this dissolution, they are restored to the indissoluble bodies, that is, the immortal ones. And thus, a deprivation of sensation occurs, not a loss of life.

But the third living being is Man, made according to the image of the cosmos. By the will of the Father, he possesses Mind <note>original: "nous"</note> beyond the other earthly animals; he has not only a sympathetic connection with the second God <note>The "second God" usually refers to the Cosmos or the Sun in Hermetic thought</note>, but also a conception of the first God. For he perceives the one as a body, but he receives a conception of the other as incorporeal.

->*BOOK IX*<-

### Of Hermes the Thrice-Greatest.
<note>original: "Hermes Trismegistus"</note>

->On thought and sense-perception [*and that the Beautiful and the Good exist in God alone, and nowhere else*].<-

<margin>1a</margin> Yesterday, Asclepius, I delivered the *Perfect Discourse*; <note>The "Perfect Discourse" likely refers to the text now known as the *Asclepius*.</note> but now I consider it necessary, as a follow-up to that one, to also go through the discourse on sense-perception.

<margin>1b</margin> For sense-perception <term>aisthesis: the physical act of perceiving through the senses</term> and thought <term>noesis: the internal process of understanding or intellect</term> seem to have a difference, because the former is material, while the latter is essential <note>or "pertaining to the true essence of being"</note>. But to me, both seem to be united and not divided—in human beings, I mean. For in the other living beings, sense-perception is united to nature, but in human beings, it is united to thought.

<margin>1c</margin> But the Mind <term>Nous: the divine or higher intellect</term> differs from thought as much as God differs from divinity. For divinity is produced by God, and thought is produced by the Mind, being the sister of speech <note>original: "logos," which can mean word, reason, or speech</note>. And these are instruments of one another; for neither is speech uttered without thought, nor is thought manifested without speech.

<margin>2</margin> Therefore, sense-perception and thought both flow together into man, as if they were intertwined. For it is not possible to think without sense-perception, nor to perceive without thought. <insert>Yet it is possible</insert> for thought to be exercised without sense-perception, just like those who experience visions through dreams.

<summary>Hermes explains to Asclepius that while sense-perception and intellect are distinct, they are inextricably linked in humans, unlike in animals. He defines God as the source of all things and the Mind as the source of thought and speech.</summary>

# BOOK VIII

God as bodiless.—*Tat.* Do you say then that this living creature <gloss>namely, man</gloss> does not perish?—*Hermes.* Speak not of man as perishing, my son. Think what God is, and what the Universe <note>original: "Kosmos"</note> is, and what is meant by a living creature that is immortal, and a living creature that is dissoluble. The Universe is made by God, and is contained in God; man is made by the Universe, and is contained in the Universe; and it is God that is the author of all, and encompasses all, and knits all things together.

---

->*BOOK IX*<-

### A discourse of Hermes Trismegistus.
->*Concerning thought and sense.*<-

<margin>1 a</margin> Yesterday, Asclepius, I delivered my crowning discourse; <gloss>The Greek original of the Latin *Asclepius* was entitled ‘The Crowning Discourse of Hermes’.</gloss> and to-day I think it necessary, by way of sequel to that discourse, to expound the doctrine of sense.

<margin>1 b</margin> Men think that there is a difference between sense and thought, in that sense is connected with matter, and thought with incorporeal and eternal substance. But I hold that sense and thought are united, and cannot be separated,—that is to say, in the case of men. In the lower animals, sense is united with instinct; in men, sense is united with thought.

<margin>1 c</margin> Mind differs from thought to the same extent that God differs from divine influence. <gloss>‘Divine influence’ probably means God’s operation in a man, i. e. divine inspiration.</gloss> Divine influence is put forth by God; and thought is put forth by mind, and is sister to speech. Thought and speech are instruments of one another; speech cannot be understood without thought, and thought cannot be uttered without speech.

<margin>2</margin> Sense and thought are infused into a man together, being intertwined with one another, so to speak; for a man can neither think without perceiving, nor perceive without thinking. It is sometimes said that men may think without sense-perception, as when one sees imaginary things in dreams; but I hold rather that

However, the God-fearing man will endure all things by holding fast to knowledge. For to such a person, all things are good, even if they are evil to others; and when he is plotted against, he refers everything to his knowledge, and he alone turns even evils into good.

# BOOK IX

Both thought and sense-perception have taken place in the dream-vision; for when we are awake, thought is always combined with sense-perception. Sense belongs in part to the body, and in part to the soul; and when the body-sense and the soul-sense are in accord, then it results that thought manifests itself, being brought forth as offspring by the mind. <note>The translator notes that the original text here is badly damaged; this rendering is a reconstruction of the likely meaning.</note>

<margin>3</margin> For all man’s thoughts are brought forth by his mind—good thoughts, when the mind is impregnated by God, and bad thoughts, when it is impregnated by some daemon <note>In this context, a "daemon" refers to a supernatural spirit or intermediary power, not necessarily the modern concept of a "demon."</note>, who enters into the man that has not been illuminated by God, and deposits in his mind the seed of such thoughts as it is the special work of that daemon to beget; and the mind brings forth those things which spring from this seed—adulteries, murders, acts of parricide and sacrilege, and all manner of impious deeds. <margin>4 a</margin> But the seeds which God deposits in the mind are few in number, but potent, and fair, and good; they are virtue, and self-control, and piety. Now piety is the knowledge of God; and he who has come to know God is filled with all things good; his thoughts are divine, and are not like those of the many.

<margin>4 b</margin> Hence it is that those who have attained to the knowledge of God are not pleasing to the many, nor the many to them. They are thought mad, and are laughed at; they are hated and despised, and perhaps they may even be put to death. For evil, as I have told you before, must needs dwell here on earth, where it is at home; for the home of evil is the earth, and not the whole universe, as some will blasphemously say in days to come. But the pious man will endure all things, cleaving to his knowledge of God. For to such a man all things are good, even though they be evil to others. When men devise mischief against him, he sees all this in the light of his knowledge of God; and he, and none but he, changes things evil into good.

<margin>5</margin> But let us return to the doctrine of sense. It is a property of man that sense in him is joined with thought; but as I have already told you, it is not every man that profits by his power of—

<margin>6</margin>The Universe also, Asclepius, has sense and thought; but its sense and thought are of a kind peculiar to itself, not like the sense and thought of man, nor varying like his, but mightier and less diversified. The sense and thought of the Universe are occupied solely in making all things, and dissolving them again into itself. The Universe is an instrument of God’s will; and it was made by him to this end, that, having received from God the seeds of all things that belong to it, and keeping these seeds within itself, it might bring all things into actual existence. The Universe produces life in all things by its movement; and decomposing them, it renews the things that have been decomposed; for, like a good husbandman, it gives them renewal by sowing seed. There is nothing in which the Universe does not generate life; and it is both the place in which life is contained, and the maker of life. The bodies of all living beings are made of matter.

<margin>7</margin>They are diversely made, but all are composite, in greater or less degree; the heavier bodies are more composite, and the lighter less. It is the swiftness of the movement of the Universe that causes the diversity of the births. For the cosmic life-breath, working without intermission, conveys into the bodies a succession of qualities, and therewith makes the universe one mass of life. ### BOOK X

## Of Hermes the Thrice-Greatest.

### The Key.

<margin>1a</margin> Yesterday’s discourse, O Asclepius, I dedicated to you; but it is only right to dedicate today’s to Tat, since it is an epitome <note>A summary or condensed version</note> of the General Discourses which were spoken to him.

<margin>1b</margin> God the Father and the Good, O Tat, possess the same nature, or rather, the same activity <note>original: "energeia"</note>. For "nature" is a term for birth and growth, which concerns things that are changeable and in motion; but the activity of God concerns things that are unchangeable and motionless—that is, the divine things—and those human things which He Himself wills to exist. Elsewhere, we have taught concerning activities, both divine and human, as we have done with other matters; these must be understood in this context as well.

<margin>2</margin> For His activity is His will; and His essence <note>original: "ousia"</note> is to will that all things exist. For what is God the Father and the Good, if not the very being of all things that do not yet exist? Rather, He is the very existence of all things that are. This is God; this is the Father. To Him belongs the Good, being such that it belongs to no one else—

### A discourse of Hermes Trismegistus.

### The Key.

<margin>1 a</margin> *Hermes.* The teaching which I gave yesterday, Asclepius <note>A legendary figure in the Hermetic tradition, often depicted as a student of Hermes</note>, I dedicated to you; and it is only right that I should dedicate to Tat <note>Hermes' son and another primary disciple in these dialogues</note> that which I am about to give to-day; for it is an abridgement of the General Discourses which I have addressed to him.

<margin>1 b</margin> Know then, Tat, that God the Father is of one nature with the Good; or rather, the working of God the Father is one with the working of the Good. 'Nature' is a term applied to birth and growth, and birth and growth have to do with things subject to change and movement; but God's working has to do with things free from change and movement, that is, with things divine; and it is God's will that what is human should be divine. Of forces at work <term>energeia: the active power or operation of a being</term>, divine and human, I have spoken elsewhere; and in dealing with our present topic, as well as in other matters, you must bear in mind what I have taught you concerning them.

<margin>2</margin> The force with which God works is his will; and his very being consists in willing the existence of all things. What else is God the Father but the being of all things when as yet they are not? It is this$^1$ that constitutes the existence of all things that are. Such then is God, such is the Father. And to him appertains the Good; for the Good is a thing that can appertain to none

---

$^1$ Namely, God's will.

It is true that the <term>Kosmos</term><note>The universe viewed as an ordered, harmonious system.</note> also is father of things which are good in so far as they partake of the Good; but the Kosmos is not, in like measure with God, the author of what is good in living creatures; for the Kosmos is not the author of their life; or if it acts as an author of life, it does so only under the compulsion imposed on it by God's will, without which nothing can be or come into being. <margin>3</margin> The Kosmos is to the things within it as a father to his children, in that it is the author of their generation and nutrition; but it has received from God its supply of good. <gloss>That is, of life, or power to give life to things.</gloss> It is the Good that is the creative principle; and it is impossible that the creative principle should come to be in any save God alone—God, who receives nothing, but wills the existence of all things. I will not say 'makes all things'; for he who 'makes' things falls short of the fulfilment of his function during long intervals of time, in that he is sometimes making, and at other times not making. And moreover, he who 'makes' things makes only qualities and magnitudes; <gloss>Qualities and magnitudes, but not substances. That is, a 'maker' works on something that already exists, and merely makes some change in it.</gloss> for he makes things have certain magnitudes and qualities at one time, and contrary magnitudes and qualities at another time. But God makes by his will the very existence of all things; and it is in this sense that he is the Father of all things. For God wills things to be, and, in <margin>4 a</margin> that way, <gloss>That is, as being willed by God.</gloss> these things also have existence. But the Good itself, my son, exists in the highest degree; for it is by reason of the Good that all other things exist.

. . . For it is a property of the Good that it becomes known <gloss>Perhaps, 'that it wills to become known'.</gloss> <margin>4 b</margin> to him who is able to see it.—**Tat.** Father, you have given me my fill of this good and most beautiful sight; and my mind's eye is almost blinded by the splendour of the vision.—**Hermes.** Nay, the vision of the Good is not a thing of fire, as are the sun's rays; it does not blaze down upon us and force us to close our eyes; it shines forth much or little, according as he who gazes on it is able to receive the inflow of the incorporeal radiance. It is more penetrating than visible light in its descent upon us; but it cannot harm us; it is full of all immortal life. and contraries. And seeing that this is so in all things that exist, . . .—

*Tat.* What then are we to think of this material God, the **Universe** <note>original: "Kosmos"</note>?—*Hermes.* The Universe is not indeed evil, but it is not good, as God is; for it is material, and subject to perturbation <note>The state of being disturbed or moved from a calm state; here referring to the instability of matter.</note>. It is first among all things that are subject to perturbation, but second among things that are. The Universe also <margin>That is, as well as God.</margin> is ever-existent; it exists in process of becoming; it is ever becoming, in that the qualities and magnitudes of things are ever coming into being. It is therefore in motion; for all becoming is material movement. That which is incorporeal and motionless <margin>Namely, the soul of the Universe.</margin> works the material **11** movement; and it does so in the following way. The Universe is a sphere, that is to say, a head; and so, all things that are united to the cerebral membrane <margin>The 'cerebral membrane' or *meninx* of the Universe is the outermost sphere of heaven; and 'the things which are united to it' are the fixed stars and planets.</margin> of this head,—the membrane in which the soul is chiefly seated,—are immortal, for they have in them more soul than body; but the things which are at a distance from the cerebral membrane <margin>That is, all things below the moon.</margin> are mortal, for they have in them more body than soul. Thus the universe is composed of a part that is material and a part that is incorporeal; <margin>That is, of body and soul.</margin> and inasmuch as its body is made with soul in it, the universe is a living creature.

The Universe is first among all living creatures; man, as a living **12** creature, ranks next after the Universe, and first among those which are mortal. Man is not merely not-good; he is evil, inasmuch as he is mortal. The Universe is not-good, as being subject to movement; but it is not-evil, as being immortal. Man, on the other hand, is both not-good, as being subject to movement, and evil, as being mortal. And the soul of man is vehicled <note>Carried or contained within a medium.</note> thus. **13** The mind has for its vehicle the soul; the soul has for its vehicle the vital spirit <note>term: "pneuma" - a subtle, air-like substance thought to connect the soul to the physical body.</note>; and the vital spirit, traversing the arteries together

And so the mind takes to itself the soul for a wrap; the soul,—for the soul also is in some measure divine,—uses as its wrap the vital spirit; and the vital spirit controls the body. --- Page 204 ---
<meta>This page continues the discourse on the nature of the Mind (Nous) and the soul's journey after death, specifically contrasting the fate of the pious and impious souls. It follows the discussion of the Mind as a divine instrument.</meta>

->THE HERMETIC CORPUS<-

The Mind has a body made of the element of fire. For being the creator of all things, the Mind uses fire as its instrument for creation. The Mind of the universe is the creator of all things, but the mind of man creates only earthly things; for being stripped of divine fire, the mind in man is unable to create divine things, being limited by its human dwelling.

<margin>19 a</margin> Not every human soul, but only the pious soul, is something demonic <note>original: "daimonia" - here meaning semi-divine or supernatural</note> and divine. Such a soul, after being released from the body and having competed in the contest of piety—the contest of piety being to know God and to wrong no human being—becomes entirely Mind. And after being released from the body, when it has become a divine spirit <note>original: "daimon"</note>, it is ordained to obtain a fiery body in order to serve the ministry of God. But the impious soul remains in its own essence, punished by itself, seeking an earthly body to enter.

<margin>19 b</margin> But it must be a human body; for no other body can contain a human soul. It is not permitted for a human soul to fall into the body of an irrational animal; for this is the law of God, to preserve the human soul from such an insult.

<margin>20</margin> —How then, O Father, is a human soul punished?
—And what greater punishment is there for a human soul, my child, than impiety? What fire has so great a flame as impiety? What biting beast has such power to ravage the body as impiety ravages the soul itself? Or do you not see what evils the impious soul suffers, as it cries out and screams: "I am burning, I am on fire! I know not what to say or what to do; I am being devoured, miserable as I am, by the evils that possess me. I can neither see nor hear." Are these not the cries of a soul being punished? Or do you believe, as the many do and as you yourself might suppose, my child, that a soul departing the body becomes a wild beast? This is a very great error. For the soul is punished in this manner: when the Mind becomes a divine spirit, it is ordained to obtain a fiery body for the service of God; <insert>but</insert> entering into the impious soul, it scourges it with the whips of its sins. Lashed by these, the impious soul is punished; for it turns to blasphemies, murders, insults, and various forms of violence through...

But the impious soul retains its own substance unchanged; it suffers self-inflicted punishment, and seeks an earthy body into which it may enter.

The divine forces are, so to speak, radiations emitted by God; the forces that work birth and growth are radiations emitted by the Universe; the arts and crafts are radiations emitted by man. The divine forces operate by means of the Universe, and their operation reaches man by means of the cosmic radiations to which birth and growth are due; and the forces that work birth and growth operate by means of the material elements. # HERMETIC CORPUS

<margin>24 a</margin> [sent by Justice.] <note>original: "ὑπὸ τῆς δίκης" — referring to the soul's punishment mentioned on the previous page.</note> [[For the soul, apart from the Mind, is able neither to say anything nor to do anything.]] For often the Mind departs from the soul; and in that hour the soul neither sees nor hears, but resembles an irrational animal. <<For the soul, apart from the Mind, "is able neither to say anything nor to do anything.">> Such is the power of the Mind. But it does not tolerate a sluggish soul; rather, it abandons the soul that is fastened to the body and strangled by it. Such a soul, my child, does not possess Mind; therefore, one should not even consider such a person to be a human being.

<margin>24 b</margin> For a human being is a divine living being, and is not to be compared to the other living beings of the earth, but to those in heaven [called the gods above]. Or rather, if one must dare to speak the truth, the true human being is even above those gods, or at the very <margin>25</margin> least they are equal in power to one another. For none of the heavenly gods will descend to earth, leaving behind the boundary of heaven; but the human being even ascends into heaven, and measures it [and knows what parts of it are high and what are low, and learns all other things with precision]. And what is greatest of all: he reaches the heights without even leaving the earth behind; so great is the magnitude of his reach. Therefore, one must dare to say that an "earthly" human being is a mortal god, and a heavenly god is an immortal human being.

Wherefore all things are governed through these two, the Cosmos and the Human, but all things are under <God>.

# CORPUS HERMETICUM

->*BOOK XI. (i)*<-

### Mind to Hermes

<margin>1 a</margin> [[Hold fast then to this discourse, O Thrice-Greatest Hermes, and remember what is said.
<margin>1 b</margin> Since it has come to me to speak, I shall not hesitate. Since many people have said many different things about the Universe and God, and yet I have not learned the truth, you, my Master, must clarify this for me; for I would trust you alone to reveal the truth of this matter. [Time.] Listen, my child, to how God and the Universe stand.]]

<margin>2</margin> God, Eternity <note>original: "Aion" — refers to the personified concept of eternal duration or the divine realm</note>, the Cosmos, Time, Becoming <note>original: "genesis" — the process of birth, change, and coming-into-being</note>.
God makes Eternity,
->Eternity makes the Cosmos,<-
->the Cosmos makes Time,<-
->and Time makes Becoming.<-

The essence of God is the Good, [the Beautiful, Happiness, Wisdom,]
->the essence of Eternity is Identity <note>meaning sameness or unchanging stability</note>,<-
->the essence of the Cosmos is Order,<-
->the essence of Time is Change,<-
->and the essence of Becoming is Life [and Death].<-

The activities <term>energeiai: the active expressions or powers of a being</term> of God are Mind and Soul,
->those of Eternity are Immortality and Duration,<-
->those of the Cosmos are restoration and counter-restoration <note>referring to the cyclical movements of the stars and seasons</note>,<-
->those of Time are increase and decrease,<-
->and those of Becoming are quality and quantity.<-

Eternity, therefore, is in God,
->the Cosmos is in Eternity,<-
->Time is in the Cosmos,<-
->and Becoming is in Time.<-

### A discourse of Mind to Hermes

God, Eternity <note>original: "Aeon"</note>, Universe <note>original: "Kosmos"</note>, Time, and Generation <note>original: "Coming-to-be"</note>.
God brings forth Eternity,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;the essence of Time is change,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;the active powers of the Universe are the restoration of things to themselves and
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;the replacement of one thing by another,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;the active powers of Time are growth and decay,

Eternity then exists within God,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;the Universe exists within Eternity,

# BOOK XI (ii)

<margin>10</margin> To which of the two does life belong in larger measure? You must understand that every living body, whether it be immortal or mortal, rational or irrational, is composed of matter and soul. All living bodies contain soul; things which are not alive are simply matter existing by itself. Likewise, there is soul by itself, held in the Maker’s keeping; for soul is the very substance <term>substance: the underlying essence or "stuff" of a thing</term> of which life is made. How then can the life found in immortal beings be different from the life in mortal creatures? And how can it be argued that the maker of immortal living beings is not also the maker of those that are mortal? He, therefore, is the author of all life, just as he is the author of the life of the immortals.

<margin>11</margin> It is clear that there is someone who makes these things. And it is manifest that the maker is one; for soul is one, life is one, and matter is one. And who is that maker? Who else can he be but God alone? To whom save God alone should it belong to instill soul into things? You have already agreed that the <term>Kosmos: the universe seen as a well-ordered and beautiful whole</term> is one, that the Sun is one, the Moon is one, and the Earth is one; would you then suggest that God himself is merely one among many? It would be absurd to suppose that there <margin>14 b</margin> are many Gods. God, therefore, is also one. Moreover, if all things—both those in heaven and those on earth—are alive, and there is one life in them all, and life is made by God, it follows that all things are made by God.

<margin>12 a</margin> And why should it be thought strange <note>original: "strange" can also be read as "a hard task"</note> for God to make both what is immortal and what is subject to change, when you yourself do <note>The original Greek verb for "do" is the same as "make," drawing a parallel between human action and divine creation</note> so many different things? You see; you speak and hear; you smell and feel by touch; you walk; you think; you breathe. It is not one person who sees, another who hears, and another who speaks; it is not one who feels, another who smells, another who walks, another who thinks, and another who breathes; but he who does all these things is a single being.

Nay, it is not possible for God to exist without doing what **12 b** I said he does. # CORPUS HERMETICUM

...on the one hand, the body dissolves, but life moves into the unseen [that which is dissolved].

By this reasoning, my dearest Hermes <note>The text addresses Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth</note>, I say that the world [which you hear is eternal] is also transformed, because a certain part <insert>of its life</insert> becomes hidden in the unseen every day, yet it is never dissolved. And these are the experiences of the world: <margin>16 a</margin> rotations and concealments. The rotation is a turning, and the concealment is a renewal. <note>original: "δίνησις" (dinesis) and "κρύψις" (krypsis). The author argues that what looks like death is merely the world "turning" its face away or renewing itself.</note> It is of all forms, not having the forms fixed within itself, but rather changing itself.

<margin>16 b</margin> Since, therefore, the world has become "all-formed," what would its Maker be? For may He not be without form; yet if He is also all-formed, He will be identical to the world. But if He has only one form, in this respect He will be inferior to the world. What then shall we say He is? Let us not bring the argument into a state of perplexity; for nothing is perplexing concerning God when understood. He has, then, one <term>Idea</term> <note>In the Platonic sense, an "Idea" or "Form" is the perfect, non-physical essence of a thing.</note> [if there is any Idea of Him], which cannot be perceived by the eyes, <margin>17 a</margin> for it is incorporeal. [And He shows all forms through bodies.] And do not wonder if there is such a thing as an incorporeal Idea; for there is—just as in paintings, mountain peaks are seen [for example] standing out prominently, yet they are by nature smooth and entirely flat. <note>A clever analogy: just as a 2D painting creates the illusion of 3D depth, the incorporeal God creates the "depth" and variety of the physical world.</note>

<margin>17 b</margin> By contemplating what has been said more boldly, <margin>17 c</margin> <insert>you will understand Him who contains all things</insert> more truly. [[For just as man cannot live without life, so God cannot exist without doing good. For this is, as it were, the life and <margin>18</margin> the motion of God: to move all things and to give them life.]] But some of these sayings must have their own specific meaning, such as what I <insert>now</insert> say [understand this]. For all things are in God, not as if lying in a place; for "place" is a body, and <insert>every</insert> body <insert>is movable; but the incorporeal</insert> is immovable, and the things situated <insert>within it</insert> have no motion; for they are situated differently within an incorporeal [imagination]. [[Understand Him who contains all things.]] And [understand that] nothing is restrictive of the incorporeal, [nor faster, nor more powerful,] but it is itself <insert>restrictive</insert> of all things.

# BOOK XI (ii)

And speaking in this way, dear Hermes <note>The speaker is likely Mind (Nous) addressing Hermes Trismegistus</note>, I say that the Universe <note>original: "Kosmos"</note> also is changing through all time, inasmuch as day by day a part of its life passes away out of our sight, but that it is never decomposed. And the things that befall the Universe are . . . . And the Universe assumes all forms; it does not contain the forms as things placed in it, but the Universe itself changes. <margin>16 a</margin>

Now if the Universe is so made that it assumes all forms, what is to be said of its Maker? Shall we say that he is formless? Surely not that! Yet if he too assumes all forms, he will be like the Universe; and if he has but one form, he will in that respect be inferior to the Universe. What then are we to say of him? We must not let the discussion end in unsolved doubt; for in our thoughts of God, no question is insoluble. We will say then that God has one form, and one alone, but it is a form that no eye can see; for it is incorporeal <term>incorporeal: existing without a physical body or material substance</term>. And marvel not that there is an incorporeal form. Such things there are; for instance, in pictures we see mountain-tops standing out high, though the picture itself is quite smooth and flat. <margin>16 b</margin> <margin>17 a</margin>

And if you boldly grasp this conception,¹ you will get a truer notion of Him who contains all things. There are terms which must be taken in a sense peculiar to the thing spoken of; and of this, what I am now saying is an instance. All things are in God; but things are not situated in God as in a place. A place is a body,² and all bodies are subject to movement; but that which is incorporeal is motionless, and the things situated in it have no movement; for it is in a different sense that things ‘are situated in’ what is incorporeal. And the incorporeal³ cannot be enclosed by anything; but it can itself enclose all things; it is the quickest <margin>17 b</margin> <margin>18</margin>

# CORPUS HERMETICUM

> “I understand nothing, I can do nothing; I fear the land <and> the sea; I cannot ascend into heaven; I do not know who I was, I do not know who I shall be;” <note>The author is mimicking the cry of a soul trapped in material ignorance.</note> what do you have to do with God? For this very reason He has made all things, so that through all things you might see Him. This is the virtue of God: to appear through all things. For nothing is invisible, not even of the incorporeal things; the Mind <term>Nous: the divine intellect or intuitive faculty</term> is seen in the act of understanding, and God is seen in the act of creating.

<margin>22 b</margin> These things have been revealed to you to this extent, O Thrice-Greatest <note>original: "Trismegiste"</note>. But consider all other things in the same way within yourself, and you shall not be deceived.

# BOOK XI (ii)

'I can do nothing; I am afraid of earth and sea, I cannot mount to heaven; I know not what I was, nor what I shall be'; then, what have you to do with God? Your thought can grasp nothing beautiful and good, if you cleave to the body, and are evil.

<margin>21 b</margin> For it is the height of evil not to know God; but to be capable of knowing God, and to wish and hope to know him, is the road which leads straight to the Good; and it is an easy road to travel. Everywhere God will come to meet you, everywhere he will appear to you, at places and times at which you look not for it, in your waking hours and in your sleep, when you are journeying by water and by land, in the night-time and in the day-time, when you are speaking and when you are silent; for there is nothing which is not God. <note>The translator suggests an alternative reading: "for there is nothing in which God is not."</note> And do you say 'God is invisible'? <margin>22 a</margin> Speak not so. Who is more manifest than God? For this very purpose has he made all things, that through all things you may see him. This is God's goodness, that he manifests himself through all things. Nothing is invisible, not even an <term>incorporeal</term> <note>Something that has no physical body or material form.</note> thing; mind is seen in its thinking, and God in his working.

<margin>22 b</margin> So far, <term>thrice-greatest one</term> <note>original: "Trismegistus" — a title for Hermes signifying his mastery over the three parts of the wisdom of the whole universe.</note>, I have shown you the truth. Think out all else in like manner for yourself, and you will not be misled.

Just as a good physician causes pain to a body already seized by disease by burning or cutting it, in the same way the Mind causes pain to the soul, weaving away from it the pleasure from which every disease of the soul arises. The great disease of the soul is <term>godlessness</term><note>original: "ἀθεότης" (atheotes) - a lack of connection to or belief in the divine</note>; since all evils follow upon the opinions <insert>of the godless</insert>, and nothing good. Does not the Mind, then, by acting in opposition to the soul, provide for its good, just as the physician provides health for the body?

But those human souls that have not obtained the Mind as a pilot suffer the same fate as those of irrational animals. For the Mind, becoming a co-worker with them and giving rein to their desires, <unclear>...</unclear> toward which they are carried by the rush of appetite, straining toward the irrational. And just like irrational animals, they do not cease being irrationally angry and irrationally desiring, nor do they have any satiety of evils; for irrational angers and desires are excessive vices. In men, this mind is <note>The original text is fragmented here; the translator suggests it may read "productive of divinity."</note> Hence some men are divine, and the humanity of such men is near to deity; for the **Good Spirit** <note>original: "Agathos Daimon" — a benevolent deity or guiding spirit in Hellenistic philosophy</note> said "gods are immortal men, and men are mortal gods." But in the irrational animals, there is instinct in place of mind. Wherever there is life, **2** there is soul; but in the irrational animals, the soul is devoid of mind. Mind is a benefactor to the souls of men; it produces good for them. In the case of the irrational animals, mind co-operates with the special form of instinct which belongs to each several kind of beast; but in men, mind works against the natural instincts. Every soul, as soon as it has been embodied, is depraved by pain and pleasure; for pain and pleasure belong to a composite body, and seethe like juices in it, and the soul steps into them and is plunged in them. Those souls then of which mind takes **3** command are illuminated by its light, and it counteracts their prepossessions; for as a good physician inflicts pain on the body, burning or cutting it, when disease has taken possession of it, even so mind inflicts pain on the soul, ridding it of pleasure, from which spring all the soul's diseases. And godlessness is a great disease of the soul; for the beliefs of the godless bring in their train all kinds of evils, and nothing that is good. Clearly then, mind, inasmuch as it counteracts this disease, confers good on the soul, just as the physician confers health on the body. But those **4** human souls which have not got mind to guide them are in the same case as the souls of the irrational animals. For mind co-operates with them, and gives free course to their desires; and such souls are swept along by the rush of appetite to the gratification of their desires, and strive towards irrational ends; and like the irrational animals, they cease not from irrational anger and irrational desire, and are insatiable in their craving for evils; for irrational angers and desires are passions that exceed all else in evil. And to punish and convict such souls as these, God has established penal law.

5 "In this case, O Father, the discourse concerning **Fate** <note>original: *heimarmene*; the Greek concept of a fixed, inescapable destiny</note> which you previously explained to me is in danger of being overturned. For if it is absolutely fated for a certain person to commit adultery, or to commit sacrilege, or to do some other evil, why is he punished when he performed the deed under the compulsion of Fate? 6 and for this reason he acts, so that he may suffer what he suffers because he acted. But for the present, our discourse is not about **wickedness** and Fate; for we have spoken of these things elsewhere. Now our discourse is about **Mind** <note>original: *nous*; the divine faculty of reason and spiritual intuition</note>: what Mind is capable of, and how it differs—being of one sort in humans, but changed in the irrational animals. And again, that in irrational animals it is not beneficent, but in humans it works good—though not equally in all, as it does not always extinguish the **spirited** <note>original: *thymikon*; the part of the soul associated with anger and courage</note> and the **desirous** <note>original: *epithymetikon*; the part of the soul associated with physical cravings</note> natures. Among these, one must distinguish between **men of reason** <note>original: *ellogimoi*; those who possess and use the *logos* or divine reason</note> and the irrational. All humans are subject to Fate, since they are subject to birth and change; for these are the beginning and the end of Fate.

7 And all humans suffer what is fated. But the men of reason, whom we said are governed by the Mind, do not suffer in the same way as others, but are set free from wickedness; for they do not suffer because they are wicked." — "How can you say this, O Father? Is the adulterer not wicked? Is the murderer not wicked, and all the others?" — "But the man of reason, O son, will suffer not because he committed adultery, but as if he had committed it; nor because he murdered, but as if he had murdered. It is impossible to escape the quality of **change**, just as it is impossible to escape

8 **birth**; but it is possible for the one who possesses Mind to escape wickedness. # BOOK XII (i)

*Tat.* But if that is so, father, it would almost seem that the doctrine of destiny <note>The Greek term is 'Heimarmene', referring to the fixed chain of causes governing the physical world.</note> which you have explained to me before is overthrown. If a man is inevitably destined to commit adultery, or sacrilege, or some other crime, why is punishment inflicted on one who has been compelled by destiny to do the deed? It is destiny that has committed all these crimes.

*Hermes.* It is true, my son, that <unclear>...</unclear>, and that nothing, whether good or bad, which has to do with the body, can come to pass apart from destiny. But it is destined also that he who has done evil shall suffer evil; and to this end he does it <note>Perhaps, 'to this end he is destined (or compelled) to do it'.</note>, that he may suffer the penalty for having done it. 

But for the present, we are not discussing evil-doing and destiny. Of those matters I have spoken elsewhere; but we are now concerned with mind <term>Mind: The Greek 'Nous', referring to the divine intellect or higher consciousness</term>, and the questions we have to consider are these—what mind can do, and how it admits of differences, being of one sort in men, and of another sort in the irrational animals. And further, we have to consider that in the irrational animals mind does not work good, whereas in men it works good, but not alike in all men; for not in all men does it quench the passions of anger and desire. 

The one sort of men we must hold to be rational, and the other sort irrational. Now all men are subject to destiny, inasmuch as all are subject to birth and death <note>Literally, 'birth and change'; but 'change' here means 'death'.</note>; for a man's destiny begins at his birth, and ends at his death. And all men undergo what destiny has appointed for them; but rational men (that is, those who, as I said, are governed by mind) do not undergo it in the same way as the irrational. They are freed from wickedness; they undergo what is destined, but they are not wicked.

*Tat.* Once more, father, what do you mean? The adulterer, and the murderer, and all the rest, are they not wicked?

*Hermes.* Nay, my son, the rational man has not committed adultery or murder, yet he must undergo what is destined, as the adulterer and the murderer undergo it. It is impossible for a man to escape from his destined death, just as it is impossible for him to escape from his destined birth; but from wickedness a man can escape, if he has mind in him. 

I will tell you, my son, what I heard the Good Spirit <note>original: "Agathos Daimon", a tutelary deity or personification of divine wisdom</note> say. If he had put forth in writing what he said, he would have conferred a great benefit on the human race; for being the first-born god, he alone,

<margin>9</margin>The first-born God, having looked upon all things, spoke words that were <insert>truly</insert> divine. Nothing is impossible for it, neither to place a human soul above Fate, nor—if the soul has been negligent, as sometimes happens—to place it under Fate. Let these things be said to this extent. <insert>The sayings of the Good Spirit are the best.</insert>

<margin>10</margin>These things are spoken divinely, O father, and truly and profitably. But clarify this further for me: you said that the Mind acts in irrational animals in the manner of nature, working together with their impulses. But the impulses of irrational animals, as I think, are passions <note>original: "pathē" — emotions, sufferings, or passive reactions to external stimuli</note>. If the Mind works together with these impulses, and the impulses are passions, then the Mind itself must be subject to passion, taking on the color of these passions. — Well said, my son! You ask a noble question, and it is right for me to answer.

<margin>11</margin>All things, my son, that are in a body are subject to passion. Strictly speaking, the bodies themselves are the things that suffer; <insert>and the incorporeal things also</insert> (...). For everything that moves is incorporeal, and everything that is moved is a body. <insert>And the incorporeal things</insert> <insert>are moved by the Mind;</insert> <insert>and movement is a passion.</insert> Therefore, both suffer: both the mover and the moved, the one ruling and the one being ruled. <insert>So also the Mind, while it is in a body, is subject to passion,</insert> but once it is released from the body, it is also released from passion. Or rather, my son, perhaps nothing is entirely free from passion, but all things are subject to it. Yet a passion differs from a thing that is acted upon. For the one acts, and the other suffers; but bodies also act on their own account. For they are either motionless or they are moved; and whichever of the two...

# CORPUS HERMETICUM

Whatever it may be, *it is a passion* <note>original: "pathos." In this context, it refers to an experience or an impression received from the outside, rather than an emotion.</note>. But incorporeal things are always active, and for this reason they are [always] capable of being acted upon. <gloss>1</gloss> Therefore, do not let these names disturb you; <gloss>C</gloss> for activity and passion are the same thing. <gloss>Ⴙ</gloss> It is no grievance to use a more auspicious name.—You have delivered this discourse most clearly, O father.—

<margin>12</margin> Observe this also, my son: that God has bestowed two gifts upon man beyond all other mortal creatures—namely, Mind <note>original: "nous," the higher intuitive intellect</note> and Reason <note>original: "logos," both the internal thought and the spoken word</note>—which are of equal value to immortality. <insert>He speaks here of the spoken word.</insert> If anyone uses these gifts for their proper purpose, they will differ in no way from the immortals; rather, <insert>they will differ only by being in a body,</insert> and when they depart from the body, they will be guided by both Mind and Reason into the choir of the gods and the blessed.—But do not the other animals use reason, O father?—No, my son, they use voice. Reason differs greatly from voice; for reason is common to all humanity, but each species of animal has its own particular voice.—But even among men, O father, is not reason different according to each nation?—It may differ, my son, <insert>in its dialect,</insert> but humanity is one, and so Reason is one; it is translated from one tongue to another, and the same Reason is found in Egypt, in Persia, and in Greece. <insert>Reason, then, is the image of Mind, and Mind is the image of God.</insert>

<margin>13 b</margin> For the blessed god, the Good Spirit <note>original: "Agathos Daimon," a tutelary deity or personification of divine wisdom</note>, said that the soul is in the body, the mind is in the soul, and <insert>God</insert> is in the mind.

<margin>14</margin> <insert>God, then, is the father of these.</insert> <insert>Reason is the image and mind of God,</insert> <insert>and the body is the image of the Form, and the Form is the image of the Soul.</insert> Therefore, the finest part of matter is air; of air, the soul; of the soul, the mind; and of the mind, God. And God is around all things and through all things; the mind is around the soul, the soul is around the air, and the air is around matter.

# CORPUS HERMETICUM

->*BOOK XII. (ii)*<-

### 〈Hermes to Tat.〉

<margin>14 b</margin> 〈...〉 Necessity, **Providence** <note>original: "pronoia"</note>, and **Nature** <note>original: "physis"</note> are the instruments of the administration of the **Cosmos** <note>the ordered universe</note> and of the ordering of **Matter** <note>original: "hyle"</note>.
<margin>14 c</margin> Each of the intelligible beings <note>beings grasped by the mind rather than the senses</note> is a single **Essence** <note>original: "ousia"</note>, and their essence is **Sameness** <note>the quality of being unchanging</note>. But each of the bodies of the universe is many. 〈〈And Matter is one.〉〉 For the simple, uncomposed bodies possess Sameness, and even when they undergo change into one another, they always preserve the indestructibility of that Sameness. But in all other composite bodies, there is a **Number** for each; <margin>15 a</margin> for without number, it is impossible for a constitution, a composition, or a dissolution to occur. The **Unities** <note>original: "monades," the fundamental units</note> generate and increase Number, and in turn, they receive it back into themselves when it is dissolved. [[And Matter is one.]]
<margin>15 b</margin> This entire Cosmos—which is the Great God and the image of the Greater One, united to Him and preserving the order according to the will of the Father—is the **Fullness of Life**. There is nothing within it, throughout the whole of eternity from the first restoration, whether of the whole or of the individual parts, which does not live. For not a single dead thing has ever been, is now, or ever shall be in the Cosmos. For the Father willed that the Cosmos <margin>16</margin> should be a **Living Being** <note>original: "zoon"</note> as long as it holds together; therefore, it must also be a God. How then, my son, could there be dead things in God, in the image of the Father, in the Fullness of Life? For "deadness" is corruption, and corruption is destruction. How then can any part of the incorruptible be corrupted, or any part of God be destroyed? — **Tat:** Do the living beings within it not die then, Father, since they are parts of it? — **Hermes:** Speak fair words, my son! You are led astray by the name given to what is happening. For they do not die, my son, but as composite bodies, they are **dissolved**. This dissolution is not death, but...

### CORPUS HERMETICUM

...the <note>original: "διάλυσις" (dialysis)</note> dissolution of the mixture. It is dissolved not so that it might be destroyed, but so that it may become new. For what is the activity of life? Is it not motion? What, then, in the cosmos is motionless? Nothing, my son.

<margin>17</margin> Does not even the earth seem motionless to you, father?

No, my son; rather, it alone is both many-motioned and stable. How would it not be ridiculous for the nurse of all things to be motionless—she who brings forth and gives birth to all things? For it is impossible for one who brings forth to do so without motion. You asked a most ridiculous thing: whether the fourth part <note>Referring to Earth as one of the four classical elements: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note> is idle; for a motionless body signifies nothing other than idleness.

<margin>18</margin> Know then, my son, that as a universal rule, everything that exists in the cosmos is moved, <insert>either by decrease or increase</insert>. And that which is moved also lives. But it is not necessary for every living thing to remain the same <insert>always</insert>. For while the cosmos as a whole is changeless, my son, all its parts are changeable; yet nothing is corruptible or destroyed. These terms <note>i.e., "death" and "destruction"</note> merely disturb mankind. For "birth" is not the <insert>beginning of life</insert>, but only the beginning of perception; nor is "change" death, but rather forgetfulness. Since these things are so, all things <insert>from which every living creature is composed</insert> are immortal: matter, <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "pneuma"; often referring to the "breath of life" or a subtle material vehicle for the soul</note>, and soul. Therefore, every living creature is immortal because of the immortality of these components.

<margin>19</margin> But above all, <insert>immortal</insert> is Man, who is both receptive of God and co-essential with God. For God speaks to this living creature alone: by night through dreams, and by day through symbols. And through all things He foretells the future to him—through birds, through entrails, through spirit, and through the oak <note>A reference to ancient methods of divination, such as the rustling leaves of the sacred oaks at Dodona</note>. Wherefore Man also professes to know things past, present, and future.

<margin>20 a</margin> Observe this also, my son: that each of the living creatures frequents one part of the cosmos—the aquatic ones the water, the land-dwellers the earth, and the winged ones the air. But Man...

Birth is not a beginning of life, but only a beginning of consciousness; and the change to another state is not death, but oblivion. And this being so, all the things of which every living creature is composed, —gross matter, and vital spirit, and soul,—are immortal; and so, by reason of their immortality, every living creature is immortal.

->*BOOK XIII*<-

### A secret discourse of Hermes Trismegistus to his son Tat [on the mountain] concerning rebirth [and the promise of silence]

<margin>1</margin> In your general discourses, O Father, you spoke in riddles and not clearly when discussing divinity. <insert>You did not reveal it</insert> for you said that no one can be saved before rebirth, <insert>you did not reveal it [to me]</insert>. Even when I became your suppliant <note>A "suppliant" is one who makes a humble, earnest plea to a superior.</note> ⌜during the passage on the mountain⌝ after you had conversed with me, and I [asked] to learn the discourse on rebirth—because this alone out of all things I am ignorant of—<insert>you did not yet deem me worthy</insert> <insert>to have it handed down to me</insert>. Who is the man that is brought into being by the Rebirth? — *Hermes*. He that is born by that birth is another; he is a god, and son of God. He is the All, and is in all; for he has no part in corporeal <note>physical or material</note> substance; he partakes of the substance of things intelligible <note>original: "noētos" — referring to things understood by the mind rather than the senses</note>,¹ being wholly composed of Powers of God. — *Tat*. Your words are riddles, father; you do not speak to me as a father to his son. — *Hermes*. This sort of thing cannot be taught, my son; but God, when he so wills, recalls it to our memory.² — *Tat*. But **3** what you say is impossible, father; it does violence to common sense. When you treat me thus, I have good reason to ask, ‘Am I an alien to my father’s race?’ Do not grudge me this boon, father; I am your true-born son; explain to me what manner of thing the Rebirth is. — *Hermes*. What can I say, my son? This thing cannot be taught; and it is not possible for you to see it with your organs of sight, which are fashioned out of material elements. I can tell you nothing but this; I see that by God’s mercy there has come to be in me a form which is not fashioned out of matter, and I have passed forth out of myself, and entered into an immortal body. I am not now the man I was; I have been born again in Mind <note>original: "Nous" — the divine intellect</note>, and the bodily shape which was mine before has been put away from me. I am no longer an object coloured and tangible, a thing of spatial dimensions; I am now alien to all this, and to all that you perceive when you gaze with bodily eyesight. To such eyes as yours, my son, I am not now visible. — *Tat*. Father, you have driven me to raving madness. **4** Will you tell me that I do not at this moment see my own self? — *Hermes*. Would that you too, my son, had passed forth out of *yourself*, so that you might have seen, not as men see dream-figures in their sleep, but as one who is awake. — *Tat*. # LITTLE BOOK XIII

Truth <gloss>1</gloss> has come to us, and on it has followed the Good, with Life and Light. No longer has there come upon us any of the torments of darkness; they have flown away with rushing wings.

<margin>10</margin>
Thus, my son, has the intellectual being <gloss>2</gloss> <note>original: "Logos"</note> been made up in us; and by its coming to be, we have been made gods. Whoever then has by God's mercy attained to this divine birth, abandons bodily sense; he knows himself to be composed of Powers of God, and knowing this, is glad.—

<margin>11 a</margin>
*Tat.* Father, God has made me a new being, and I perceive things now, not with bodily eyesight, but by the working of mind.—*Hermes.* Even so it is, my son, when a man is born <margin>13 a</margin> again; it is no longer body of three dimensions that he perceives, but the incorporeal.—*Tat.* Father, now that I see in mind, I see myself to be the All. I am in heaven and in earth, in <margin>11 b</margin> water and in air; I am in beasts and plants; I am a babe in the womb, and one that is not yet conceived, and one that has been born; I am present everywhere.—*Hermes.* Now, my son, you know what the Rebirth is.—

<margin>11 c</margin>
[*Tat.* But tell me further; how is it that the torments of darkness, which are twelve in number, are driven off by ten Powers? How does this come about, thrice-greatest one?—*Hermes.* This earthly tabernacle, <gloss>3</gloss> <note>A metaphor for the physical body, common in Hellenistic and early Christian thought.</note> my son, out of which <margin>12</margin> we have passed forth, has been put together by the working of the Zodiac, which produces manifold forms of one and the same thing <gloss>4</gloss> to lead men astray; and as the Signs of which the Zodiac consists are twelve in number, the forms produced by it, my son, fall into twelve divisions. But at the same time they are inseparable, being united in their action; for the reckless vehemence of irrational impulse is indivisible. It is with good reason then that they all depart together, as I said before. And it is also in accordance with reason that they are driven out by ten Powers, that is, by the Decad; <term>Decad: The number ten, considered by Pythagoreans and Hermeticists as a symbol of perfection and the return to unity.</term> for the Decad, my son, is

<gloss>1</gloss> Or 'Reality'.
<gloss>2</gloss> I. e. that which was previously called the Logos.
<gloss>3</gloss> I. e. the body.
<gloss>4</gloss> These 'manifold forms' are the several 'torments', i. e. the twelve different kinds of evil passion.

## THE HERMETIC BODY OF WRITINGS

For the number ten, my son, is the generator of souls. Life and Light are united as a unity <note>original: "henas" (ἑνάς). # BOOK XIII

> Thou, my Unselfishness <note>original: "autousia" - likely referring to the essential self or the divine essence within</note>, praise the All through me;

# CORPUS HERMETICUM
<note>The "Hermetic Body of Writing," a collection of Greek texts attributed to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note>

### BOOK XIV

### Hermes Trismegistus to Asclepius: Greetings.
<note>original: "Ἑρμοῦ τοῦ τρισμεγίστου Ἀσκληπιῷ εὖ φρονεῖν." The phrase "εὖ φρονεῖν" literally means "to be of sound mind" or "to think well," used here as a formal greeting wishing the recipient wisdom.</note>

**1** Since my son Tat, in your absence, desired to learn the nature of existing things, and would not allow me to postpone the matter—as he is my son and has only recently arrived at the threshold of knowledge—I was compelled to speak at greater length about each particular point, so that the contemplation <term>theoria: a way of seeing or understanding divine truths</term> might be easy for him to follow. But for you, I have selected the most essential chapters of what was said and wished to send them in a brief letter, interpreting them in a more mystical <note>or "more secret"</note> way, as is fitting for one of your great stature and knowledge of nature.

**2** If all visible things have been born and continue to be born <note>original: "γέγονε καὶ γίνεται" — have come into being and are coming into being</note>—and that which is born is not made by itself but by another—and since there are many things born, or rather, all visible things are born, and all are different and not alike—and since that which is made is made by another, there must be someone who makes these things. And this Creator must be unborn, so that he may be older than the things that are born. For I say that things born are made by another; and among things that are born, it is impossible for anything to be older than all else, except for that which is unborn.

**3** This Creator is one, and superior to all, and alone truly wise in all things, as he has nothing older than himself. For he rules over the multitude of things being made by his greatness, and over the variety of things made by the continuity of his creation. Since the things born are visible, he too is visible; for he creates for this very purpose: that he may be visible. Therefore, as he is always creating, he is always visible.

**4** Thus it is worthy to understand, and having understood, to wonder, and having wondered, to count oneself blessed, as one who has come to know the Father.

---

In Book XIV, I have used the readings of manuscript R and the Turnebus edition.

->*BOOK XIV*<-

### Hermes Trismegistus writes to Asclepius, wishing him health of mind.

<margin>1</margin>In your absence, my son Tat desired to be taught the nature of things, and would not let me postpone his instruction; and as he was young, and had only just begun to learn the <term>gnosis</term> <note>Gnosis refers to "spiritual knowledge" or direct insight into the divine nature, rather than mere intellectual learning.</note>, I was obliged to discourse to him on each several matter at some length, in order to make it easy for him to understand the doctrine. But since you are older, and have knowledge of the nature of things, I have thought fit to select and send to you in writing, in the form of a short summary, the most important of the truths I taught him.

<margin>2</margin>The things presented to our sight are many, and all different, and not like to one another; and seeing that all these things have come into being, and are ever coming into being, and that things which come into being are brought into being by another, there must be one who makes these things. And he who makes them cannot have been generated <note>original: "not generated" - meaning he was not created or born, but has always existed.</note>; for he must be prior to the things that are generated. These things, as I said, are brought into being by another; and it is impossible that anything should be prior to them all, save only that which has not been generated.

<margin>3</margin>And the Maker is one; he is mightier than all, and he alone is truly wise in all things, for there is nothing that is prior to him. He rules over the multitude of things made, in virtue of his greatness; and he rules over all their differences, because he makes things without intermission. And inasmuch as the things generated are seen, the Maker also can be seen; for to this end he makes them, that he may be seen. Since then he is at all times making things, he can be seen at all times.

<margin>4</margin>Thus is it meet for us to think, and thus thinking, to marvel, and marvelling, to deem ourselves blest, in that we have come to

# CORPUS HERMETICUM

For what is sweeter than a true father? Who then is this, and how shall we come to know him? Is it right to assign to him alone the title of "God," or that of "Creator," or that of "Father"? Or perhaps all three: "God" because of his power, "Creator" because of his activity <note>original: "energeia," referring to the actualizing force of the divine</note>, and "Father" because of his goodness. For in his power he is distinct from the things that come into being, but his activity consists in the very fact that all things are coming into being <insert>and he is good...</insert>.

**5** Therefore, having rid ourselves of talkativeness and idle speech, we must understand these two things: that which is produced and the one who produces. For there is nothing in between these, nor any third thing. Thus, when you think of all things and hear of all things, remember these two; and consider that these are the All, placing nothing in doubt <insert>or in a hidden corner</insert>, whether of the things above or the things below, whether of the divine or the changeable <note>The text emphasizes that the entire universe, from the highest heavens to the lowest matter, follows this binary rule</note>. For the All is two things: that which is produced and the one who produces. And it is impossible for the one to be separated from the other; for it is not possible for the producer to exist without the product, <insert>nor the product without the producer.</insert> For each of them is exactly this: therefore, one cannot be separated from the other, <insert>just as</insert> a thing cannot be separated from itself. For if the producer is nothing else than the act of producing alone—simple and uncompounded—it is necessary that <insert>he produces this very thing for himself, for whom the act of producing is the very birth of the producer</insert>. And it is impossible for anything produced to be produced by itself; but since it is produced, it must be produced by another. Without the producer, the thing generated neither comes into being nor exists. For the one without the other loses its own nature <note>The author argues that "Creator" and "Creation" are relative terms that define each other's existence</note>. If, then, it is admitted that beings are two—the produced and the producer—they are one by their union: the one leading and the other following. God the producer is the leader, and the thing produced is the follower, of whatever sort it may be.

**7** And do not be on your guard because of the variety of things produced, fearing that you might attach lowliness or lack of glory to God. For he has only one glory: the making of all things, and this is the very essence of...

# BOOK XIV

recognize our Father; for what is dearer to a son than his true father? Who is he then, and how are we to recognize him? Are we to say that it is right that the name of God alone should be assigned to him, or that of Maker, or that of Father? Nay, all three names are his; he is rightly named God by reason of his power, and Maker by reason of the work he does, and Father by reason of his goodness. In power he surpasses the things that come into being; he is at work in bringing all things into being; (and his goodness is shown in . . .). <note>The text is fragmentary here; the original Greek likely continued to describe the specific manifestation of divine goodness.</note>

We ought therefore to get rid of superfluous and idle talk, and **5** keep our thoughts fixed upon these two, the thing made and the Maker. Between them there is nothing; there is no third. In all your thoughts then, and in all that you are told, keep in mind these two, and hold them to be all that is, making no difficulty or mystery about anything in heaven above or here below, divine or mutable <note>original: "mutable" refers to things subject to change or decay</note>. All things are but two, that which is made and that which makes. And the one cannot be separated from the other; the Maker cannot exist apart from the thing made, nor the thing made, apart from the Maker. Each of them is just that and nothing else; and so the one can no more be parted from the other than it can be parted from itself. For **6** if the Maker is nothing else but that which makes, and that alone, simple and incomposite, he must of necessity make . . . . And again, what is made cannot be made by itself; if it is made, it must of necessity be made by another; without the Maker, the thing made can neither come into being nor exist. If the one is wanting, the other ceases to be itself. If then it is admitted that there are two things, that which is made and that which makes, these two are one in virtue of their union, the one of them going before, and the other following after. It is the Maker, that is, God, that goes before: and it is the thing made, whatsoever it be, that follows after.

And if the things made vary in quality, do not for that reason **7** hesitate through fear of degrading God, or impairing his glory. For God's glory is this, and this alone, that he makes all things;
