<meta>This page continues the philosophical discourse on the nature of God as the sole Creator and the origin of perceived "evil" or "imperfection" in the material world.</meta>

# CORPUS HERMETICUM
<note>The "Hermetic Corpus" is a collection of Greek texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, exploring theology, philosophy, and the divine nature of the universe.</note>

The making of things is, as it were, the very essence of God; and for Him who makes, one must not consider anything to be evil or shameful. For these are the "passions" <note>original: "pathe" — here meaning accidental qualities or side effects</note> that follow upon the process of becoming <note>original: "genesis" — the act of being born or created into the material world</note>, just as rust attaches to copper or grime to the body. But the coppersmith did not create the rust, nor did the one who fathered <insert>the body</insert> create the grime. In the same way, God did not create evil; rather, the persistence of the process of becoming causes it to bloom forth, as it were. And for this reason, God created change, as a kind of purification of the process of becoming.

**8** Furthermore, if it is possible for the same painter to create heaven, earth, and sea, and gods, and men, and all the unreasoning creatures and inanimate things, is it then impossible for God to make all things? Oh, the great folly and ignorance concerning God! For such people suffer the most strange of all things: while claiming to speak well of God by not attributing the making of all things to Him, they neither know God, and in addition to this ignorance, they commit the greatest impieties against Him, attributing to Him a "passion" <note>a limitation or human-like emotion</note> of either arrogance or inability. For if He does not make all things, He either does not make them because He is prideful, or because He is unable; both of which are impious thoughts.

**9** For God has only one "passion": the Good. And He who is Good is neither prideful nor unable. <insert>For this is what God is: the Good; to whom belongs all power to make all things.</insert> Everything that is created has come into being by God—that is, by the Good and the One who is able to make all things. <insert>For this is what God is: the Good; and to the Good belongs all power to make all things.</insert>

**10** If you wish to learn how He makes things, and how the things that are made come into being, you may see a most beautiful and perfect image. Observe a farmer casting seed into the earth: here wheat, there barley, and elsewhere some other kind of seed. Observe—

# BOOK XIV

and the making of things is, so to speak, God’s very being. In relation to the Maker himself, nothing is to be deemed evil or foul. Evil and foulness are accidents <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that is not essential to the nature of a thing, like the color of a shirt rather than the shirt itself.</note> which follow on the making of things, just as rust forms on metal, or dirt collects on a man’s body; but the metal-worker did not make the rust, nor did the father who begot the body make the dirt. And even so, God is not the author of evil; but it is the lasting on of the things made that causes evil to break out on them. And that is why God has subjected things to change; for by transmutation <note>original: "transmutation" — the process of changing from one form or state into another.</note> the things made are purged of evil.

<margin>8</margin>The same painter can make heaven and earth and sea, gods and men, and beasts of every kind, and things without life; and is it impossible for God to make all things? What fools men are! How little they know of God! It is a strange mistake; such men profess to honour God by refusing to ascribe to him the making of all things; but they know not God, and not only that, but they are guilty of the worst impiety against him; for they attribute a bad quality to God; they make him out to be either disdainful or incapable. If God does not make all things, it must be either because he disdains to make things, or because he is not able; and it is impious to say that. God has one quality, <margin>9</margin>and one alone, the quality of goodness; and he who is good is neither disdainful nor incapable. All that has come into being then has been brought into being by God, that is, by him who is good, and is able to make all; for God is the Good, and the Good has all power to make all.

<margin>10</margin>And if you wish to know how God makes things, and how the things made come into being, you may see an image of it,— a goodly sight, and very like. <note>1</note> Perhaps, '⟨And some people will find it difficult to understand.⟩ For my teacher', etc.
<note>2</note> Perhaps, 'his', or 'our'.
<note>3</note> Perhaps, 'with a devout mind'.
<note>4</note> That is, from the Egyptian language.

This passage is quoted in a different form by Nicephorus Gregoras <note>A 14th-century Byzantine scholar and historian.</note>. According to him, it runs thus: 'As far as it is in your power, my King, keep ⟨untranslated⟩ the teaching which I have transmitted to you, in order that secrets so holy may not be revealed to Greeks, and that the disdainful mode of speech of the Greeks, with its showy tricks of style, may not reduce to impotence the impressive strength of the language, and the cogent force of the words. For such teachings, when expressed in our native language, convey their meaning clearly; for the very quality of the sounds, and the power of the Egyptian words, have in it (that is, in our native language?) the efficacy of the things signified; but when distorted (by translation), these teachings become obscure and ineffectual.'

After "they possess the efficacy," Nicephorus adds: "but when distorted they become both obscure and ineffectual."

# BOOK XVI

In this way the <term>Demiurgus</term> <note>The "Craftsman" or Creator-God who fashions the physical world</note> (that is, the Sun) brings together heaven and earth, sending down true being <note>original: "οὐσία" (ousia); here referring to light or life-force</note> from above, and raising up matter from below. And he <unclear>orders all things</unclear> <note>Reconstructed from fragmentary text</note> in connection with himself, both drawing <unclear>life</unclear> to himself, and giving forth <unclear>life</unclear> from himself; for he lavishes light on all things without stint. For the Sun is he whose beneficent workings operate not only in heaven, but also <margin>6</margin> upon earth, and penetrate even to the lowest depths. The material body of the Sun is <unclear>the source of visible light</unclear>; and if there is such a thing as a substance not perceptible by sense <note>original: "νοητὴ οὐσία" (noētē ousia); often translated as 'intelligible substance' or that which is understood by the mind rather than the eyes</note>, the light of the Sun must be the receptacle of that substance. 

But of what that substance consists, or whence it flows in, God only knows. The Sun, being near to us in position, and like to us in nature, presents himself to our sight. God does not manifest himself to us; we cannot see him, and it is only by conjecture, and with hard effort, that we apprehend him in thought. But it is not by conjecture that we <margin>7</margin> contemplate the Sun; we see him with our very eyes. He shines most brightly on all the universe, illuminating both the world above and the world below; for he is stationed in the midst, and wears the <term>Kosmos</term> <note>The universe conceived as an ordered, harmonious system</note> as a wreath around him. And so he lets the Kosmos go on its course, not leaving it far separated from himself, but, to speak truly, keeping it joined to himself; for like a skilled driver, he has made fast and bound to himself the chariot of the Kosmos, lest it should rush away in disorder. And the reins are <unclear>his light-rays</unclear>.

In this wise he makes all things <note>Meaning he gives life to all things</note>. He assigns to the immortals <margin>8</margin> their everlasting permanence, and with that part of his light which tends upwards (that is, the light which he sends forth from that side of his light which faces heaven), he maintains the immortal parts of the Kosmos <note>Referring to the heavenly bodies or stars</note>; but with the light which is shed downward, and illuminates all the sphere of water, earth, and air, he puts life into the things in this region of the Kosmos, and stirs them up to <unclear>change</unclear>.

<margin>9</margin> Within these parts of the world, he <note>Referring to the Sun or the Creator</note> transforms and reshapes living beings [in the manner of a spiral], changing them from one genus to another and from species to species, exchanging them through a mutual transformation, just as he does when crafting the great bodies <note>The celestial bodies or elements</note>. The equality of all these multiform images is varied, so that infinite types of qualities appear to be born from the intervals between them; yet they are joined together <margin>3 a</margin> for this purpose: so that the whole appears to be one, and all things appear to proceed from the one. Therefore, the elements from which the entire world is formed are four: fire, water, earth, and air. There is one world, one soul, and one God.

For the logic of divinity, which must be known by a divine intention of the senses, is most like a torrential river rushing headlong from the heights with grasping speed; because of this, it outruns the attention not only of those listening, but even of those treating the subject themselves, by its swift velocity.

<margin>3 c</margin> Heaven, therefore—the god perceived by the senses—is the administrator of all bodies, whose increases and decreases are allotted to the sun and the moon. But of Heaven itself, and of the soul, and of all things that are within the world, the governor is God himself; he is the creator <note>original: "effector"</note> of all genera and all species through the nature of things. For from all the aforementioned things, of which the same God is the governor of all, the frequent movement of the soul is carried, flowing through the world and through the soul of all genera and all species through the nature of things. The world, moreover, was prepared by God as a receptacle for all-formed species; and nature, by imaging the world through these species by means of the four elements, <margin>4</margin> leads forth all things to the heavens so that they may be pleasing in the sight of God. Furthermore, all things hanging from above are divided into species in the manner I am about to describe. The species of all things follow their own <term>genus|The general category or "family" to which a specific type (species) belongs</term>, so that the genus is the substantiality of the species, and the species is a small part of the genus.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue known as the Asclepius, a core text of the Hermetic tradition, focusing on the hierarchy of being and the relationship between universal "kinds" and individual "forms."</meta>

# ASCLEPIUS

The genus <note>The Latin *genus* refers to a general "class" or "category" of being.</note> of the gods, therefore, creates species <note>The Latin *species* refers to the specific "forms" or "individuals" that belong to a genus.</note> of gods out of itself. Likewise the genus of demons; similarly the genus of humans, of birds, and of all things which the world contains within itself; each genus generates species similar to itself. There is also another genus of living thing, which is indeed without a soul, and yet not lacking in senses, whereby it both rejoices in benefits and suffers from adversities by which it is diminished and harmed: I speak of all those things which live upon the earth by the health of their roots, whose species are scattered throughout the whole earth. Heaven itself is full of gods; their species are immortal. Moreover, the aforementioned genera inhabit the regions up to the places of the gods; the species of all these things are immortal. For a species is a part of a genus, as a human is a part of humanity; it must necessarily follow the quality of its own genus. From this it follows that, although all genera are immortal, not all species are immortal. For in the case of divinity, both the genus itself and its species are immortal. Regarding the other things, although they perish as individuals, the genera—whose eternity is inherent to the genus—are preserved by the fecundity of birth. Therefore, the species are mortal, while the eternity of the genus remains; thus, a human is mortal, but humanity is immortal.

**5** All species are very similar to their genera; nevertheless, the species of all genera are mixed among all genera.

There are certain things which were made beforehand, and certain things which are made from those things which have been made. These things which are made, therefore, are made either by gods and demons, or by humans. For it is impossible for bodies to be conformed to a genus without the divine will, or to be shaped into species without the help of demons; and inanimate things cannot be established or cared for without humans.

Whosoever of the demons, therefore, flowing down from their genus into a species, are joined by chance to the divine genus through proximity and fellowship with some species of the divine genus, they are considered similar to gods. But those species of demons which persist in the quality of their own genus—

# ASCLEPIUS I

The individual is a part of the kind. Thus the god-kind produces individual gods, and the daemon-kind <note>The term "daemon" here refers to intermediary spirits between gods and humans, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> produces individual daemons. And so too the kind or race of men, and that of birds, and those of all beings which the universe contains, generate individuals of like form to their kind. And there is yet another kind of living beings, <gloss>original Latin: *animalis*, corresponding to the Greek for "living thing"</gloss> which are devoid of soul <gloss>original Latin: *sine anima*, corresponding to the Greek for "soulless"</gloss> indeed, yet not without sensation, <gloss>original Latin: *sensus*, corresponding to the Greek for "perceptions"</gloss> so that they are gladdened by all that does them good, and suffer pain from all that impairs and harms them. This kind consists of all things which are implanted in the soil, and spring into life with firm-fixed <gloss>original Latin: *incolumitas*, implying safety or stability</gloss> roots; and the individuals of this kind are spread abroad over all the earth. 

Heaven itself is filled with gods; and the gods are individually immortal. The other kinds of which I have spoken dwell in the space which extends from earth to the abode of the gods; and in all these kinds, the individuals are mortal. For the individual is a part of the kind—as a man, for instance, is a part of mankind—and must necessarily agree in quality with the kind of which it is a part. Hence, though all kinds are immortal, not all individuals are immortal. In the case of the gods, both the kind and the individuals are immortal. All other kinds, though they perish in their individuals, are kept in being by their reproductive fertility. <gloss>original Latin: *nascendi*, referring to the process of birth or generation</gloss> Thus the individuals are mortal, but the kind is everlasting; <gloss>The Greek sense implies that while the specific forms are mortal, the genus is eternal</gloss> so that men are mortal, but mankind is immortal.

# ASCLEPIUS

...those who truly love mankind are called <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, daemons are not evil spirits but intermediary divine beings or guardian spirits</note>. The nature of man is similar, and even more expansive. For the human race is multiform and varied; coming from the aforementioned source above, it creates many necessary connections with almost all other species through its shared fellowship. Because of this, the person who joins himself to the gods through divine religion—using the mind by which he is linked to the gods—comes close to the gods themselves. So too does he who joins himself to the daemons. Those who are content with the middle-ground of their own race remain purely human. Other types of men will be similar to those species with whom they have joined themselves.

## 6 a

For these reasons, O Asclepius, man is a great miracle, a living being to be adored and honored. For he passes into the nature of a god as if he were a god himself; he understands the race of daemons, knowing he originates from the same source. He even looks down upon the purely human part of his nature, putting his trust in the divinity of his other part. O, how much more happily tempered is the nature of man! He is joined to the gods by a shared divinity; he despises that part of himself which is earthly; and all other things to which he knows himself necessary by celestial arrangement, he binds to himself with a bond of love. He looks up to heaven and <insert>he tends the earth</insert>. Now of all the different kinds or races, those which possess soul <note>original: "Animalia" (Greek: ἔμψυχα), referring to living beings with a soul, including animals and humans</note> have roots extending downward to them from above; and those which are soulless <note>original: "inanimalia" (Greek: ἄψυχα), referring to plants or inanimate objects</note> sprout from roots which reach upward from below. <meta>This page continues the Hermetic dialogue "Asclepius," specifically discussing the creation of the cosmos and the unique dual nature of humanity as a bridge between the divine and the earthly.</meta>

# ASCLEPIUS

I call this second god "perceivable" <note>original: "sensibilem." This refers to the physical universe (the Cosmos) which can be experienced through the senses, as opposed to the purely intellectual first God.</note> not because he himself possesses senses (for whether he senses or not is a matter we shall discuss at another time), but because he falls within the perception of those who see. Since, therefore, the Supreme God made this second god from himself as the first, and second only to himself, and since he appeared beautiful to him, being most full of the goodness of all things, God loved him as the offspring of his own divinity. Therefore, because he is so great and good, he willed there to be another who could contemplate that being whom he had made from himself; and at the same time, he made man to be an imitator of his own reason and care. For the will of God is itself the highest perfection, since for him, willing and perfecting are completed in one and the same moment of time.

When, therefore, he had made man <term>essential</term> <note>original Greek: "οὐσιώδη" (ousiōdē), meaning consisting of true essence or spiritual substance.</note>, and noticed that man could not be mindful of all things unless he were covered with a worldly garment, he sheltered him in a bodily home. He ordained that all men should be so, blending and mixing from both natures into one as much as was necessary. Thus, he shapes man from soul and body—that is, from eternal and mortal nature—blending and mixing from both natures into one as much as was necessary, so that a living being thus shaped could satisfy both of his origins: both to wonder at and adore celestial things, and to tend to and govern earthly things.

By "earthly things," however, I do not mean only water and earth, which are two of the four elements that nature has subjected to humans, but those things which are done by humans, either in these elements or from them: such as the cultivation of the earth itself, pastures, building, harbors, navigation, communication, and the mutual exchange of services, which is the strongest bond of humanity among themselves...

# ASCLEPIUS I

In the same way, does he not worthily and fittingly obey God’s will? For since the world is God’s handiwork, he who maintains and heightens its beauty by his care is co-operating with the will of God; he contributes the aid of his bodily strength, and by his daily care and labor, he ensures things assume the shape and appearance that God’s purpose designed. What shall be his reward? Shall it not be that which our ancestors received, and which we pray with heartfelt piety that we too may receive, if God in his mercy <note>original Latin: *pietas*, perhaps translating the Greek *eleos* meaning mercy or compassion</note> is pleased to grant it? And that reward is this: when our term of service is ended, when we are stripped of our guardianship <note>original Latin: *custodia*, referring to the soul's duty as a 'watchman' or 'prisoner' in the material world</note> of the material world and freed from the bonds of mortality, he will restore us, cleansed and sanctified, to the primal condition of <margin>**12 a**</margin> that higher part of us which is divine.

—*Asclepius:* That is right and true, Trismegistus.

—*Trismegistus:* Yes, such is the reward of those who spend their lives in piety toward God above, and in care <note>original: *diligenter viventes*, likely meaning "living in a state of service or attendance"</note> of the world around them. But those who have lived evil and impious lives are not permitted to return to heaven. For such men, a shameful transmigration <note>The movement of a soul into a new body after death</note> into bodies of another kind is ordained—bodies unworthy to be the home of a holy mind. <note>The translator suggests this refers to the bodies of beasts.</note>

—*Asclepius:* According to your teaching <note>original: *rationis sermo*, the "discourse of reason"</note> then, Trismegistus, souls have at stake in this earthly life their hope of eternity <note>original: *aeternitas*</note> in the life to come.

—*Trismegistus:* Yes. But some cannot believe this; and some regard it as an empty tale; and to some, perhaps, it seems a thing to mock at. For in our bodily life on earth, the enjoyment derived from possessions is a pleasant thing; and the pleasure which they yield grips the soul by the throat, so to speak, and holds it down to earth, compelling it to cling to man’s mortal part.

Moreover, there are some whose ungenerous temper grudges <note>original: *invidens immortalitate*, "envying them their immortality"</note> <margin>**12 b**</margin> men the gift of immortality, and will not allow them to gain knowledge of that part of them which is divine. For speaking as a prophet speaks, I tell you that in times to come, no one will pursue philosophy in singleness of heart. Philosophy is nothing else than striving through constant contemplation <note>original: *frequens obtutus*, a "steady gazing" or "frequent looking" upon the divine</note> and saintly piety to attain to knowledge of God; <note>original: *cognoscere divinitatem*, "to know the divinity"</note> but there will be many who will...

<summary>Hermes Trismegistus explains that humans serve as co-creators by caring for the physical world, earning a return to a divine state, while the impious face reincarnation into lower forms. He warns that future generations will lose the true path of philosophy, distracted by material pleasures and greed.</summary>

Therefore, the men who come after us, deceived by the cunning of <term>sophists</term> <note>rhetoricians or philosophers who use clever but fallacious arguments</note>, will be turned away from true, pure, and holy philosophy. For to worship the divinity with a simple mind and soul, to venerate his works, and to give thanks to the will of God—which alone is most full of goodness—this is a philosophy violated by no intrusive curiosity of the mind.

Matter⁸ is the recipient⁹ of all forms;¹⁰ and the changes and unbroken successions¹¹ of the forms (are wrought by means of spirit). The process is directed by God, who distributes (life) to all things in the universe, giving to each one of them as much as it needs. Into all things he infuses spirit, assigning it to each in larger measure, in proportion as the thing stands higher in the scale of being.¹²

These¹³ then are the primary things, the prior things, the heads <margin>17 c</margin> or first principles¹⁴ of all things in the universe; for all cosmic¹⁵ things are contained in them, or wrought by means of them, or made of them.

# ASCLEPIUS III

Regarding this matter of importance, <note>original Latin: "Quod etiam... quam plurimis"; likely translating the Greek: "which also seems to be a great thing to most people"</note> I hold that no such thing as void exists, or can have existed in the past, or ever will exist. For all the several parts <note>original: "membra," likely translating "moria" (parts/limbs)</note> of the Kosmos <term>Kosmos: the universe viewed as a well-ordered and beautiful whole</term> are wholly filled with bodies of various qualities and forms, <note>original: "qualitate formaque diversis"</note> each having its own shape and magnitude; and thus the Kosmos as a whole is full and complete. <note>original: "perfectus," translating "teleios" (perfect or finished)</note> Of these bodies, some are larger, some are smaller; and they differ in the greater or lesser firmness <note>original: "validitas," referring to solidity or density</note> of their substance. Those of them which are of firmer substance are more easily seen, as are also those which are larger; whereas smaller bodies, and those which are of less firm substance, are almost or quite invisible, and it is only by the sense of touch that we are made aware of their existence. Hence many people have come to think that these bodies do not exist, and that there are void spaces; but that is impossible. 

And the like holds good of what is called ‘the extramundane’ <term>extramundane: that which exists outside the physical boundaries of the world</term>, if indeed any such thing exists; for I hold that not even the region outside the Kosmos is void, seeing that it is filled with things apprehensible by thought alone, that is, with things of like nature with its own divine being. <note>The translator reconstructs the lost Greek original here: "For not even that which is called the region outside the world, if indeed it is anything, seems to me to be void, being thus full of intelligible things, that is, things similar to its own divinity."</note> And so our Kosmos also,—the sensible universe <term>sensible universe: the world that can be perceived by the five senses</term>, as it is called,—is wholly filled with bodies, and living bodies, suited to its character. The shapes presented by these bodies to our sight differ in magnitude; some of these shapes are very large; others are very small, when the distance of the objects makes them appear small to us; and some things, on account of their extreme minuteness or tenuity, are wholly invisible to us, and are consequently supposed by many people to be non-existent.

<margin>33 c</margin>
And so, Asclepius, you must not call anything void, without saying what the thing in question is void of, as when you say that a thing is void of fire or water or the like. For it is possible for <note>The translator suggests the Greek original meant: "For even if it should happen that something appears to be void—for it is possible to be void of such [material] things—nevertheless, not even the smallest of things appearing to be void could be void of spirit and air."</note>

->ASCLEPIUS<-

[A space] cannot be empty of such things; even if what appears to be empty is small [or large], it cannot be a vacuum, for it is filled with <term>spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritu"; in this context, it refers to a vital, invisible breath or gas that permeates the universe</note> and air.

<margin>34 a</margin> We must say the same regarding "place"; this word by itself has no meaning to the intellect. For a "place" only becomes apparent by what it contains: if you remove the primary object, the meaning of the name is cut short. Therefore, we correctly speak of a "place for water," a "place for fire," or similar things. Just as it is impossible for a void to exist, so too a "place" cannot be identified on its own. For if you propose a place without that which occupies it, the place will seem empty; and I do not believe such a thing exists in the world. If there is no such thing as a void, then "place" does not appear as a thing in itself. <insert>Unless you add to it the dimensions of length, width, or height, just as one uses signs to mark the bodies of men.</insert>

<margin>18 b</margin> Thus, the World nourishes bodies, and the <term>spirit</term> nourishes souls. But <term>Sense</term> <note>original: "Sensus"; here meaning a higher spiritual perception or divine intelligence</note> is added to these, a heavenly gift by which humanity alone may be blessed—though not all people, but only the few whose minds are so constituted that they can receive such a great benefit. For just as the world is brightened by the sun, so the human mind shines with that light, and even more so. For whatever the sun illuminates is eventually deprived of light by the intervention of the earth when night comes; but once Sense has been mixed with the human soul, they become a single nature through a well-fused mixture, so that minds of this kind are never hindered by the errors of darkness.

Therefore, they have rightly called *Sense* the soul of the gods. I, however, do not say this of all gods, but of certain great and primary ones.

# ASCLEPIUS III

a thing to be void of such things as these, and it may consequently come to *seem* void; but the thing that seems void, however small it be, cannot possibly be empty of spirit <note>original: "pneuma" (πνεῦμα); can also be translated as "breath" or "wind"</note> and of air.

<margin>34 a</margin>
And the like must be said of Space. <note>original: "Locus" (τόπος)</note> The word 'space' is unmeaning when it stands alone; for it is only by regarding something which is in space, that we come to see what space is; and apart from the thing to which it belongs, <note>original: "Principali dempto" (ἀπόντος τοῦ προηγουμένου); literally "when the primary thing is taken away"</note> the meaning of the term 'space' is incomplete. Thus we may rightly speak of the space occupied by water, and fire, and so on, (but not of space alone.) For as there cannot be a void, so it is impossible to determine what space is, if you regard it by itself. For if you assume a space apart from something which is in it, it will follow that there is a void space; and I hold that there is no such thing as that in the universe. If void has no existence, <note>original: "Nihil" (μὴ ὄν); literally "non-being"</note> then it is impossible to find any real thing answering to the word 'space' taken by itself.

By the light of mind the human soul is illumined, <note>original: "Clarescit" (φωτίζεται)</note> as the world is illumined by the sun,—nay, in yet fuller measure. For all things on which the sun shines are deprived of his light from time to time by the interposition of the earth, when night comes on; but when mind has once been interfused with the soul of man, there results from the intimate blending of mind with soul a thing <note>original: "Natura" (φύσις); a "nature" or "essence"</note> that is one and indivisible, so that such men's thought is never obstructed by the darkness of error. <note>original: "Caliginum erroribus" (τῷ σκότῳ τῆς πλάνης); literally "the darkness of wandering"</note>

The Ruler of Heaven, or of whatsoever is included under the name ‘Heaven’, is Zeus the Highest <note>original: "Hypatos"</note>; for life is given to all beings by Zeus through the medium of Heaven.

The Ruler of the Decani <note>term: Decani (The thirty-six spirits or star-groups that rule over ten-degree segments of the zodiac)</note>,—that is, the thirty-six fixed stars which are called Horoscopes,—is the god named the Giver of All Forms <note>original: "Pantomorphos"</note>; he it is that gives to the individuals of each kind their diverse forms.

The seven spheres <note>The seven planetary bodies: Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, as they are called, have as their Ruler the deity called Fortune or Destiny, who changes all things according to the law of natural growth, working with a fixity which is immutable, and which yet is varied by everlasting movement.

The air is the instrument <note>original: "organum vel machina" / "organon"</note> with which all these gods work, and by means of which all is done. The Ruler of the air is the subordinate distributor <note>original: "dispensator" / "tamias"</note> of life; to him belongs the region <margin>**27 c**</margin> between heaven and earth; and we call him Zeus the Lowest <note>original: "Neatos"</note>.

Earth and sea are ruled by Zeus of the Underworld <note>original: "Chthonios"</note>; he it is that supplies nutriment to all mortal beings that have soul <note>original: "animantium" / "empsychōn", referring to living animals</note>, and to all trees that bear fruit; and it is by his power <note>original: "viribus" / "dynamei"</note> that the fruits of the earth are produced.

And there are other gods beside, whose powers and operations <note>original: "effectus" / "energeiai"</note> are distributed through all things that exist.

But God, who dwells above the summit of the highest heaven, <margin>**27 b**</margin> is present everywhere, and from all around he watches all things; his abode is beyond heaven, in a starless region, far removed from all things corporeal <note>Physical or bodily things</note>.

<summary>This page outlines the Hermetic hierarchy of the universe, identifying specific deities (various aspects of Zeus and the Giver of All Forms) who govern the stars, the planetary spheres, the air, and the earth. It concludes by distinguishing the supreme, incorporeal God who exists beyond the physical heavens.</summary>

# ASCLEPIUS

<margin>Chapter 19 c</margin> In this way, mortal things are joined to immortal ones, and things perceived by the senses are connected to those beyond the senses; indeed, the highest authority of governance obeys that supreme Lord. Since things are arranged in this manner, as they move from the lowest to the highest, all things are so interconnected and related to one another—mortal to mortal, and sensible to insensible—that they do not seem to be many, but rather one. For since all things hang from the One and flow down from Him, they are believed to be many when they are seen at a distance, but when united, they are one. <insert>Or rather two: that from which all things are made, and He by whom they are made; that is, the matter from which they arise, and the will of Him by whose command they are brought into being.</insert>

<margin>Chapter 34 c</margin> This world, which is called "sensible" <note>original: "sensibilis"; referring to the physical world perceived through the five senses</note>, is the receptacle of all sensible forms, qualities, or bodies; none of these can be given life without God. For God is all things, and from Him all things come, and all things are the product of His will and inimitable wisdom. This "All" is good, fitting, and wise, and it is perceptible and intelligible to Him alone: without this, nothing was, nor is, nor shall be. For all things are from Him, in Him, and through Him—various and multiform qualities, great quantities, magnitudes exceeding all measure, and forms of every kind. If you understand these things, O Asclepius, you will give thanks to God.

But if you observe the whole, you will learn by true reason that the sensible world itself, and all things within it, are woven from that higher world like <margin>Chapter 17 b</margin> a *garment.* For <term>Matter</term> <note>original Greek: "hyle" (ὕλη); the raw substance of the universe</note> is:

For every living being <note>original: "animal" - literally "that which has life"</note>, Asclepius, whatever be its kind <note>original: "genus"</note>, and whether that kind be mortal or immortal, rational <note>original: "rationalis" or "logikos"</note> or irrational, endowed with soul <note>original: "animans" or "empsychos"</note> or devoid of soul, bears the likeness of its kind, according as the character of that kind may be. But though each living being has in all respects the form which is proper to its kind, the individuals, while one and all have the same form, yet differ among themselves. For instance, though the human race has a common form, so that we can know from a man's appearance that he is a man, at the same time individual men, for all their sameness of form, yet differ one from another. For it is impossible that any single form should come into being which is exactly like a second, if they originate at different points of time, and at places differently situated; but the forms change at every moment in each hour of the revolution of that celestial circle <note>This refers to the Zodiac, the belt of heavens through which the planets move</note> in which resides the god whom we have named Pantomorphos <note>Greek for "The All-Formed One" or "He who takes all shapes"</note>. Thus the type <note>The generic or universal form of a species</note> persists unchanged, but generates at successive instants copies of itself as numerous and different as are the moments in the revolution of the sphere of heaven <note>original: "mundus" - here meaning the cosmos or the celestial firmament</note>;

<margin>36</margin>
*Asclepius.* And does the <term>Kosmos</term><note>The Universe, viewed as an ordered and harmonious system.</note> also, Trismegistus, change its forms?¹—*Trismegistus.* Why, you must have been asleep, Asclepius; you cannot have heard what I have been telling you all this while. What is the Kosmos, and of what is it composed, if not of things which have all come into being?² When you speak of the Kosmos then, you are speaking of sky, and earth, and the elements.³ And do not these change their forms as often as anything that exists? The sky⁴ is moist and dry, cold and hot, bright and obscured by turns; these are the rapidly alternating (sensible) forms included under the one (ideal or universal) form of the sky. The earth is ever passing through many changes of form; it generates produce, it nourishes the produce it has generated, it yields all manner of crops, with manifold differences of quality and quantity; and above all, it puts forth many sorts of trees, differing in the scent of their flowers and the taste of their fruits. Water takes different forms, now standing and now running. Fire undergoes many changes, and assumes godlike forms; thus the aspects⁵ of the sun and moon pass through all manner of forms; they are like our mirrors, and reproduce (the ideal or universal form) in visible copies with rival brilliance.

# ASCLEPIUS III

entered his mind through his senses, whenever he wills to do so;¹ <note>The Latin text suggests that God reveals his will through mental perceptions or sensory experiences.</note> and if a name is nothing more than a few syllables, and is restricted in length, so as to render possible the indispensable intercourse of man with man by speech and hearing;—if this is so, the full name of God must include the names of sense, and breath, and air, and all names that are contained in sense and breath and air,² or are uttered by means of them, or are composed of them. For I deem it impossible that he who is the maker of the universe in all its greatness, the Father or Master of all things, can be named by a single name, though it be made up of ever so many others; I hold that he is nameless <note>original: "innominem", meaning without a name</note>, or rather, that all names are names of him <note>original: "omninominem", meaning having all names</note>.³ For he in his unity is all things; so that we must either call all things by his name, or call him by the names of all things.

<margin>20 b</margin>
He, filled with all the fecundity of both sexes in one, and ever teeming with his own goodness,⁴ <note>original: "bonitas", referring to the Platonic concept of the Good</note> unceasingly brings into being all that he has willed to generate; and all that he wills is good. From his divine being has sprung the goodness of all things in this world below; and hence it is that all things are productive, and that their procreative power is adequate to ensure that all shall hereafter be as it is now, and as it has been in the past. For if you observe that final moment of time when, through frequent friction, we reach the point where both natures pour themselves into one another—as one <insert>the male</insert> emits the offspring and the other <insert>the female</insert> greedily seizes it and hides it within—at that moment, through the shared mingling, the females acquire masculine vigor and the males grow weary with feminine languor.

...to pursue the <insert>treatise</insert>, and to explain [[the treatise]] why the Divinity has deigned to bestow his own intelligence and discipline upon humans alone. Listen, therefore. <margin>23 b</margin> And since our discussion is now led toward the kinship and fellowship between men and gods, learn, O Asclepius, the power and strength of man. But the forms of the gods which humanity fashions are shaped from two natures: from the divine, which is purer and much more ⌜divine⌝, and from that which is below humans, that is, from the matter out of which they are fabricated. They are shaped not only with heads alone, but with all their limbs and their entire bodies. Thus humanity, always mindful of its nature and origin, perseveres in that imitation of divinity; just as the Father and Lord made the eternal gods to be like himself, so humanity fashions its own gods in the likeness of its own countenance. — *Asclepius:* Are you speaking of statues, Trismegistus? — *Trismegistus:* Statues, Asclepius. ->### ASCLEPIUS<-

[...of them; but whoever survives will be recognized as Egyptian only by his language, while in his actions he will seem like a foreigner.] Why do you weep, O Asclepius? <note>Asclepius is the student of Hermes Trismegistus in this dialogue.</note> Egypt will be persuaded to even more and much worse things than these, and she will be steeped in greater evils. She who was once holy, most loving of divinity, the only place on earth where the gods were brought down in reward for her devotion—the teacher of holiness and piety—will become an example of the greatest cruelty. **"And the number of the dead will far exceed the living; the survivor will be known as Egyptian only by his tongue, but in his behavior he will seem a stranger."**

**"O Egypt, Egypt! Of your religions only fables will remain, and these incredible to your descendants; only words carved in stone will remain to tell of your pious deeds."** And then, because of men's weariness, the world will no longer seem a thing to be wondered at or adored. This entire "Good" <note>original: "bonum"; referring to the created universe as a manifestation of God's goodness</note>—than which nothing better has been, is, or ever shall be seen—will be in danger. It will become a burden to men, and because of this, it will be despised. This whole world will no longer be loved: this inimitable work of God, this glorious construction, a "Good" composed of a multiform variety of images, a machine of God's will supporting his work without envy—a unified heap of all things in one that can be venerated, praised, and finally loved by those who behold it.

For darkness will be preferred to light, and death will be judged more useful than life. No one will look up to heaven. The religious man will be thought insane, the irreligious will be thought wise; the madman will be thought brave, and the worst man will be held as good. For the soul, and all things surrounding it—by which it was either born immortal or presumes it will attain immortality, according to what I have explained to you—will not only be a target for mockery but will even be considered vanity.

But believe me, a capital penalty will be established for anyone who devotes himself to the religion of the mind. <note>original: "mentis religioni"; likely referring to Gnosis or internal spiritual discipline</note> New rights will be established, a new law.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical dialogue known as the Asclepius, specifically discussing the relationship between God, Eternity, Time, and the Cosmos.</meta>

# ASCLEPIUS

Indeed, by the returns of the stars to the same places, they run in a seasonal revolution. And the world <note>original: "mundus"; here referring to the ordered universe or cosmos</note> is the receptacle of time, by whose course and motion it is animated. Time, moreover, is maintained by order: order and time bring about the renewal of all things that are in the world through alternation. Since all things are thus disposed, nothing is stable, nothing is fixed, nothing is immobile—neither among things being born, nor things in the heavens, nor things on the earth. 

God alone is ⟨stable⟩, and rightly [alone]; for He is in Himself, and from Himself, and is entirely around Himself, full and perfect. He is firm in His own stability, and cannot be moved from His place by any impulse, since all things are in Him and He alone is in all things; unless someone should dare to say that His motion exists within eternity: but rather, eternity itself is also immobile, into which the motion of all times returns, and from which the motion of all times takes its beginning. 

God, therefore, has been stable, and eternity has always stood together with Him in like manner, holding within itself the unborn world, which we rightly call ⟨in⟩sensible <note>original: "insensibilem"; referring to the intelligible or spiritual world that cannot be perceived by the physical senses</note>. This world we see was made as an image of that [God], an imitator of eternity. Time, however, ⟨⟨although it is always in motion,⟩⟩ possesses the force and nature of its own stability by that very necessity of returning into itself. Therefore, although eternity is stable, immobile, and fixed, nevertheless, because the motion of time (which is mobile) is always recalled into eternity, it results that eternity itself, though immobile—

Indeed, [eternity] alone <note>original: "sola"</note> <insert>seems to be moved</insert> through the time in which it exists, and all movement exists within it. In this way, it is believable that God is moved within himself by that same immobility. For his stability is an immobile movement within his own magnitude; for the law of his magnitude is immobility. Therefore, this which is of such a nature that it is not subject to the senses—<insert>whether it be God, or eternity, or both, or one within the other, or both within each other</insert>—is undefined, incomprehensible, and immeasurable; for it can neither be sustained, nor carried, nor tracked. Because of this, eternity is without the definition of time: but time—which can be defined either by number, or by alternation, or by the return of its circuit—is eternal. Both, therefore, are infinite, and both appear eternal: but the stability <insert>of eternity</insert>, being fixed so that it can support those things which are movable <insert>by possessing an immobile firmness</insert>, rightly holds the primary place by the benefit of its firmness.

# ASCLEPIUS III

Hence it follows that on the one hand eternity, stable though it be, is also mobile, and on the other hand, time, mobile though it be, is rendered stable by the immutability of the law by which its movement is determined. And in this way it is possible to hold that God also moves within himself, <note>original Latin: "Agitari in se ipsum"; Greek: "to move within himself"</note> though God, like eternity, is motionless; for the movement of God, being made stable by his greatness, is no movement, inasmuch as his greatness is necessarily motionless. <note>The translator suggests the Greek original might mean: "For in his greatness, movement is established as motionless; for the law of his greatness is immobility."</note> The being, then, of which I speak,—whether it is to be called God, or eternity, or both, and whether God is in eternity, or eternity in God, or each in the other,—this being, I say, is imperceptible by sense; <note>original Latin: "That which is such that it is not subjected to the senses"</note> it is infinite, incomprehensible, immeasurable; <note>likely translating the Greek terms for "undefined," "ungraspable," and "unmeasurable"</note> it exceeds our powers, and is beyond our scrutiny. changeless in virtue of the unalterable law by which its motion is determined, revolves with an everlasting movement. That movement has had no beginning, and will have no end; it manifests itself and disappears by turns in the several parts of the Kosmos <note>The universe conceived as a beautiful, ordered system</note>, and that in such fashion that again and again in the chequered course of time it manifests itself anew in those same parts in which it disappeared before. Such is the nature of circular movement; all points in the circle are so linked together, that you can find no place at which the movement can begin; for it is evident that all points in the line of movement both precede and follow one another for ever. And it is in this manner that time revolves.

# ASCLEPIUS

And so it happens to men that we see the things that are in heaven as if through a mist, as much as is possible through the condition of human perception. This focus of ours is very narrow when compared to the greatness of the things to be seen; yet, when it does see, it is the broadest happiness of the conscience. [[You see therefore, O Asclepius, in what circumstances we are placed, what things we treat, or what we dare to touch upon. But to You, Supreme God, I give thanks, who have illuminated me...]]

And to this day he renders to the sick by his divine power all the aid which he used to render to them by his medicinal art. Again, there is my grandfather Hermes, whose name I bear. These things are done to the end that, gladdened by oft-repeated worship, the heavenly beings who have been enticed into the images may continue through long ages to acquiesce in the companionship of men. Thus it is that man makes gods.

# ASCLEPIUS

<margin>38 b</margin> And do not think, Asclepius, that the influence of these earthly gods is merely *ineffective* <note>original: "irritos". The translator notes a correction from "fortuitos" (accidental) to "irritos" (useless/ineffective).</note>: the celestial gods inhabit the highest reaches of heaven, each one fulfilling and guarding the rank they have received. These gods of ours, however, care for specific matters individually; they predict certain things through lots and divination, and provide for others through foresight, coming to our aid according to their means—helping humanity through a kind of friendly kinship. <insert>Thus, the celestial gods rule over universal matters, while the earthly gods dwell in specific places.</insert>—

<margin>39</margin> *Asclepius:* In what part of the cosmic plan, then, do <term>Fate</term> <note>original: "εἱμαρμένην" (heimarmene). The Greek term for the fixed destiny or the "allotted" portion of one's life.</note> or the Fates reside, O Trismegistus? <insert>The celestial gods rule over universal matters, while the earthly gods dwell in specific places.</insert>—*Trismegistus:* That which we call <term>Fate</term>, Asclepius, is the <term>Necessity</term> <note>original: "necessitas". In Hermetic thought, this is the irresistible force that ensures the laws of the universe are carried out.</note> that brings about all things that happen, always bound to itself by the linked chains of necessity. This, therefore, is either the <term>Actualizer of all things</term> <note>original: "effectrix rerum". The force that turns potential into reality.</note>, or the supreme God himself, or the power established by that very God who was made second <note>Likely referring to the "Second God" or the Cosmos/Logos in Hermetic hierarchy.</note>, *and it is the discipline of all celestial and earthly things established by divine laws.* Thus, this Fate and Necessity are both bound to one another by an inseparable glue; of these, the former, Fate, gives birth to the beginnings of all things, while Necessity compels to completion those things which depend on those beginnings. Following these is <term>Order</term> <note>original: "ordo".</note>, which is the weaving together and the arrangement of time for the things that must be accomplished. For nothing exists without the composition of order; <insert>this world is perfect in all things</insert> for the world itself is carried along <insert>most especially</insert> by order, or rather the world is entirely order.

# ASCLEPIUS III

<margin>38 b</margin>And you must not suppose, Asclepius, that the operations <note>original: "effectus" (Latin), likely translating the Greek "energeia" meaning active power or manifestation</note> of the terrestrial gods are to no purpose <note>original: "irritus," meaning empty or in vain</note>. The celestial gods dwell in the heights of heaven, and there each one of them unswervingly accomplishes the part assigned to him <note>original: "ordo," referring to their specific rank or station</note> in the ordering of the Kosmos <note>The Greek term for the universe, implying a beautiful and harmonious system</note>; but these our gods on earth below see to things one by one, predict events by means of sacred lots and divination, foresee what is coming and render aid accordingly; they assist, like loving kinsmen, in the affairs of men. Thus the celestial gods rule over things universal; the terrestrial gods administer particulars.

<margin>39</margin>*Ascl.* But tell me, Trismegistus, what part of the government <note>original: "ratio," perhaps translating "oikonomia" or the divine management of the world</note> of the universe is administered by Destiny? <note>original: "fata" or "heimarmene," the inescapable chain of events</note>—*Trism.* That which we name Destiny, Asclepius, is the force by which all events are brought to pass; for all events are bound together in a never-broken chain by the bonds of necessity. Destiny then is either God himself, or else it is the force which ranks next after God; it is the power which, in conjunction with Necessity, orders all things in heaven and earth according to God's law. Thus Destiny and Necessity are inseparably linked together and cemented <note>original: "conexae sunt glutino," literally glued or bonded together</note> to each other. Destiny generates the beginnings of things; Necessity compels the results to follow. And in the train of Destiny and Necessity goes Order, that is, the interweaving <note>original: "textus," like a woven fabric</note> of events, and their arrangement in temporal succession. There is nothing that is not arranged in order; it is by order above all else that the Kosmos itself is borne upon its course; nay, the Kosmos consists wholly of order.

### ASCLEPIUS III

Of these three, the first is Destiny <note>original: *Heimarmene*</note>, which sows the seed, as it were, and thereby gives rise to all that is to issue from the seed thereafter; the second is Necessity, by which all results are inevitably compelled to follow; and the third is Order, which maintains the interconnection of the events which Destiny and Necessity determine. But Destiny, Necessity, and Order, all **40 a** three together, are wrought by the decree <margin>¹ Decree <note>Latin: *Nutus*; Greek: *neuma*</note></margin> of God, who governs the Kosmos <note>The universe conceived as a complex and harmonious system</note> by his law <margin>² Law <note>Latin: *Lex*; Greek: *nomos*</note>: ordinance <note>Latin: *ratio*; Greek: *logos*</note></margin> and by his holy ordinance. Hence all will to do or not to do is by God's ruling wholly alien from them. They are neither disturbed by anger nor swayed by favor <margin>³ Favor <note>Latin: *gratia*; Greek: *charis*</note></margin>; they obey the compulsion of God's eternal ordinance, which is inflexible, immutable, indissoluble.

Yet chance or contingency <margin>⁴ Chance or contingency <note>Latin: *Eventus vel fors*; Greek: *tyche* or *to symbebekos*</note></margin> also exists in the Kosmos, being **40 c** intermingled with all material things <margin>⁵ Material things <note>Latin: *Mundana*; Greek: *hylika*</note></margin>. . . .

# ASCLEPIUS

<margin>28</margin>
[The fear of] death tortures those who are ignorant of true reason. For death is brought about by the dissolution of the body when it is exhausted by labor, and by the completion of the number <note>original: "numeri conpleti"; likely referring to the predetermined lifespan or "number" of years assigned by fate</note> by which the limbs of the body are fitted into a single machine for the uses of life. The body dies when it ceases to be able to carry the vital functions of a human being. This, therefore, is death: the dissolution of the body and the destruction of bodily sense—concerning which anxiety is unnecessary. 

But there is another [death] which is necessary, which human ignorance or unbelief disregards. — **Asclepius:** What is it, O Trismegistus, that they either do not know or doubt can exist? — **Trismegistus:** Listen then, O Asclepius. When the departure of the soul from the body has taken place, then the judgment and the examination of its merit shall occur. For it shall pass into the power of the highest spirit <term>daemon: in this Hermetic context, a high-ranking spiritual being or mediator, not a "demon" in the modern sense</term>; and when he perceives the soul to be pious and just, he permits it to remain in places suitable to itself. 

<margin>5</margin>
<margin>10</margin>
But if he sees it smeared with the stains of crimes and forgotten by its vices, he casts it down from above to the depths, handing it over to storms and whirlwinds of air, fire, and water, which are often in conflict with one another. ((In the religion of God and in [supreme] piety there is (one) protection: for God protects such people from all evils. This man, once the darkness of error has been shaken off from his soul and the clarity of truth perceived, mingles himself with his whole sense into the divine intelligence; through the love of this intelligence, he is freed from that part of nature which is mortal, and he conceives a confidence in the immortality to come. # ASCLEPIUS

->〈Epilogue〉<-

<margin>40 d</margin> *Trismegistus:* "I have spoken to you of each matter as far as human capacity allowed, and as the Divinity willed and permitted. Only this remains for us: that, having blessed God and offered our prayers, we return to the care of our bodies; for we have sufficiently satisfied ourselves with the food of the soul, as it were, while treating these divine matters."

<margin>41 a</margin> Indeed, having stepped out from the inner sanctum <note>original: "adyto"; the most sacred part of a temple</note>, they began to pray to God, looking toward the South—for when one wishes to petition God at sunset, they ought to direct themselves there, just as at sunrise they should face toward the East <note>original: "subsolanus"; the direction of the rising sun</note>. Now, as they were beginning the prayer, Asclepius said in a low voice: "O Tat, do you wish that we suggest to your father that we say the prayer to God with the addition of incense and spices, according to the ritual?" Hearing him, Trismegistus was moved and said: "A better omen, a better omen, Asclepius! <note>A polite way of saying "Heaven forbid" or "Speak more auspiciously."</note> For it is something like sacrilege to burn incense and other things when you pray to God. For nothing is lacking to Him who is Himself all things, or in whom all things are. Rather, let us worship by giving thanks; for these are the 'incense' of the highest God: thanksgivings offered by mortals."

<margin>12-17 ‘A better omen... by mortals.’ Quoted by Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250 – c. 325 AD) who frequently cited Hermes Trismegistus to support monotheism.</note> in *Divine Institutes* 6. 25.</margin>
<margin>11: ‘Hermes Trismegistus... in that "Perfect Discourse," when he had heard Asclepius asking his son whether it would please his father for incense and other odors to be brought for the sacrifice to God, he exclaimed:</margin>
> “Speak well, speak well, O Asclepius! For it is the greatest impiety to entertain such a thought in the mind concerning that one and singular Good. These and things similar to these do not suit Him; for He is full of all things that exist, and stands in need of nothing at all. Let us rather worship by giving thanks; for His sacrifice is blessing alone.”’

# EPILOGUE

### *Epilogue.*

*Trismegistus.* ‘I have explained each of these matters to you,¹ as far **40 d** as my human powers availed, and as far as God willed and allowed. This only remains for us to do, that we should praise God and pray to him, and then turn our attention to the needs of the body; for our minds have been fed full with discourse **41 a** concerning things divine.’

Having come forth from the sanctuary, they began their prayers to God, looking towards the South; for when a man wishes to pray to God at sunset, he ought to face southward, as at sunrise he ought to face eastward.² But when they had begun to pray, Asclepius whispered, ‘Tell me, Tat, shall we propose to your father that we should add to our prayer, as men are wont to do, an offering of incense and perfumes?’³ Trismegistus heard; and much disturbed, he said, ‘Hush, hush,⁴ Asclepius; it is the height of impiety to think of such a thing with regard to Him who alone is good.⁵ Such gifts as these are unfit for him; for he is filled with all things that exist, and lacks nothing.⁶ Let us adore him rather with thanksgiving; for words of praise⁷ are the only offering that he accepts.

---

¹ <note>original: "Vobis"</note> To you <note>plural, indicating he is addressing both Tat and Asclepius</note>.
² <note>original: "Subsolanus" = "apēliōtēs"</note> The East wind or the direction of the rising sun.
³ <note>original: "Pigmenta (alios odores Lactant.)" = "arōmata"</note> Spices or aromatic herbs <note>Lactantius was an early Christian author who quoted these Hermetic texts</note>.
⁴ <note>original: "Melius ominare" = "euphēmei" or "euphēmēson"</note> Speak words of good omen <note>a ritual command to keep silence or avoid speaking ill-omened words during a rite</note>.
⁵ <note>original: "De uno illo ac singulari bono (Lactant.)" = "peri ekeinon ton hena kai monon agathon onta"</note> Concerning that one and only being who is good.
⁶ <note>original: "Omnium minime indigens (Lactant.)" = "pantōn aprosdeēs" (or "anendeēs")</note> Needing nothing at all from anyone.
⁷ <note>original: "Benedictio (Lactant.)" = "eulogia"</note> Blessing or words of praise.

<summary>The dialogue concludes with Hermes Trismegistus leading his students, Tat and Asclepius, in prayer, emphasizing that God desires only the "incense" of human praise and thanksgiving rather than material offerings. This passage highlights the Hermetic shift from physical sacrifice to a purely spiritual and intellectual form of worship.</summary>

<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Asclepius, Tat, prayer, ritual orientation, spiritual sacrifice, thanksgiving, Lactantius, Hermetica</keywords>

# EPILOGUE

->‘We thank thee, O thou Most High<note>original: *Exsuperantissime*. This Latin term might represent the Greek *hyperochōtate* (most excellent) or *hypsiste* (highest/most high).</note>, with heart and soul wholly uplifted to thee;
for it is by thy grace alone<note>original: *tantum*. It is unclear if this means "only" or "this great light."</note> that we have attained to the light,
and come to know thee.
We thank thee, O thou whose name no man can tell,
but whom men honour by the appellation ‘God’, because thou alone art Master,
and bless by the appellation ‘Father’, because thou hast shown in act<note>The original translator likely interpreted the Greek word for "activity" or "efficacy" as a description of God's direct action.</note> toward all men and in all things loving-kindness and affection such as a father feels, nay, yet sweeter than a father’s;
for thou hast bestowed on us mind, and speech, and knowledge:
mind, that we may apprehend thee;
speech, that we may call upon thee;
and knowledge, that having come to know thee, and found salvation in the light thou givest, we may be filled with gladness.
We are glad because thou hast revealed thyself to us in all thy being;<-

***

# ASCLEPIUS

->**The Concluding Prayer**<-

We rejoice because you have deigned to consecrate us to your eternity while we are yet placed in these bodies <note>original: "in corporibus sitos"; the text emphasizes the miracle of experiencing the divine while still physically incarnate</note>. For this is the only human thanksgiving: the knowledge of your majesty. We have known you, O greatest light, perceivable by the intellect alone; *we have known you, O true life of (human) life.*

We have known you, O fertile womb of all things <note>original: "matrix rerum omnium"; a metaphor for the divine source as a mother-creator</note>, pregnant by the father’s sowing; we have known you, who are most full of the conception of all nature, the eternal perseverance. In all this prayer, as we worship you, the only Good, we ask only this of your goodness: that you wish us to be preserved persevering in the love of your knowledge <note>term: "cognitionis" (Gnosis) — a transformative, experiential knowledge of God rather than mere intellectual learning</note>, and that we never be separated from this kind of life.

'With these hopes expressed, let us turn ourselves toward a pure meal, free from animal sacrifice.' <note>This reflects the Hermetic practice of vegetarianism, viewing the "bloodless sacrifice" of prayer and praise as the only fitting offering to God</note>

---

### Critical Notes on the Latin Text
<note>The following notes refer to scholarly reconstructions of the Latin manuscript</note>
1 *your eternity* I have written: *to eternity* in the manuscripts: *perhaps* your eternal life | 5 *and* omitted in F: excluded by Thomas | *of the sensible things* I have written: *by the sensible* in the manuscripts | 7 *we have known* I have written: *we understand* in the manuscripts | *Perhaps* O true life of ⟨human⟩ life | 8 *we have known you* transposed here by Reitz. | 9 *Perhaps* ⟨pregnant through the father's⟩ impregnation | 10 *most full* Reitz. : *most full* (corrected) B | 13 *Perhaps* we pray to you | *to be preserved* I have written: *to preserve* in the manuscripts | 16 *let us turn* I have written: *we turn* in the manuscripts

---

### Greek Original Text
<note>This is the original Greek version of the prayer above, reconstructed from papyrus fragments</note>

> We rejoice that while we are in created forms, you have deigned to deify us <note>original: "ἀποθεῶσαι" (apotheosai); the Greek is more explicit than the Latin about the human becoming divine through knowledge</note> by your [eternity].
> The one grace of man toward you is to recognize your greatness.
> We have recognized you, O true life of human life;
> We have recognized you, O greatest light of all knowledge.
> We have recognized you, O all-bearing womb, pregnant by the planting of the Father;
> We have recognized you, the eternal endurance of him who carries the All in [circular] motion.
> Having worshipped you with this word as the only one who is Good, we ask no grace from your goodness except this alone: wish for us to be kept safe in your knowledge and love, and never to fall away from such a life.

<summary>This page contains the final prayer of the Asclepius in both Latin and Greek, expressing gratitude for the "deification" of man through the knowledge (Gnosis) of God. It concludes with a call to a pure, meatless meal, emphasizing the ethical life of the Hermetic initiate.</summary>

# EPILOGUE

> we are glad because, while we are yet in the body, thou hast deigned to make us gods by the gift of thine own eternal life.
> Man can thank thee only by learning to know thy greatness.
> We have learnt to know thee, O thou most brightly shining light of the world of mind; <note>original: "solo intellectu sensibilium" / "tōn noētōn". The author refers to the "intelligible world," a realm of pure thought beyond physical senses.</note>
> we have learnt to know thee, O thou true life of the life of man. <note>The Greek papyrus source swaps the order of this and the previous line.</note>
> we have learnt to know thee, O thou all-prolific Womb, made pregnant by the Father's begetting; <note>original: "praegnatio" / "phyteia". This uses the metaphor of a divine womb to describe the creative power of the universe.</note>
> we have learnt to know thee, O thou eternal constancy of that which stands unmoved, yet makes the universe <note>original: "totius naturae" / "tou pantos". Referring to the "All" or the totality of existence.</note> revolve.
> With such words of praise do we adore thee, who alone art good; and let us crave from thy goodness no boon save this: be it thy will that we be kept still knowing and loving thee, and that we may never fall away from this blest way of life. <note>This refers to the spiritual bliss experienced by those who achieve "Gnosis" or direct knowledge of God.</note>

'Having prayed thus, <note>Likely an aorist participle in the original Greek text.</note> let us betake ourselves to a meal unpolluted by flesh of living things.' <note>original: "animalia" / "empsycha". This indicates a vegetarian ritual meal, common in certain ancient philosophical and mystery traditions.</note>

# THE HERMETICA OF STOBAEUS

### EXCERPT I

Stobaeus 2. 1. 26, volume ii, page 9 in the Wachsmuth edition (*Florilegium* 80. 9 in the Meineke edition).

### From the writings of Hermes to Tat.
<note>Hermes Trismegistus is the legendary sage of this tradition; Tat is his son and disciple.</note>

**1** To conceive of God is difficult, but to describe Him is impossible, even for one who is able to conceive of Him. For [it is impossible to signify the incorporeal <term>incorporeal: that which has no physical body or substance</term> by means of a body, and] it is ⌜not possible⌝ for the perfect to be grasped by the imperfect, and it is hard for the eternal to associate with the short-lived. For the one always exists, while the other passes away; the one is truth, while the other is ⌜shadowed⌝ by appearance. [Therefore, as far as the weaker stands apart from the stronger and the lesser from the greater, **2** so far] does the mortal stand apart from the divine. The distance between these two obscures the vision of the Beautiful. For while bodies are visible to the eyes [and things seen are expressible by the tongue], that which is incorporeal and invisible and formless, and not ⌜composed⌝ of underlying matter, cannot be grasped by our senses. ⌜I perceive in my mind, O Tat, I perceive that which is impossible to speak out; this is God.⌝

---

Manuscripts of Stobaeus: S (early 11th century), M (early 12th or late 11th century), A (14th century), B (16th century).
Pseudo-Justin, *Exhortation to the Greeks* 38 (Otto, Vol. II, *Works of Justin of Doubtful Authenticity*, 1879): Hermes... saying: “To conceive of God is difficult, but to describe Him is impossible, even for one who is able to conceive of Him.”
Lactantius, *Epitome* 4. 5 (Brandt): “The beginning of his (*namely* Hermes Trismegistus’) writing to his son is as follows: ‘To understand God is indeed difficult, but to speak of Him is impossible, even for one to whom understanding is possible: for the perfect cannot be comprehended by the imperfect, nor the invisible by the visible.’”
Cyril, *Against Julian* 1. 31 (Migne *Greek Patrology* 76. 549): Hermes Trismegistus says something like this: “To conceive of God is difficult... shadowed by appearance. Therefore, as far as the weaker stands apart from the stronger and the lesser from the greater, so far does the mortal stand apart from the divine and immortal.”

**1** *from the writings of* I have written : omitted in S : *from the writing of* in other manuscripts. **2** *to conceive indeed* Cyril, Stobaeus A : *to conceive indeed is* Pseudo-Justin : *indeed to conceive* Stobaeus SM : *indeed to understand* (that is, *to conceive indeed*) Lactantius. **2-3** *even for one who is able to conceive* Pseudo-Justin : *even for one to whom understanding is possible* (that is, *and for whom to conceive is possible*) Lactantius : *if even to conceive is possible* Cyril (Aubert) : *if for anyone even to understand is possible* (that is, *if for someone even to conceive is possible*) Cyril (Oecolampadius) : omitted in Stobaeus manuscripts. **3** *and the* Stobaeus A : *for the* others | *to happen* Stobaeus A : *to signify* other Stobaeus manuscripts and Cyril. **3-4** *incorporeal... and the* Stobaeus manuscripts and Cyril : omitted by Lactantius.

<summary>This excerpt from Hermes Trismegistus to his son Tat discusses the ontological gap between the divine and the mortal, arguing that God's incorporeal nature is beyond human speech and sensory perception. It includes a critical apparatus comparing the text across various ancient sources like Lactantius and Cyril of Alexandria.</summary>
<keywords>Hermes Trismegistus, Tat, ineffability of God, incorporeal, Stobaeus, Greek philosophy, theology, manuscript variants</keywords>

# STOBAEUS

### EXCERPT I

### *An extract from the Discourses of Hermes to Tat.*

To conceive God is difficult; and to describe Him is impossible, even if one is able to conceive Him. For it is not easy for that which is imperfect to apprehend that which is perfect, and it is hard for that which is of short duration to have dealings with that which is everlasting. The one ever is, the other passes; the one is real, the other is but shadowed forth by sense-picturing. So widely is that which is mortal separated from that which is divine. And the wide interval between them dims men's vision of the Beautiful. With our eyes we can see bodies; but that which is incorporeal and invisible and without shape, and is not composed of matter, cannot be apprehended by senses such as ours. . . .¹

---

¹ Perhaps, 'When I have in my mind a conception of this, my son', (viz. of 'that which is incorporeal', &c.,) 'I have a conception which it is impossible to express in words; and such is God' (i. e. God is incorporeal, &c., and therefore, is something that cannot be told in words).

---

<meta>This page begins the translation of Excerpt II A from the anthology of Stobaeus, representing a fragment of the Hermetic dialogues between Hermes Trismegistus and his son/disciple Tat. It focuses on the ontological distinction between absolute Truth and the material world.</meta>

# THE HERMETICA OF STOBAEUS

->*EXCERPT II A*<-

Stobaeus 3. 11. 31, vol. iii, p. 436 Hense (*Florilegium* 11. 23 Meineke).

### From the works of Hermes to Tat.

**1** Concerning truth, O Tat, it is not possible <note>original: "κατ’ ἀξίαν εἰπεῖν" - to speak worthily or adequately</note> for a human being to speak, since man is an imperfect living being, composed of imperfect parts, and <insert>possessing</insert> a frame <note>The Greek "σκῆνος" literally means a "tent" or "tabernacle," a common metaphor for the physical body as a temporary dwelling for the soul.</note> assembled from many foreign bodies. But what is possible and right, this I say: that truth exists only in eternal beings. **2** And these eternal bodies are, in and of themselves, true: fire is fire-itself, earth is earth-itself, air is air-itself, and water is water-itself. But our bodies are composed of all of these; for they have something of fire, and they also have earth and water and air. Yet in them there is neither <insert>true</insert> fire, nor earth, nor water, nor air, nor anything true. And if our composition did not possess truth from the beginning, how could it either see or speak truth? [To understand truth is <insert>possible</insert> only if God wills it.]

**3** Therefore, O Tat, all things upon the earth are not true; they are imitations of the truth, and not even all of them, but only a few. The rest are falsehood and error, O Tat, composed of <term>phantasia</term> <note>Phantasia (φαντασία) here refers to "appearance" or "imagination"—the way things seem to our senses rather than how they truly are.</note>. **4** Whenever this appearance receives an "in-flow" from above, it becomes a <term>mimesis</term> <note>Mimesis (μίμησις) means "imitation" or "representation."</note> of the truth. But without that activity from above, it remains a falsehood. Just as a portrait in a painting shows <insert>the body</insert> according to the appearance of the person seen, but is not the body itself. It is seen as having eyes, yet it sees nothing; <insert>and ears,</insert> yet it hears nothing at all. The painting has all the other features, but they are false, [deceiving] the eyes of those who look upon them.

# EXCERPT II A. HERMES TO TAT

### From the Discourses of Hermes to Tat.

*Hermes.* Concerning reality <note>original: "aletheia" - truth or the fundamental nature of things</note>, my son Tat, it is not possible for one who is but a man to speak adequately; for man is an imperfect creature, composed of parts <gloss>1</gloss> which are imperfect, and his mortal frame is made up of many alien bodies. But what it is within my power to say, that I do say, namely, that <gloss>2</gloss> reality exists only in things everlasting . . . . The everlasting bodies, <margin>2</margin> as they are in themselves,—fire that is very fire, earth that is very earth, air that is very air, and water that is very water,—these indeed are real. But our bodies are made up of all these elements together; they have in them something of fire, but also something of earth and water and air; and there is in them neither real fire nor real earth nor real water nor real air, nor anything that is real. And if our composite fabric has not got reality in it to begin with, how can it <gloss>3</gloss> see reality, or tell of reality?

All things on earth then, my son, are unreal; but some of <margin>3</margin> them,—not all, but some few only,—are copies of reality. The rest are illusion and deceit, my son; for they consist of mere appearance. When the appearance flows in from above, <gloss>4</gloss> it <margin>4</margin> becomes an imitation of reality. But apart from the working of power from above, it remains an illusion; just as a painted portrait presents to us in appearance the body of the man we see in it, but is not itself a human body. It is seen to have eyes, and yet it sees nothing; it is seen to have ears, and yet it hears nothing at all. The picture has all else too that a living man has, but all this is false, and deceives the eyes of those who look

4 Or 'receives the influx (of . . . ?) from above'.
