A thing is "untrue to itself" when it fails to remain what it is from one moment to the next.</note> how could they possibly be real? Everything that changes is illusory, because it does not stay in the state in which it is, but presents appearances that vary.

# EXCERPT II A. HERMES TO TAT
## C C 2

And all things on earth are overtaken by destruction; for <margin>16</margin> without destruction things cannot come into being. The things which come into being must needs arise out of those which are destroyed; and the things which come into being must needs be destroyed, in order that coming-into-being may not stop. The things which come into being out of destruction must therefore be illusory, because they come to be different things at different times. For it is not possible that the same things should come into being again; and how can that be real, which is not the same that it was before? Inasmuch as things change, <margin>18</margin> they are illusory. But at the same time you must understand, my son, that these illusory things are dependent on Reality itself, which is above; and that being so, I say that the illusion is a thing wrought by the working of Reality.<note>The material world is an unreal appearance, but this unreal appearance is produced by God’s working.</note>—

*Tat.* But what of man, father? Is not man real?—*Hermes.* In <margin>11</margin> so far as he is man, my son, he is not real. For the real is that which consists of itself alone, and continues to be such as it is in itself; but man is composed of many different things, and does not continue to be such as he is in himself, but shifts and changes from one time of life to another, and from one form to another. Oftentimes men fail to recognize their own children after a short interval, and children likewise fail to recognize their parents. And when a thing so changes that it is not known, how can that <margin>12</margin> thing be real, my son? Is it not an illusion, inasmuch as its changes manifest themselves in varying appearances? You must understand that that which ever is, and that alone, is real. But man is not a thing that ever is; and therefore man is not real, but is only an appearance. # THE HERMETICA OF STOBAEUS

->*EXCERPTUM II B*<-

Stobaeus book 1, chapter 41, section 1 a; volume 1, page 273 in the Wachsmuth edition (*Eclogues* I. 698, Heeren edition).

### From the writings of Hermes to Tat
<note>Hermes Trismegistus addresses his son/disciple Tat, a common framing device in these mystical philosophical texts.</note>

**1** I write this first work <insert>I write this first work</insert> <note>original: "πρῶτον τόδε συγγράφω"</note>, [my child], both for the sake of my love for humanity and for the sake of piety toward God. For there could be no <insert>more righteous</insert> piety than to understand the things that are, and to acknowledge thanks to the one who made them; a practice which I shall never cease to perform.

**2** "What then, O father, could a person do to lead their life well, if there is nothing true here on earth?" —By being pious, my child. And he who <insert>seeks to be pious</insert> will practice philosophy [to the highest degree]. For without philosophy, it is impossible to be [perfectly] pious. But he who has learned what <insert>the things that are</insert> truly are, and how they have been ordered, and by whom, and for what purpose, will give thanks for all things to the Creator <term>Demiurge: the "craftsman" or creator of the physical world</term> as to a good father, a kind nurse, and a faithful guardian. And he who acknowledges thanks will be pious.

**3** And he who practices philosophy <insert>to the highest degree</insert> will <insert>learn</insert> both where the truth is and what it is. And having learned this, he will be even more pious, <insert>and will no longer be able to depart from the Good.</insert> For never, my child, can a soul [being in a body] that has lifted itself up to the comprehension of the truly Good and True, slide back to the opposite. For the soul, having learned of its own forefather, possesses a terrible <note>In this context, "terrible" (deinos) implies an overwhelming or awe-inspiring intensity.</note> love and a forgetfulness of all evils. [[And it can no longer depart from the Good.]]

**4** This, my child, this is the end <note>The "telos" or ultimate goal/purpose.</note> of piety. Reaching this, you will both live well and die happily, since your soul will not be ignorant of where it must fly back to.

**5** <...> For this alone, my child, is the way to truth; the way which our ancestors also traveled, and having traveled it—

### An extract from the Discourses of Hermes to Tat.¹

<margin>1</margin>
I esteem² this treatise more highly than any other, on account of the benevolence towards men and piety towards God that is expressed in it; for there is nothing that could more rightly be called piety than to apprehend in thought the things that are, and to give thanks for them to Him who made them. And this I will continue to do without ceasing.

<margin>2</margin>
*Tat.* If then there is nothing real here below, what must a man do, father, to live his life aright?—*Hermes.* He must be pious, my son. And he who seeks to be pious will pursue <term>philosophy</term> <note>In this context, philosophy is not just academic study, but a spiritual "love of wisdom" that leads to the knowledge of God.</note>. Without philosophy, it is impossible to be pious; but he who has learnt what things are, and how they are ordered, and by whom, and to what end, will give thanks for all things to the Maker, deeming him a good father and kind fosterer and faithful guardian; and thus rendering thanks, he will be pious.

<margin>3</margin>
And he who pursues philosophy to its highest reach will learn where Reality is, and what it is; and having learnt this, he will be yet more pious. And thenceforward it will be impossible for him to fall away from the Good. For never, my son, can a soul that has so far uplifted itself as to grasp the truly good and real slip back to the evil and unreal; for the soul acquires a wondrous yearning for the Good, and oblivion of all evils, when it has learnt to know its own Forefather. This, my son, <margin>4</margin> this³ is the consummation of piety; and when you have attained to it, you will live your life aright, and be blest in your death; for your soul will not fail to know whither it must wing its upward flight.

<margin>5</margin>
. . . For this,⁴ my son, is the only road that leads to Reality. It is the road our ancestors⁵ trod; and thereby they attained

### EXCERPT III. HERMES TO TAT

That which is acted upon by forces is mastered. And that which has the mastery is free, and takes the lead; but that which is mastered is in servitude, and is passively borne along.

<margin>9</margin>Moreover, the forces work not only in bodies that have souls in them, <note>The original editor suggests the writer ought rather to have said ‘in bodies that *have had* souls in them’.</note> but also in soulless bodies, such as logs and stones and the like, increasing their bulk and bringing them to maturity, corrupting, dissolving, rotting and crumbling them, and carrying on in them all processes of that sort that it is possible for soulless bodies to undergo. For this, my son, is the very meaning of the <term>term ‘a force-at-work’</term> <note>original: "energeia" (ἐνέργεια), often translated as energy or activity</note>; it signifies <insert>that by which is worked</insert> every sort of process that goes on.

<margin>10</margin>And there must be going on at all times many processes, or rather, every kind of process. For the <term>Kosmos</term> <note>The universe conceived as an ordered, harmonious system</note> is never bereft of any of the things that are; ever in movement, it is ever breeding within itself the things that are.

<margin>11</margin>You must understand then that every force is incorporeal, whatever force may be at work in any kind of body.

<margin>1</margin>For forces, my son, though they are themselves incorporeal, are in bodies, and work by means of these bodies. And so, my son, inasmuch as they are incorporeal, I say that they are immortal; but inasmuch as they cannot work apart from bodies, I say that they are always in a body.

<margin>4</margin>Hence it follows that there are always bodies in existence. And for this reason I say that the production of bodies must be everlasting. For if earthly bodies are dissoluble, and there must be bodies to serve as places and instruments for the working of the forces, and the forces are immortal, and that which is immortal exists for ever, then it follows that the production of bodies must go on for ever.

<margin>6</margin>The forces, though they are themselves incorporeal, are dependent on the bodies; for they come from the <term>divine bodies</term> <note>original: "theia somata," referring here to the heavenly bodies or stars</note>, and enter into mortal bodies. But each of them acts either on

8 The soul of irrational beings consists of anger and desire. For this reason, these living things were called "irrational" <term>aloga; literally 'without logos' or reason</term>, due to the deprivation of the rational part of the soul.

9 Consider a fourth <insert>activity</insert>, that of inanimate things, which, being external to the bodies, acts by moving them. This would be the <insert>soul</insert> moving in the divine body, moving these things as if in passing.

There are three different kinds of souls—divine soul, human <margin>5</margin> soul, and irrational soul.

The divine soul is that which moves the divine body <note>The "divine body" likely refers to the celestial spheres or the heavens.</note>. . . its motive force <note>The original text is fragmented here; it likely meant "Its motive force acts in two ways."</note>; it moves itself in the divine body, and it moves that body.

But the soul of irrational animals consists of repugnance and <margin>8</margin> desire; and that is why these animals are called ‘irrational’, because they are deprived of the rational part of the soul.

And you must understand that there is a fourth kind of motive <margin>9</margin> force, which acts on soulless bodies. It is outside the bodies, and is operative in moving them. This must be the soul that is in motion in the divine body, and moves soulless bodies incidentally, so to speak.—

->*EXCERPT IV B*<-

Stobaeus I. 41. 6 a, vol. i, p. 284 Wachsmuth (*Eclogues I.* 726 Heeren).

### From the writings of Hermes to Tat.

**1** **Tat:** You have demonstrated these points correctly, O Father; but teach me one thing further. For you said somewhere that knowledge <note>original: "episteme" — systematic or scientific knowledge</note> and craft <note>original: "techne" — technical skill or art</note> are activities of the rational soul. But now you say that irrational animals are called "irrational" <note>original: "aloga" — literally "without logos" (reason/speech)</note> because they are deprived of reason. It is clear, then, according to this argument, that irrational animals must have no share in knowledge or craft, because they are deprived of reason.—

**2** **Hermes:** That is necessarily so, my son.—**Tat:** How is it then, Father, that we see certain irrational creatures using knowledge and craft? For instance, the ants storing up their food [for the winter], and the creatures of the air likewise constructing nests for themselves, and the four-footed animals

**3** recognizing their own dens?—**Hermes:** These things, my son, they do not do by knowledge or craft, but by nature <note>original: "physis" — the innate, biological drive</note>. For knowledge and craft are things that can be taught; but none of these irrational creatures is taught anything. Things that happen by nature are produced by a universal activity; but things produced by knowledge and craft come only to certain individuals [who know], not to all.

**4** [Things produced by nature are energized by it.] For example, [all] men look upward; [for this is energized by nature;] but not all men are musicians, nor are all archers or hunters, nor [do all men do] all other things; rather, only some of them do, [those who] have learned something through the activity of knowledge and craft.

**5** In the same way, [if] some ants did this and others did not, you would be right to say that they collect their food by knowledge and craft. But if all are led toward this goal by nature, even without their will, it is clear that they do not do this by knowledge or craft, [but are led by nature].

---

<header>EXCERPT IV B. HERMES TO TAT</header>

->*EXCERPT IV B*<-

### From the Discourses of Hermes to Tat.¹

*Tat.* You have explained these things rightly, father; but there **1** is another thing about which I ask you to give me further instruction. You said before that knowledge and skill <note>The original Greek terms are *episteme* (scientific knowledge) and *techne* (applied craft or art).</note> are forces put in action by the rational part of the soul. But now you tell me that it is because the irrational animals are deprived of the rational part of the soul, that they are irrational and are so called; and it is clear that it follows of necessity from this that the irrational animals have no portion of knowledge or skill, since they are deprived of the rational part.—*Hermes.* Yes, my son, it necessarily follows.—*Tat.* How is it then, father, that we see **2** some of the irrational animals using knowledge and skill,—the ants, for instance, storing up their food, and the birds of the air building nests for themselves, and the four-footed beasts knowing their own lairs?—*Hermes.* It is not by knowledge or skill, my son, **3** that they do these things, but by natural instinct <note>original: *physike energeia*, literally "natural activity" or "working of nature".</note>. Knowledge and skill are things that are taught; but none of the irrational animals are taught to do the things you speak of. And the things that are done by instinct are done by a force that is universal in its working; but the things that are done by knowledge and skill are acquired by some, and not by all. For **4** instance, all men look upward;² for this is done by nature's working; but not all men are musicians, nor are all men archers or hunters; and all other such things also are done, not by all men, but by some of them, that is, by those who have learnt to do this or that; for it is knowledge and skill that are work. In the same way, if some ants only did this, and others did not, **5** you would have been right in saying that it is by knowledge and skill that they collect their food; but if all of them alike are led to do this, and do it involuntarily, it is clear that it is not by knowledge or skill that they do it, but by nature's leading.

---

¹ Excerpt IV B appears to be a continuation of Excerpt IV A.
² That is, men stand erect with upturned face, in contrast to the beasts, which 'look downward'.

---

The manuscripts add: "For activities, O Tat, being themselves incorporeal, etc." See *Excerpt III*.

# STOBAEUS’S HERMETICA

### EXCERPT V

Stobaeus, Book I, Chapter 41, Section 8; Volume I, page 290 in the Wachsmuth edition (Eclogues I. 744 in the Heeren edition).

### From Hermes: From the [to Ammon] to Tat.
<note>The title in the manuscript originally said "To Ammon," but scholars believe this was a copying error repeated from the previous chapter; it should be addressed to Hermes's son, Tat.</note>

**1** And indeed, the [Lord and] Creator of all eternal bodies, O Tat, having made them once, did not make them again, nor does he continue to make them. For having handed these bodies over to themselves and having united them with one another, he let them go to be carried along <note>referring to the celestial orbits of the stars and planets</note>, lacking nothing [as eternal beings]. If they do require anything, they will require it of one another, but they require no external influx from the outside, <...> being immortal. For it was necessary that the bodies created by Him should possess such a nature.

**2** But our own creator <note>The "secondary" creator or demiurge who shapes the physical world</note>, being himself in a body, made us, and makes us always, and will continue to make us, <possessing> bodies that are dissoluble and mortal. For it was not lawful for him to imitate his own Creator, especially since <...> it was impossible. For the Great Creator made things out of the primary essence, which is incorporeal <note>original: *asōmatos*, meaning without physical matter</note>; but our creator made us out of a physical embodiment that had already come into existence.

**3** It is reasonable then [according to right reason] that those celestial bodies, having been generated from an incorporeal essence, are immortal; but our bodies are dissoluble and mortal, since our matter is composed of physical bodies.

**4** For this reason <also> our bodies are weak and in need of much assistance. For how could the bond of our bodies hold out against even a chance occurrence, if it did not have a certain incoming nourishment from [similar] elements, and if this <nourishment> did not build up our bodies every day? For there is an influx of earth, water, fire, and air into us, which, by renewing our bodies, holds this "tent" <note>original: *skēnos*, a common philosophical metaphor for the physical body as a temporary shelter for the soul</note> together.

**5** <...> Consequently, we are too weak even for movements, being unable to bear <them> for even a single day. For know well, my son, that if our bodies did not rest during the nights, we would not have held out for a single day. Therefore, the Creator, being good and foreknowing all things, created sleep for the preservation of the living creature, as the greatest <remedy> for exhaustion.

<margin>1</margin>And the Maker of the everlasting bodies <note>The "everlasting bodies" refer to the stars and planets, which were believed to be divine and unchanging.</note>, my son, having once made them, did not thereafter make them, nor does he make them now; he gave them over into their own keeping, and having united them to one another, left them to go their way, as things in need of nothing. <margin>2</margin>But the Maker by whom we men were made,² being himself embodied, made us, and ever is and will be making us, as beings whose bodies are dissoluble and mortal. <margin>3</margin>It is with good reason then that the everlasting bodies are immortal, inasmuch as they have been made of incorporeal substance; but our bodies are dissoluble and mortal, inasmuch as our fabric is composed of bodies. And for this reason our <margin>4</margin>bodies are weak, and need much help. How could the bond that holds our bodies together have endured even for a little time, were it not that they receive into them nutriment which comes from the elements, and that this nutriment renews our bodies day by day? **15** Below the Moon are other stars that are perishable and idle, existing only for a short time. These have a nature similar to the useless creatures on earth, which are brought into being for no other purpose than to perish, such as the race of flies, fleas, worms, and other such things. For just as those creatures, O Tat <note>Hermes' son and disciple in these dialogues</note>, are useful neither to us nor to the cosmos, but on the contrary cause distress by being a nuisance—mere by-products of nature that arise as a superfluity—in the same way, the stars exhaled from the earth do not reach the upper region. They are unable to do so, as they rise from below; having much heaviness, they are dragged down by their own matter and quickly disperse. Having dissolved, they fall back to earth, having accomplished nothing other than disturbing the air above the earth.

**16** There is another kind, O Tat, called the Comets. They appear at intervals and then become invisible again after a short time, neither rising nor setting nor dissolving. These appear as messengers and heralds of universal events that are about to happen. These [occupy] the...

<margin>16</margin>And there are stars of another kind, my son, which are called comets. They appear at their appointed times, and disappear again after a little while. ### From Hermes to his son.

**1** You have told me all things rightly, O father. ->*EXCERPT VIII*<-

### A discourse of Hermes to his son.

*Tat.*<gloss>The translator notes that Excerpt VIII, as found in the original manuscripts, is entirely meaningless and has been reconstructed here to make sense of the philosophical argument.</gloss> In all this, father, you have spoken rightly. But go on, **1** and tell me again what are the incorporeal <note>term: "incorporeal" — things that have no physical body or material form, such as the soul or mind.</note> things in us that are according to Providence, and likewise what are those that are according to Necessity, and those that are according to Destiny.—

*Hermes.* I told you, my son Tat, that there are in us three **2** kinds of incorporeals. The first of these<gloss>Namely the mind—that part of the soul in which reason resides.</gloss> is apprehensible by thought alone . . . This is a thing without colour and without shape; it issues from nothing else than the primary intelligible substance.<gloss>That is, from God, or the divine Mind.</gloss>

But there is also in us a second kind of incorporeal thing,<gloss>Namely that part of the soul in which the passions reside.</gloss> . . .<gloss>Perhaps: "which is in itself irrational, but is capable of being moved rationally."</gloss> **3** For when the irrational part is moved by the intelligible substance,<gloss>That is, by the mind.</gloss> it is moved rationally in some degree,<gloss>Literally, "it is moved according to some reason." This phrase appears again in section 6.</gloss> and being so moved, is at once transformed into an image of the Maker's thought.

# EXCERPT IX. HERMES TO TAT

God is the germ from which has sprung its coming-into-being,¹ and has thereby come into being. And it came into being as a thing that is mutable <note>subject to change</note>; and it takes many forms, being fashioned into various shapes; for in passing through its changes it is governed by God’s working, which fabricates the forms taken by it in the course of its mutation. In respect of its formlessness then, matter was without beginning; but in respect of God’s working on it, it has come into being.

->*EXCERPT X*<-

### An extract from the Discourses of Hermes to Tat.

. . . concerning the three times² . . . For they are neither independent of one another nor united with one another; and again, they are both united and independent.³

If you suppose the present time to be separate from the past time (and the future from the present, you will find yourself in a difficulty. For) it is impossible for the present to come into being unless the past also has come into being, (and for the future to come into being unless the present has;) for the present issues from the past, and the future from the present. And inasmuch as the past joins on to the present, and the present to the future, they are made one by their continuity. They are therefore not separate from one another.

(On the other hand, if you suppose them to be united with one another, you will again find yourself in a difficulty . . .⁴). Thus it appears that, though time is one and the same throughout, its parts are separate.

If we are to investigate the matter yet further, let us reason

² I.e. past time, present time, and future time.
³ Perhaps, ‘For they are not independent, but are united with one another; and again (in another sense) they are not united, but are independent’.
⁴ Here must have followed a passage, now lost, in which reasons were given for saying that the three times are not ‘united’.

**1** And now, my son, I shall go through all things in summary; for you will understand what is being said by remembering what you have already heard.

**2** (1) All bodies <note>The Greek text here distinguishes between "beings" and "bodies."</note> are in motion; only the incorporeal <term>incorporeal: that which has no physical body or material form</term> is motionless.
(2) Every body is subject to change; but not every body is subject to dissolution. <insert>Some bodies are dissoluble.</insert>
(3) Not every living being is mortal; yet not every living being is immortal.
(4) That which is dissoluble is perishable; only that which cannot be dissolved is eternal.
(5) That which is always coming into being is also always perishing, but that which is brought into being once and for all never perishes <insert>nor does it become anything else</insert>.
(6) First is God, second is the Cosmos, third is Man.
(7) The Cosmos exists for the sake of Man, and Man exists for the sake of God.
(8) <insert>Of the soul, the part governed by the senses is mortal, but the rational part is immortal.</insert>
(9) Every essence <term>essence: "ousia," the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</term> is subject to change; but not every essence is perishable.

# EXCERPT XI. HERMES TO TAT

(10) Everything that exists is in motion; nothing that exists stands still. <gloss>Perhaps: "All bodies are movable; no bodies are fixed."</gloss>
(11) Not all things are moved; but <gloss>Possibly "Not all... but" should be removed.</gloss> everything that is moved is moved by a soul. <note>In ancient philosophy, the "soul" or "psyche" was considered the primary source of animation and movement in living things.</note>
(8) The part of the soul that perceives through the senses is mortal; but the part of the soul that reasons is immortal.
(12) Everything that possesses sensation is subject to external influence; <gloss>Or "is disturbed by passion."</gloss> the mind alone is free from such influences. <gloss>Or "disturbing passions."</gloss> <note>The term "passive affections" refers to the Greek "pathos," meaning things that happen to a person or emotions that overcome the intellect.</note>
(13) Everything that feels pain also feels pleasure; but not everything that feels pleasure feels pain. <gloss>Perhaps: "and everything that feels pleasure feels pain also."</gloss>
(14) Not all bodies are subject to disease; but all bodies that are diseased are capable of being dissolved. <gloss>Possibly aphorisms 13 and 14 were originally one: "Everything that feels pain is diseased; and everything that is diseased is dissoluble."</gloss>
(15) The Mind is within God; and reason <gloss>Or "speech" (Greek: logos).</gloss> is within the Mind.
(16) Nothing that has a physical body is truly real; only that which is without a body is free from deception.
(17) Everything that has been created is subject to change; but not everything that has been created can be destroyed.
(18) There is nothing truly good to be found on earth; there is nothing bad to be found in heaven.
(19) God is the essence of good; man is prone to bad.
(20) That which is good is chosen by will; that which is bad happens against the true will.
(21) The gods choose things that are good; men choose things that are bad, mistakenly believing them to be good.
(22) . . . <gloss>Perhaps: "Obedience to law is being of one mind with God; lawlessness is struggling against God."</gloss>
(23) . . . <gloss>Perhaps: "God's law is virtue; man's law is vice."</gloss>
(24) . . . <gloss>Perhaps: "For the Universe (Kosmos), time is a circular movement; for man, time is destruction."</gloss> <note>The original Greek text for these lines is fragmented or missing in the primary manuscripts.</note>
(25) Everything in heaven is unchangeable; everything on earth is subject to change.
(26) Nothing in heaven is enslaved; nothing on earth is truly free.

# THE HERMETICA OF STOBAEUS

(27) Nothing is unknown in heaven; nothing is known upon the earth. <note>This suggests that divine reality is fully transparent, while earthly life is defined by ignorance or "forgetting."</note>

(28) The things in heaven do not commune with those on earth, but the things on earth <insert>commune with</insert> those in heaven.

(29) All things in heaven are without blemish; all things on earth are full of blemish.

(30) That which is immortal is not mortal; that which is mortal is not immortal. <note>original: "οὐ θνητόν" (not mortal). A scholar's note suggests this might originally have read "not subject to suffering."</note>

(31) That which is sown is not necessarily brought to birth, but that which is brought to birth has necessarily been sown. <note>The author distinguishes between the "seed" or potential of a thing and its actual manifestation in the world.</note>

(32) For a dissoluble body <note>A body that can break down or die.</note> there are two periods of time: the one from sowing until birth, and the one from birth until death. For the eternal body, there is only the time starting from its coming into being.

(33) Dissoluble bodies increase and decrease; <insert>eternal bodies neither increase nor decrease.</insert>

(34) Dissoluble matter <note>original: "ὕλη" (hyle). Some scholars suggest this should be "essence" (ousia).</note> changes into its opposites through decay and generation, but eternal matter changes either into itself or into things like itself.

(35) The birth of man is the beginning of decay; the decay of man is the beginning of birth. <note>This reflects the cyclical view of nature where death provides the material for new life.</note>

(36) That which passes away <insert>comes into being again; and that which comes into being</insert> also passes away.

(37) Of the things that exist, some are bodies, some are forms, and some are activities. Form and activity, <insert>being incorporeal,</insert> exist within a body. <term>Incorporeal: existing without a physical body or material form.</term>

(38) The immortal does not partake of the mortal, but the mortal partakes of the immortal.

(39) The mortal does not enter into an immortal body, but the immortal comes to be within a mortal body. <note>This likely refers to the soul (immortal) inhabiting the human frame (mortal).</note>

### EXCERPT XI. HERMES TO TAT

(27) Nothing is unknown <note>The original Greek term implies something that cannot be perceived or understood; it may also be translated as "unknowable."</note> in heaven; nothing is known <note>Or "knowable."</note> on earth.

(28) The things in heaven have no communion <term>communion: a shared participation or spiritual connection</term> with the things on earth; but the things on earth have communion with the things in heaven.

(32) A dissoluble <term>dissoluble: capable of being decomposed or broken down</term> body has two times, namely, . . . and . . .; an everlasting body has only one time, namely, . . . <note>Based on the context of paragraph 33, this likely refers to the time of increasing and the time of diminishing.</note>

(34) . . . <note>A missing passage, possibly stating: "Dissoluble things are changed into their opposites (the elements); everlasting things are changed into things like themselves."</note>

(35) Coming into being is the beginning of destruction, and destruction is the beginning of coming into being.

(36) That which goes out of being also comes into being; and that which comes into being also goes out of being.

(37) Of the things that are, some are bodies, some are forms, and some are forces. Forms and forces are incorporeal <term>incorporeal: having no physical body or material form</term> things, but are in bodies.

(38) That which is immortal has no part in that which is mortal; but that which is mortal has part in that which is immortal.

(39) That which is mortal does not go into an immortal body; but that which is immortal enters into a mortal body.

**1** That which sustains the whole world is Providence <note>original: *pronoia*; the divine foresight that orders the universe</note>; that which ⌜binds and encompasses it⌝ is Necessity <note>original: *ananké*; the inescapable laws of the cosmos</note>. And while Providence (...) provides for all, Fate is the cause ⌜of the arrangement of the stars.⌝
⌜This⌝ is an inescapable law according to which all things have been ordered.

### From the writings of Hermes to Ammon.

**1** The soul, therefore, is an incorporeal essence <note>original: *ousia asomatos*</note>; even when it is within a body, it does not depart from its own essential nature. For it happens to be eternally in motion according to its essence, and self-moving according to its intellect. It does not move *in* something, nor *toward* something, nor *for the sake of* something. For it is prior in power, and that which is prior does not stand in need of things that come after.

**2** That which is "in something," therefore, is place, time, and nature <note>original: "φύσις" (physis). In this context, it refers to the inherent driving force of the physical world.</note>. That which is "relative to something" is harmony, form, and shape.

[These things share in one another according to a kindred affinity.] [Since, therefore, the body required a place,] for it was impossible for a body to subsist without a place, [and it changes by natural motion,] and it is impossible for a change of body to exist without time and motion according to nature. [Nor is it possible for the constitution of a body to exist without harmony.]

**4** Place, therefore, exists for the sake of the body; for by receiving the changes of the body, it does not allow that which is changing to be destroyed. In changing, the body falls from one state into another; it is deprived of its previous condition <note>original: "ἕξις" (hexis), meaning a stable quality or disposition</note>, but not of its being a body. Having changed into another state, it possesses the condition of that other. <<The body, therefore, changes according to its disposition;>> for the body, insofar as it is a body, remains a body, but the specific quality of its disposition does not remain. [[The body, therefore, changes according to its disposition.]]

**5** Place, time, and natural motion, therefore, are for the sake of the body.

**6** Each of these attains its own particular property. The property of place is reception; of time, interval and number; of nature, motion; [of harmony, friendship;] and of the body, change. The property of the soul is motion according to its intellectual essence <note>original: "νοητὴν κίνησιν" (noēten kinēsin). # EXCERPT XVI. HERMES TO AMMON

. . . place and time . . . ;<gloss>That in which things are is place and time; <note>original: "for it is in place and time that"</note> physical movement goes on</gloss> and that for the sake of<gloss>Or 'because of'</gloss> which these things exist is body. Place exists for the sake of body; for it receives into itself the changes of the body, and so prevents the thing which is changing from being destroyed. The body, when it changes, is transformed into something different, and ceases to be in the state in which it was before, but it does not cease to be a body; and when it has changed into something different, it is in the state which belongs to that different thing. The body then changes merely in condition; for the body, *as* body <note>original: "qua"</note>, persists, but the particular condition in which it was before does not persist.

# EXCERPT XIX. HERMES

. . . For it is <note>The translator suggests: "The soul rules over the irrational thing which is joined to it, bringing into that thing a movement similar to the soul's own thought, and giving life to it when it comes into life; for it is..."</note> a peculiar property of soul, that it gives to **2** other things something similar to its own . . . <note>The translator suggests: "similar to its own substantive existence (or reality of being)."</note>

. . . not partaking of the physical body. For if . . . , it has **4** neither reason nor intelligence. <note>The translator suggests: "When the soul's movement is the kind of movement which corresponds to true being, the soul is moved by love of 'intelligible substance' (i.e. by desire for that which truly is—the incorporeal and divine), and has no part in (i.e. is not affected by) the physical body. If it takes part in the body (or 'is mastered by love of the body'), it is unable to think rationally or intelligently."</note> For all bodies are devoid of intelligence; but when a body has received a portion of true being, it becomes a living creature that has in it the breath of life.

The <term>vital spirit</term> <note>original: "pneuma"; the life-breath or animating force that connects soul to body.</note> is that part of the body to which belongs **5** sensation; the reason is that part of the intelligent substance which has understanding. With the reason coexists knowledge of . . . ; with the vital spirit coexists opinion. The reason contemplates the . . . , <note>The missing text likely referred to "the real" or "that which truly is."</note> but the vital spirit discerns appearances. The vital spirit is parcelled out among the organs of sense; there is a part of it that sees, a part that hears, a part that smells, a part that tastes, and a part that feels by touch. This vital spirit if, . . . , <note>The translator suggests: "if it is brought into connection with discursive thought (which is the function of the 'reason')."</note> discerns things rightly; but if not, it merely receives illusory impressions.

. . . For the vital spirit gets the force with which it works **7** from the <term>Kosmos</term> <note>The universe or the ordered world-system; the translator suggests the spirit may draw this force specifically from the surrounding atmosphere.</note> by which it is environed; but the soul gets from itself the force with which it works.

# THE HERMETICA OF STOBAEUS

->*EXCERPT XX*<-

Stobaeus I. 49. 3, volume i, page 320 Wachsmuth (*Eclogues* I. 798 Heeren).

### From Hermes.

**1** The soul, therefore, is an incorporeal <term>essence</term> <note>original: "ousia"; the fundamental nature or "being" of a thing</note>; (. . .). For if the body does not possess a soul, it will no longer be capable of preserving itself. For every body requires life—that life which is established in the order of the soul—in order to exist.

**2** For it is necessary that decay follow everything that possesses birth and change. For that which is brought into being is brought into being within a certain magnitude, and having been brought into being, it possesses growth; and for everything that grows, there follows a decrease, and after decrease, destruction.

**3** But that which has partaken of the soul lives, and it shares in existence by means of the soul. And the soul itself is the primary cause of existence for the other <note>i.e., the body</note>. By "existence" I mean now the state of participating in <term>intellectual life</term> <note>original: "zoē noera"; a life characterized by mind or spirit rather than just biological function</note>. [[The soul provides this intellectual life.]]

**4** Now, <term>man</term> <note>original: "anthropos"; used here in the universal sense of "humanity"</note> is called a "living being" because of life, "rational" because of the intellect, and "mortal" because of the body. The soul, then, is incorporeal, possessing the unchanging power of providing life <insert>to man</insert>; and the soul provides intellectual life. For how is it possible to call man an intellectual living being if there were no essence that actually provided life? Nor would it be possible to call him rational if there were no thinking essence providing the intellectual life.

**5** However, the intellectual quality does not reach its fulfillment in all people, because in some, the constitution of the body is not fitted according to the <term>mean</term> <note>The "mean" refers to the Greek ideal of balance; if the bodily elements are out of proportion, the mind cannot function perfectly</note>. For if heat predominates in the constitution, the man becomes flighty and passionate; but if cold predominates, he becomes heavy and sluggish. For nature fits the constitution of the body—

### *From the teachings of Hermes.*

<margin>1</margin> The soul then is an incorporeal substance <note>original: "ousia" - a fundamental reality or essence</note>; . . . $^1$ For if the body has not soul, it will no longer be real. For all bodies need life to make them real, and life resides in soul.

->*EXCERPT XXI*<-

### From the teachings of Hermes.

**1** The <term>Pre-existent</term><note>The Primal Being or God, existing before all creation</note> then is beyond all existent things, being prior even to the things which *really* exist. <note>In this Platonic context, "things which really exist" refers to eternal truths or "objects of thought" rather than physical matter</note> For <note>The author likely argues that the word "exist" is used in two different ways</note> the term ‘substantive existence’, employed as all-inclusive, is applicable both to the objects of thought and to the objects of sense. . . . the things which really exist, and which are regarded by thought as existing of themselves. But the objects of sense are contrary to the objects of thought, and exist in the other way; for they are not existent of themselves. . . . The world of nature <note>The material or corporeal world</note> is an existent object of sense, and contains within itself all objects of sense.

Intermediate between the objects of thought and the objects of sense are the <term>objects of opinion</term>;<note>Things that are perceived or believed but not necessarily known through pure reason</note> and of these, some partake of the objects of thought, but others do not. <note>Opinions may be true or false; only a true opinion connects to the higher reality of thought</note>

->*EXCERPT XXII*<-

Stobaeus I. 42. 7, volume i, page 295 Wachsmuth (*Eclogae* I. 754 Heeren).

### From Hermes, from the book "Of Aphrodite."

I shall set forth the reason why infants come to be like their parents <insert>or are assigned to their kin</insert>. When <insert>nature</insert> treasures up the seed as it is skimmed from the "tasty" blood <note>The text uses a term suggesting the foam or essence of the blood, which ancient physiology believed was the source of semen.</note>, it happens somehow that a certain essence from the whole body <insert>of the limbs</insert> exhales by a divine energy, as if the same human being were being recreated. It is likely that the same thing happens in the case of the woman. Whenever, <insert>therefore</insert>, the flow from the man prevails and remains undissolved, the infant will be shown to be like the father, just as, conversely, it would be like the mother in the same manner. But if the prevalence occurs <insert>only in</insert> some specific part, the infant is made like to that part. ...And sometimes, even across many generations, ...the infant is compared to the form of the one who begat it ...<insert>of that</insert> <term>Decan</term><note>The Decans are 36 Egyptian astral deities, each ruling ten degrees of the zodiac, believed here to influence the physical appearance of the child at the moment of conception.</note> which has the governance over the hour in which the woman was conceiving.

### EXCERPT XXII

->*From the discourse of Hermes which is entitled* APHRODITE.<-

How does it come about that children resemble their parents <note>The original text is fragmented here; it likely added "or other relatives"</note>? I will explain this. When <insert>nature</insert> stores up semen that is foamed forth from productive blood, it comes to pass that there is exhaled from the whole body a certain substance <note>This refers to the "vital spirit" or pneuma, believed to be the active life-force within the seed</note> by the working of a divine force, inasmuch as it is a human being that is being brought into existence <note>The author suggests that while animals reproduce naturally, human conception involves a specific divine intervention</note>. And it is to be presumed that the same thing takes place in the case of the woman also. When then the efflux from the man is prepotent <note><term>prepotent</term>: having greater power or influence in determining hereditary characters</note>, and its vigour is not impaired, the child that is produced will be like its father; and in the same way, if the conditions are reversed, the child will be like its mother. And if there is such a prepotency in respect of some part of the body, the child comes to resemble the father or the mother in that part . . . and sometimes even to remote generations . . . to compare the child with the form of its father . . . of that <term>Decanus</term> <note>A "Decan" is a deity presiding over ten degrees of the zodiac; here, the author links physical appearance to the astrological ruler of the hour of birth or conception</note> who had to do with the hour in which the woman was bearing the child.

<summary>This page discusses the Sun as a physical manifestation of the divine Creator and provides a Hermetic explanation for heredity, attributing physical resemblance to the strength of parental "efflux" and the influence of astrological Decans.</summary>

->*EXCERPTUM XXIII*<-

### From the Sacred Book of Hermes Trismegistus entitled "The Virgin of the World."

**32** "Pay attention, my son Horus; for you are listening to a secret theory, of which my forefather Kamephis <note>original: "Kamēphis." An Egyptian deity often identified with the "Kneph" or a primordial creator figure.</note> was the leader. Hermes received it from Kamephis, the eldest of all beings; I received it from Hermes, the recorder of all deeds, at the time when he honored me with the perfect black <note>original: "tō teleiō melani." This likely refers to the "black rite" or a specific mystical pigment/ink used in Egyptian initiation.</note>; and now you receive it from me."

**1** Having said these things, Isis first pours for Horus a sweet draught of ambrosia, which souls are accustomed to receive from the gods, and thus Isis begins the most holy discourse.

**2** "Since the many-crowned heaven, my son Horus, is situated above the whole nature of those things lying below, and since it is in no place deprived of anything which the whole universe now possesses, it is an absolute necessity that the whole nature lying below be ordered and filled by the things situated above. For surely the things below are not able to provide order to the arrangement above. It is necessary, therefore, that the lesser mysteries yield to the greater. The arrangement of the celestial things is greater than those things lying below; it is secure in every way, and it does not fall under the comprehension of mortals."

->*EXCERPT XXIII*<-

### *From the holy book of Hermes Trismegistus which is entitled THE VIRGIN OF THE WORLD.*¹ <note>original: "KORE KOSMU". While "Kore" can mean "pupil of the eye," in this context it refers to the "Virgin" or "Maiden" of the Cosmos.</note>

**32** *Isis.* Give heed, my son Horus; for you shall hear secret doctrine, of which our forefather Kamephis <note>A primordial Egyptian creator deity, often associated with the generative force of the sun or a serpent.</note> was the first teacher. It so befell that Hermes heard this teaching from Kamephis, the eldest of all our race; I heard it from Hermes the writer of records, at the time when he . . . ;² and you shall hear it now from me.—

**1** Having thus spoken, Isis first poured forth for Horus a sweet draught of ambrosia <note>The food or drink of the gods, granting immortality.</note>, such as the souls are wont to receive . . . ;³ and thereupon she thus began her most holy discourse:

**2** Inasmuch as heaven with its many circles, my son Horus, is placed above all the world of things below, . . . ,⁴ it must be that all the world which lies below has been set in order and filled with contents by the things which are placed above;⁵ for the things below have not power to set in order the world above. The weaker mysteries⁶ then must yield to the stronger; and the system of things on high is stronger than the things below, and is wholly steadfast, and cannot be apprehended by the thoughts of mortal men.⁷

---
->\*&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;\*&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;\*&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;\*&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;\*<-

¹ I. e. ‘the Eye-pupil of the Universe’. <note>The translator notes a double meaning: "Kore" is both "maiden" and the "pupil" of the eye, suggesting the world's most precious or central part.</note>
² Perhaps, ‘when he initiated me in the Black (?) Rites’ (or possibly, ‘in the great rites’).
³ Perhaps, ‘such as are the draughts which souls in bliss are wont to receive when they dwell among the gods’.
⁴ Perhaps, ‘and the whole universe is not in any of its regions deprived of (i. e. left unprovided with) any of the things it needs’.
⁵ I. e. we see that the terrestrial world is organized, and filled with living beings; and this must have been done by the celestial gods.
⁶ <term>Mysteries</term>: ‘Mysteries’ seems here to mean supernatural powers or forces. But it might perhaps be better to write ‘the weaker things’.
⁷ Perhaps, ‘is stronger than the things below, inasmuch as it is secure from disturbance and not subject to death’.

It outlines the Hermetic principle of "as above, so below," asserting that the celestial realm governs and organizes the terrestrial world.</summary>

# EXCERPT XXIII (THE VIRGIN OF THE WORLD). ISIS TO HORUS

<margin>3</margin> Thereupon <note>original: "ἐκ τούτου" - This passage describes the state of early humanity before the revelation of divine knowledge.</note> men moaned, being afraid, regarding the beautiful and everlasting duration of the things above. For it was a sight to behold the beauty of the sky when it was flooded with light by the Sun, and the well-nigh equal majesty of the night, torch-lit with light less than the Sun's, yet bright, when in their turn the other holy Powers <note>The moon and stars.</note> moved along their paths in heaven with ordered movements in fixed periods of time, and by certain secret effluences <term>effluences: invisible spiritual or physical flows believed to influence earthly life</term> wrought order and growth in the things below. And thus arose fears upon fears, and ceaseless questionings.

<margin>4</margin> And as long as the Craftsman <term>Craftsman: the Demiurge or Creator of the physical universe</term> who made the universe willed not to be known, all was wrapped in ignorance. But when he determined to reveal himself, he breathed into certain godlike men a passionate desire to know him, and bestowed on their minds a radiance ampler than that which they already had within their breasts, that so they might first will to seek the yet unknown God, and then have power to find him. But this, Horus my <margin>5</margin> wondrous son, it would not have been possible for men of mortal breed to do, if there had not arisen one whose soul was responsive to the influence of the holy Powers of heaven. And such a man was Hermes, he who won knowledge of all. Hermes saw all things, and understood what he saw, and had power to explain to others what he understood. <note>The text likely implies he did not reveal everything at once.</note> For what he had discovered he inscribed on tablets, and hid securely what he had inscribed, leaving the larger part untold, that all later ages of the world might seek it.

<margin>6</margin> And Hermes, having been bidden to attend on the gods to whom he was akin <note>Meaning he was summoned to die and ascend to the stars.</note>, was about to ascend to the stars; but to him succeeded Tat, who was his son, and therewith inheritor of the knowledge which Hermes had acquired; and not long after, Asclepius, also named Imuthes <note>The Egyptian name Imhotep, identified with the Greek god of healing.</note>, the son of Ptah, who is also named Hephaistos <note>The Greek god of fire and craftsmanship, equated here with the Egyptian creator-god Ptah.</note>, and all those other men who, by the will of that Providence which reigns over all, were destined to search out with the utmost accuracy...

Clenching his fists tightly, he said, “Take, O sacred Earth, take, O most honored one, you who are destined to be the mother of all things, and see that you lack for nothing from this moment on.” So spoke God, and stretching out his hands [as is fitting for a God to have], he released all things [into the composition of all that exists].

This was a translucent substance, which the Craftsman alone beheld. This [composition] God called "Animation" <note>original: "psychōsin" - the process of ensoulment or making into soul</note> [from its auspicious name and its activity according to likeness]. From this congealed mass he generated myriads of souls, fashioning the bloom of the mixture [from himself] into whatever he desired with perfect order.

<meta>This page continues the Hermetic dialogue regarding the descent of souls into material bodies. The previous context likely established the souls' original divine state before their "fall" or incarceration in human form.</meta>

# THE HERMETICA OF STOBAEUS

From the fluid expanse and the ⟨place⟩ near ⟨the⟩ pole and the blessed life [with the gods], we shall thus be imprisoned in dishonorable and lowly dwellings. <note>The "dwellings" refer to the human body, viewed here as a prison for the divine soul.</note> [[What so unseemly has been done by us wretches? What have we done to deserve these punishments?]] What ⟨necessities⟩ await us miserable ones [for our sins]; what things shall we suffer [because of our wicked hopes], so that we may provide the necessities for a body [watery and] quickly dissolved. Our eyes will contain [the souls no longer belonging to God] but a little, and [[altogether a small amount]] by the moisture in these ⟨circles⟩, seeing their own ancestor, heaven, through ⟨⟨an altogether small space⟩⟩, we shall groan forever. [And there are times when] even ⟨while looking⟩ we shall not see ⟨⟨clearly⟩⟩; [hence Orpheus says: "With brightness we look, but with our eyes we see nothing."] <note>original: "τῷ λαμπρῷ βλέπομεν, τοῖς δ’ ὄμμασιν οὐδὲν ὁρῶμεν." This refers to the Orphic belief that physical sight is a form of blindness compared to spiritual vision.</note> For ⟨darkness⟩ has been condemned upon us wretches. “...and you, who serve my ageless sovereignty, <note>original: *skēptouchian*, literally 'the bearing of the scepter'</note> you have surely recognized that you undergo this punishment [of incarnation] because of your previous actions. For you know that as long as you were without sin, you inhabited the regions neighboring the heavens. But since a certain blame has attached itself to you, you are condemned to mortal inward parts, <note>original: *splangchnois*, referring to the physical organs or 'guts' of a body</note> and you shall inhabit the place allotted to them. <margin>39</margin>

But I have not established the laws for your changes <note>The transitions between lives or states of being</note> blindly or at random. Rather, just as they lead toward the worse if you commit any unseemly act, so they lead toward the better if you purpose anything worthy of your own origin. For I myself [and no other] shall be the overseer and witness. If your failings are moderate, you shall leave behind the frail bond of the flesh and once more, without lamentation, embrace your own heaven. But if you should be the authors of greater sins, you shall no longer inhabit heaven nor even the bodies of men after your fashioned forms reach their end; instead, you shall pass into unreasoning animals <note>original: *zōia aloga*, 'beasts without speech/reason'</note> and continue wandering upon the earth.”

<margin>40</margin>

And as soon as he saw the souls entering into their bodily frames, he asked (though he well knew the answer to his question), ‘What are these creatures called, Hermes, you record-writer of the gods?’ ‘They are called *men*,’ said Hermes. Then Momus <note>In Greek mythology, Momus is the personification of mockery and criticism; here he acts as a cosmic skeptic questioning the creation of humanity.</note> said, ‘Hermes, you are doing a rash thing in making man; for he is like to be a creature that sees with inquisitive eyes, and hears things he has no right to hear, and indulges greedily his sense of taste, and makes voluptuous use of his sense of smell,$^1$ and misuses to all extremes his sense of touch. Tell me, you that are the author of his being, is it your settled purpose to leave him free from care, this being that is going to look with audacious gaze upon the beauteous mysteries of nature? Is it your will to let him be exempt from sorrow, this man that is going to send forth his designing thoughts to the very ends of the earth? And if so, will not men put forth audacious hands against the elements? They will dig up roots of plants, and investigate the properties of stones. They will dissect the lower animals,—yes, and one another also,—seeking to find out how they have come to be alive, and what manner of thing is hidden within . . . . $^2$ They will cut down the woods of their native land,$^3$ and sail across the sea to seek what lies beyond it. They will dig mines, and search into the uttermost darkness of the depths of the earth. And all this might be borne, but they will do yet more: they will press on to the world above, seeking to discover by observation the laws of movement of the heavens. Are they then to meet with no impediment? Shall they never be overpowered by the cruel stings of fear, and shall they luxuriate in a life exempt from cares? Teach them henceforth to . . . . $^4$ <Make them . . . ,> that they may fail to get the things they hoped for, and be subdued by the pangs of grief. Let their presumptuous eagerness be disappointed of its expectations. Let their souls be a prey...

**52**
And having filled his balanced hands with the surrounding substances of nature, and having gripped his handfuls firmly, he said, "Take, O sacred Earth, take, O most honored one, you who are destined to be the mother of all, and see that you lack for nothing from this moment on." **53**
And at the beginning, these things were entirely unknown. For the souls, having been recently imprisoned <note>The Greek *katheirchtheisai* implies being shut up in a dungeon; the Hermetic tradition views the physical body as a prison for the divine soul.</note> and unable to bear the dishonor, began to quarrel with the gods in heaven. Holding fast to their own noble birth and claiming their rights, since they too had obtained the same Creator, they fell into sedition. And the stronger souls, using the inferior human bodies as their instruments, caused them to attack and oppose one another, and to wage war against each other. And so it was that strength had such great power over weakness that the strong burned and slaughtered the weak; they enslaved the living and even cast out the dead without burial within the sacred sanctuaries.

**54**
When the evil had already become widespread, the elements <note>The four basic building blocks of the universe: Fire, Air, Water, and Earth.</note> grew indignant and resolved to petition God the Monarch concerning the savage conduct of men. Since the evil was now so great, the elements approached God, who had made them, and used such words as these in their complaint.

**55**
And indeed, Fire spoke first, for it held the authority of speech. "O Master," it said, "and Architect of this new world, whose name is revered among the gods and hidden among all men until now, how long, O Divinity, do you intend to leave the life of mortals without God? They do not allow me to remain in the state for which I was created, improperly defacing my incorruptible nature. For I am being defiled, O Master, by the godless audacity of the men who have been made.

**56**
I am forced to melt flesh." <note>A reference to the violence of war and perhaps the improper use of fire in sacrifices or cremations that offended the natural order.</note> "Reveal yourself now to the world which needs you, and dissolve the savagery of life. I am dishonoured; . . . <note>original: "..." The translator suggests the missing word might be 'trouble' or 'strife'.</note> has risen up against me from mankind. Having naught to fear, they commit all manner of crimes; slaughtered by every sort of cruel device, men fall dead on my plains, O Lord, and I am soaked through and through with the juices of rotting corpses. Thus spoke the Elements; and God filled the universe with **62** the sound of his holy voice, and said, ‘Go your ways, my holy children, that are worthy of your great Father; make no attempt to violate my laws, and leave not my universe bereft of your services. Another <note>Referring to the god Osiris.</note> shall now come down to dwell among you, an efflux of my being, who shall keep holy watch on men’s deeds. He shall be judge of the living,—a judge that none can deceive,—and a terrible king of the dead; and every man shall meet with such retribution as his deeds deserve.’ Thereon the Elements **63** ceased from their entreating, and kept silence; and at their Master’s bidding, each of them continued to wield the power committed to him.—

# EXCERPT XXIV. ISIS TO HORUS

Over all else likewise, rules the Maker of the universe; in the aether <note>The highest, purest layer of the atmosphere, thought to be made of fire or spirit</note> dwell stars, over whom rules that great luminary, the Sun; in the air dwell souls, over whom rules the Moon; and upon earth dwell men, over whom rules he who is king for the time being; for the gods, my son, cause to be born at the right time a man that is worthy to govern upon earth. <margin>**2**</margin> The other rulers <note>original: "οἱ λοιποὶ ἄρχοντες" referring to the Sun, the Moon, and the earthly king</note> are effluxes <note>Flowing out or emanations</note> of Him who is king in heaven; and among them, he who is nearer to Him is more kingly than the others. The Sun, inasmuch as he is nearer to God, is greater and mightier than the Moon; (and the Moon is mightier than the earthly king.) <margin>**3**</margin> He who is king on earth is the last of the four rulers, but the first of men. As long as he is on earth, he has no part in true deity; <note>original: "θεότης" - meaning he is not literally a god while in the flesh</note> but as compared with other men, he has in him something exceptional, which is like to God; for the soul which is sent down to dwell in him comes from a place which is situated above the places whence souls are sent down to dwell in other men. <note>The author suggests kingly souls originate from a higher stratum of the heavens than common souls.</note>

<margin>**4**</margin> Now souls are sent down thence to reign as kings, my son, for these two reasons. Souls that have well and blamelessly run their appointed race, and are about to be transmuted into gods, are sent down to earth in order that, by reigning here as kings, they may be trained to use the powers which are given to gods; and souls that are already godlike, and have in some little thing transgressed God's ordinances, are sent down to be kings on earth in order that they may undergo some punishment in being incarnated, and yet may not suffer in like measure with the rest, but in their bondage may still retain the same pre-eminence which they enjoyed while they were free.

<margin>**5**</margin> The differences in the characters of kings are not determined by the nature of their souls (for all kingly souls are godlike), but by that of the angels and <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses, not necessarily evil</note> that have escorted the—

² I. e. he is not a god.

# THE HERMETICA OF STOBAEUS

...of angels and spirits <note>original: "daimones" — in this context, intermediary spirits rather than evil demons</note>. For such souls, when descending for such purposes, do not descend without an escort and a bodyguard; for Justice on high knows how to assign to each their due, even if they are being thrust away from the **6** region of prosperity. Whenever, therefore, the angels and spirits who lead the soul down, my child Horus, are warlike, <then the soul itself also wages war;> [for the soul is overpowered by their disposition, forgetting its own proper works, and remembering only those things added to it by its <from the> sacred escort;] but when they are peaceful, then the soul also [follows its own course] and makes peace; and when they are judicial, then it also judges; when they are musical, then it also sings; and when they are lovers of truth, then it also practices philosophy. For by necessity these souls are mastered by the disposition of those who lead them down; for they fall into humanity forgetting their own nature [and insofar as they have stood far apart from it], but remembering the character of those who have shut them in.—

**7** "Well have you <unfolded> [all] <these things> for me, O Mother," said Horus; "but how souls become noble, you have not yet narrated to me."— [How noble souls are produced.] In the same manner as there are certain states on earth, my child Horus, that differ from one another, so it is also among souls. For these too have places from which they set out, and a soul that has set out from a more glorious place is nobler than one that is not so situated. For just as among men the free man is thought to be nobler than the slave—for that which is superior and kingly [[among souls]] by necessity makes a slave of that which is surpassed—so indeed, my child, it <is> also <<among souls>>.—

**8** <How, O Mother,> do souls become male and female?— [How male and female souls are produced.] Souls, my child Horus, are of the same nature in themselves, as if they existed from a single place where the Creator <note>original: "demiurge" — the divine craftsman of the universe</note> shaped them, and they are neither male nor female. For such a [disposition] <<distinction>> occurs in bodies, and not in—

# EXCERPT XXIV. ISIS TO HORUS

...soul on its way down to earth. For souls that are of this quality,¹ and come down to earth for this purpose,² do not come down without escort and attendance; for the Justice that rules on high knows how to assign to each his due, even though they be exiled from the Happy Land <note>The "Happy Land" refers to the celestial or divine realm from which souls originate before incarnation.</note>. And so, my son Horus, when **6** the angels and <term>daemons</term> <note>In this context, "daemons" are not evil spirits, but intermediary spiritual beings or "guardian spirits" who guide the soul.</note> who bring the kingly soul down from above are warlike, then that soul wages war; when they are peaceful, then it maintains peace; when they are disposed for judicial work, then it sits in judgement; when they are given to music, then it sings; when they are truth-lovers, then it pursues philosophy. For these souls, as of necessity, cling to the temper of the angels and daemons who bring them down to earth; for when they sink into the condition of man, they forget their own nature, and bethink them only of the disposition of those who have shut them up in the body.'—

'Mother,' said Horus, 'you have full well explained these **7** things to me; but you have not yet told me what is the origin of noble souls.'—*Isis.* 'Just as on earth, my son, there are certain grades of social standing which differ one from another, even so it is with the souls. For the souls also have certain places whence they come; and the soul which has come from a more glorious place is nobler than one that is not thus exalted. For just as among men the free man is held to be nobler than the slave, because that which is of superior and kingly nature necessarily enslaves that which is inferior, even so it is, my son, in the case of the souls.'—

*Horus.* 'Tell me, mother, what is the origin of *male and female* **8** *souls*.'—*Isis.* 'The souls, my son Horus, are all of one nature, inasmuch as they all come from one place, that place where the Maker fashioned them;³ and they are neither male nor female; for the difference of sex arises in bodies, and not in—

¹ I. e. that are godlike.
² I. e. to reign as kings there.
³ Namely, the atmosphere.

**9** ...of incorporeal beings. The cause <note>original: αἰτία</note> why the souls of males are more vigorous <note>original: ὀβριμωτέρας; implying strength or spiritedness</note> while those of females are more delicate, is <insert>not</insert> the air, my child Horus, in which all things are generated—for the air is the soul’s <insert>environment before it is embodied</insert>—but rather the very body with which the soul is clothed, which is a mixture <term>phurama|a kneaded mass or dough</term> of the elements: earth, water, air, and fire. Since the composition of females has an abundance of the moist and the cold, but is lacking in the dry and the hot, the soul shut up in such a mold becomes damp and tender. Conversely, in males, one finds the opposite: for in them the dry and the hot abound, while the cold and the moist are lacking. Because of this, souls in such bodies are hardy and more active.

**10** *“How do souls become intelligent, O Mother?”*—And Isis answered: The faculty of sight, my child, is wrapped in tunics <note>The "tunics" or "coats" of the eye refer to the anatomical layers or membranes</note>. When these tunics are dense and thick, the eye is dim-sighted; but if they are porous and thin, then it sees most sharply. It is the same with the soul. For the soul also has its own coverings, which are incorporeal, just as the soul itself is incorporeal. These coverings are the "tunics" of the air that is within us. When these are thin, porous, and transparent, then the soul is intelligent; but when, on the contrary, they are dense, thick, and clouded—as if in a storm—then the soul does not see far, but only those things lying at its feet.

**11** And Horus said: *“For what reason then, O Mother, are the people outside of our most holy land not as intelligent in their minds as our own people?”*—And Isis said: The earth lies flat in the middle of the universe, like a human being <margin>facing</margin>...

When these coats are thin and rare and transparent, then the soul is intelligent; but when on the other hand they are dense and thick and muddied, as the outer air is in stormy weather, then the soul cannot see far, but sees only what is close at hand.’—

Because of the way these things are carried back up to that place, they say that our own river <note>The Nile</note> flows from there, when the frost melts in that region. ### Critical Notes on the Greek Text
<note>These notes reflect scholarly corrections made to the original Greek manuscript to ensure the English translation is accurate.</note>

**14-15** *serenity*: I have written this in place of "carelessness" found in the manuscripts.
**15** *intelligent*: I have added this word (perhaps "more intelligent"?).

# STOBAEUS: HERMETICA

Having journeyed through the plain of truth, I shall explain to you each of the things that exist, telling you this first: that which is composed and does not vanish possesses a place <note>The Greek text here is fragmentary; scholars suggest it refers to the "place" or "receptacle" where souls reside.</note> (...).

**3** But someone might say—as if it were my own argument—"Where do the souls dwell once they are released from their bodies?" This would be like water taken from vessels below, which cannot be held again in the same places from which it was taken; nor, even if it were taken and poured out immediately, does it regain its own specific place, but instead mixes with the whole mass of water.

Therefore, that which is from a single source and not from many cannot be mixed with something else; hence, its union with the body must be a harmony of God brought about by necessity.

**5** That souls are not sent back to one and the same place in a common heap, nor randomly and just as it happens, but each to its own proper region, is clear from what the soul experiences while still in the body and the physical form, even when it has been thickened <note>The text suggests the soul becomes "dense" or "heavy" through its contact with the material world.</note> contrary to its own nature. Pay close attention, O most beloved Horus, to the following comparison. Suppose that men, eagles, doves, swans, hawks, and swallows were all shut up together in one and the same enclosure...

### Concerning Incarnation and Transmigration.
<note>Original: "Peri empsychōseōs kai metempsychōseōs." These terms refer to the process of a soul entering a body and moving between bodies across lifetimes.</note>

<margin>1</margin> The space between earth and heaven is divided, my son Horus, according to measure and harmony. These regions are called by our ancestors "zones" by some, "firmaments" by others, and "folds" by still others. In these regions dwell both the souls released from bodies and those not yet embodied. Each of these, my son, holds a place according to its merit, so that the divine and royal souls inhabit the highest region of all, while those lowest in honor—and all those that are earth-bound—dwell in the lowest of all, and the middle souls in the middle region.

For such souls, the Providence from above <note>Original: "pronoia," the divine foresight or plan that governs the universe.</note> [casts down] into the lower regions according to the measure of their sins...

For if, according to the bodily solidification, fire should predominate, then the soul—being hot by nature and receiving an additional heat [becoming more fiery]—makes the living being more active and spirited [and the body sharp and quick-moving]. But if air should predominate, then it becomes light and bouncy and unstable.

# STOBAEUS: HERMETICA

**16** ...the living being in both soul and body. If water should predominate, then the living being becomes, in its soul, fluid <note>original: "euchroun" - literally "well-colored," but emended here to mean "well-flowing"</note> and adaptable, able to fall upon and cling to others sufficiently because of the unifying and social nature of water. For water settles upon all things; when it is plentiful and encompasses them, it dissolves them into itself, but when it is present in small amounts and sinks down, it becomes that with which it was mixed. However, the bodies, due to their moisture and looseness, are not drawn together into a firm grip, but are dissolved by any small occasion of disease <note>The text suggests the physical structure lacks the "binding" necessary for resilience.</note>.

The body, while solid, is sluggish and heavy, and is moved by the will only with great effort. 

If, however, the composition of all elements should be symmetrical, then the living being is prepared as one who is hot for action, light for movement, well-tempered in touch, and noble in its firm constitution. For the earthy part is the solidification of the body, the liquid is the diffusion within it that leads to a compact state, the airy part is the principle of movement within us, and fire is the awakener of all these.

In man, the excess of the hot element has been turned into intelligence. For the mind in us is a hot thing; it has no power to burn, but it penetrates all things. or diminution caused by the operation of the environment, <note>For example, an increase in body heat caused by sitting near a fire.</note> nor by that change in bodies which takes place in the course of growth, <note>In healthy growth, the total amount of elements increases, but their proportions to one another remain the same.</note> but an increase or diminution that results from an alteration in the mixing of the elements of which the body is composed—when, I say, the hot element, or one of the other elements, is increased or diminished, then the creature is diseased.

<margin>28</margin>
Now just as the vapour that is produced by the first coming together and mixing of the elements in the body, whatever the quality of that vapour may be, mingles with the soul and assimilates it to itself, even so . . . <note>The text is broken here; the translator suggests: <insert>even so every alteration in the quality of the vapour causes a corresponding alteration in the quality of the soul</insert>.</note>

<margin>29</margin>
As long as the soul continues to be in its original condition, it maintains its good order unimpaired; but when either the mixed mass as a whole, or some one part of it, <note>For instance, an increase of fire in a specific limb resulting in inflammation.</note> receives, by subsequent addition from without, a portion of one of the elements larger than that which was originally assigned to it, then there is an alteration in the vapour thence produced, and the altered vapour alters the condition of the soul. <note>The following section in the original manuscripts appears to be from a different document. Reconstructed, it suggests that when heat and air—elements that move upward—interact with the soul's "habitation," the living being becomes distracted or "beside itself." Meanwhile, water and earth—downward-tending elements—settle upon the physical body.</note>

There are seven wandering stars <term>wandering stars: the planets, from the Greek 'planētai'</term> which circle at the threshold of Olympus, and among them ever revolves unending Time. # STOBAEUS’S HERMETIC EXCERPTS

And Zeus is the primal source of all birth, from whom nature first sprouted.
The same gods have obtained by lot the race of mortal men; for within us dwell
the Moon, Zeus, Mars, Venus <note>original: "Paphia," an epithet for Aphrodite/Venus derived from her sanctuary at Paphos</note>, Saturn, the Sun, and Mercury.
Therefore, from the ethereal spirit we are allotted to draw forth
tears, laughter, anger, birth, speech, sleep, and desire.
Saturn is tears, Zeus is birth, Mercury is speech,
Mars is wrath, the Moon is sleep, Cytherea <note>Another name for Venus, referring to the island of Cythera</note> is desire,
and the Sun is laughter; for by him, and rightly so,
both the mortal mind and the infinite cosmos rejoice.

---

**1** primal source of birth: reading from manuscript P²; others read "first-born." **2** obtained by lot: reading from manuscripts F and P; the *Anthology* reads "they drive."
**3** Perhaps the order should be: Zeus, Mars, Venus, Moon. **4** allotted: emendation by Meineke.
**5** tears: manuscript P spelling error | anger: manuscript F; others read "gall" or "bile." **6** tears: manuscript P spelling error | Zeus is birth: the *Anthology* reading; manuscripts F and P are slightly corrupted. **7** Cytherea: spelling variations in F and P. **8** and: the *Anthology* reading; Stobaeus's manuscripts read "both" | Perhaps: "for through his rays all things..."
