# EXCERPT XXIX

From whom Nature has sprung. To those same stars is assigned the race of men; and we have in us the Moon, Zeus <note>Jupiter</note>, Ares <note>Mars</note>, the Lady of Paphos <note>Aphrodite or Venus</note>, Kronos <note>Saturn</note>, the Sun, and Hermes <note>Mercury</note>. Wherefore it is our lot to draw in from the aetherial life-breath <note>original: "pneuma"; the subtle substance of the upper atmosphere</note> tears, laughter, wrath, birth, speech, sleep, and desire. Tears are Kronos; birth is Zeus; speech is Hermes; anger is Ares; the Moon is sleep; Aphrodite is desire; and the Sun is laughter, for by him <note>Perhaps: "for by reason of his radiance"</note> laugh all mortal minds, and the boundless universe.

---

¹ That is, from the aether, which is the life-breath of the universe.
² Perhaps, ‘for by reason of his radiance’.

# FRAGMENTS

1. *Tertullian, On the Soul, 33.*
(Egyptian Mercury <note>original: "Mercurius Aegyptius," the Roman name for Hermes</note> says) that the soul, having departed from the body, is not poured back into the soul of the universe, but remains distinct, so that it may give an account to the Father of those things which it performed while in the body.

2. *Cyprian (?), That Idols are Not Gods, 6.*
Hermes Trismegistus <note>The "Thrice-Greatest" Hermes</note> also speaks of one God, and confesses Him to be incomprehensible and beyond estimation.

3. *Lactantius, Divine Institutes, 1. 6. 4.*
(Mercury Trismegistus calls God) Lord and Father. . . . These are his very words: "But God is one. And the one does not require a name; for He who is, is nameless." <note>original Greek: ὁ δὲ θεὸς εἷς. ὁ δὲ εἷς ὀνόματος οὐ προσδέεται· ἔστι γὰρ ὁ ὢν ἀνώνυμος</note>¹

4. *Lactantius, Divine Institutes, 1. 7. 2.*
(Mercury the Thrice-Greatest) calls God not only "motherless" <note>original Greek: ἀμήτορα</note>, . . . but also "fatherless" <note>original Greek: ἀπάτορα</note>, because He has no origin from elsewhere. For He who Himself generated all things cannot have been generated by anyone.

5. *Lactantius, Divine Institutes, 1. 11. 61.*
(Trismegistus), when he said that there have been very few in whom perfect learning existed, named among these Uranus, Saturn, and Mercury, his own kinsmen.

<column-break/>

*Lactantius, Epitome, 4. 4.*
(Hermes) names God "Lord and Father," and says that He is without a name, because He does not stand in need of a proper title, since He is alone.¹

*Divine Institutes, 4. 13. 2.*
For God the Father Himself, since He lacks parents, is most truly named "fatherless" and "motherless" by Trismegistus, because He was procreated from no one.

*Epitome, 4. 4.*
Nor does (God) have any parents, because He exists from Himself and through Himself.

*Epitome, 14. 3.*
Trismegistus, when saying that there were very few men of perfect learning, enumerated among them his own kinsmen: Uranus, Saturn, and Mercury.

---

¹ <note>Translator's note on the Greek text</note> Perhaps: "But God is one. And He, being the one, is nameless; for He does not require a name, since He is alone."

# FRAGMENTS <note>original: "FRAGMENTS¹" - These are short excerpts from lost Hermetic works preserved by other ancient authors.</note>

1. The soul, when it has quitted the body, does not flow back into <note>original: "into²" - i.e. is not reabsorbed into</note> the soul of the universe, but remains separate <note>original: "ἀφωρισμένη" - set apart or distinct</note>, that it may be called to account by the Father for the deeds which it has done in the body.

2. There is one God; he is beyond comprehension <note>original: "ἀκατάληπτος?" - incomprehensible or unknowable by the human mind</note> and beyond appraisement.

3. God is called Master and Father.—God is one. And he that is one is nameless; for he does not need a name, since he is alone.

4. God is without father and without mother; for he has been generated by none but himself.

5. There have been very few men that have had perfect knowledge <note>original: "γνῶσις?" - Gnosis; specifically, a deep spiritual knowledge of God is intended here.</note>. Among those few are my kinsmen Uranos, Kronos, and Hermes <note>The Hermetic writer here makes Hermes Trismegistus the teacher speak of another Hermes, whom he perhaps assumes to have been the teacher's grandfather, as in the Latin Asclepius, Book III, section 37.</note>.

15. Lactantius, *Divine Institutes* 7. 13. 3.
<note>Lactantius was a 4th-century Christian advisor to Constantine who often cited Hermes to show that ancient pagans anticipated Christian truths.</note>
Hermes, describing the nature of man in order to teach how he was made by God, introduced these words: "And the same" <note>original: καὶ τὸ αὐτὸ</note> from both natures, the immortal and the mortal, he made one nature, that of man, making the same being partly immortal and partly mortal. And bringing this being, he established him in the midst of the divine and immortal nature and the mortal and changeable nature, so that seeing "all things," he might wonder at "all things."¹

16. *Abammon’s Response to Porphyry*² 8. 6 a.
<note>This text is better known as "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians" by Iamblichus. Abammon is a pseudonym for an Egyptian priest.</note>

For man has two souls, as these same writings say: one is from the First Intelligible <note>The "Intelligible" refers to the realm of pure thought or divine reality, beyond the physical senses.</note>, participating also in the power of the Creator; the other is instilled from the revolution of the heavenly bodies, into which the soul that sees God <note>original: θεοπτικὴ ψυχή</note> creeps.³

<note>Zosimus was a 3rd-century alchemist; Panopolis was a center of Egyptian wisdom.</note>

² <note>Alternative reading</note> Perhaps, ‘skilful’.
³ <note>Reconstruction</note> Perhaps, ⟨‘appointing his Word to govern the material world’⟩, or something to that effect.
⁴ The meaning of this phrase is doubtful; but the God denoted by it is the first or supreme God. *Compare Fragments 12, 17, and 30.*
⁵ That is, the <term>Kosmos: The universe conceived as an ordered and beautiful whole</term>.
⁶ Perhaps rather, ‘and Time’.
⁷ Probably taken from a Greek *Hermeticum* <note>A text belonging to the Hermetic tradition</note> in which the teacher was Agathos Daimon.

<summary>This page details the Hermetic view of creation, where God establishes a hierarchy of the spiritual over the material and defines the "second God" as the visible universe. It also cites the Persian scholar Shahrastani regarding the five first principles of the philosopher Agathodaimon.</summary>
